(p-326) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Ma'idah

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle, except what is recited to you﴾. Here He did not specify what this exception is, which is recited to them and excluded from the permissibility of the beasts of cattle. But He clarified it in His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], up to His saying: ﴿and what is sacrificed on the stone altars﴾. So the things mentioned in this noble verse, such as the animal killed by a blow (al-mawqudhah) and the animal that falls to its death (al-mutaraddiyah), even if they are of the cattle, are forbidden because of these accidents.

The verified view is that the cattle (al-an'am) are the eight pairs, as we mentioned earlier in Surah Al 'Imran. Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, and more than one of the scholars have used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of eating the fetus (al-janin) when its mother is slaughtered and it is found dead in her belly.

And there came from the Prophet ﷺ: "The slaughter of its mother is a slaughter for it," as recorded by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Majah from the hadith of Abu Sa'id.

al-Tirmidhi said: it is hasan. And Abu Dawud narrated it from Jabir, from the Prophet ﷺ.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 2:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you are released from the state of ihram, then hunt﴾, meaning: if you wish. This command does not indicate that hunting is obligatory upon release from ihram. Inductive survey (istiqra') of the Qur'an supports this, for everything that was permissible, then prohibited due to a cause, and then commanded after that cause ceased, the command in the Qur'an in all such cases indicates permissibility. Examples include his saying here: ﴿And when you are released from the state of ihram, then hunt﴾,

- and his saying: ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse through the land﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10],
- and his saying: ﴿So now, have relations with them﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Baqarah: 187],
- and his saying: ﴿And when they have purified themselves, then come to them﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Baqarah: 222].

This is not refuted by his saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Tawbah: 5]. This is because their killing was obligatory before its temporary prohibition due to the four months, whether we say that these are the months of respite mentioned in his saying: ﴿So travel freely through the land for four months﴾ [al-Tawbah: 2], or we say that they are the sacred months mentioned in his saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Four of them are sacred﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36].

From this you know that the verified conclusion indicated by complete induction of the Qur'an is that a command to do something after its prohibition indicates a return to the ruling that applied before the prohibition, whether permissibility or obligation. Thus hunting was permissible before ihram, then it was forbidden because of ihram, then it was commanded after release from ihram by his saying: ﴿And when you are released from the state of ihram, then hunt﴾, so it returns to what it was before the prohibition, namely permissibility. And the killing of the polytheists was obligatory before the sacred months began, so it was forbidden because of them, then it was commanded after they had passed, in his saying: ﴿And when the sacred months have passed﴾, to the end of the verse, so it returns to what it was before the prohibition, namely obligation.

This is the truth in this legal-theoretical (usuli) question.

Ibn Kathir said in his commentary on this verse: "This is a command after a prohibition. The correct position, which is established upon examination (sabr), is that the ruling is returned to what it was before the prohibition. If it was obligatory, it returns as obligatory; if it was recommended, it is recommended; or if permissible, it is permissible."

Whoever says it indicates obligation is refuted by many verses, and whoever says it indicates permissibility is refuted by other verses. What unifies all the evidences is what we have mentioned, as chosen by some of the scholars of legal theory (usul al-fiqh). And God knows best. [End of quotation from Ibn Kathir in his own wording.]

On this question there are other opinions, which he set forth in Maraqi al-Su'ud (The Ascents of Felicity) in his saying:

[Rajaz meter]
"The command indicates obligation after prohibition, and after a question it has come to indicate the original (ruling),
or it requires permissibility for the most part, when it is connected to a similar cause,
except that this is the position, and the majority hold to its requiring obligation."

It is established in the principles of jurisprudence that complete induction is an authoritative proof without disagreement, and incomplete induction, known as "attaching the individual to the majority" (ilhaq al-fard bi-al-aghlab), is a probable proof. As he set this out in Maraqi al-Su'ud in the book on "Inference" (al-Istidlal), in his saying:

[Rajaz meter]
"And among it is induction by the particular upon establishing the ruling for the universal,
if it is general and not one of disagreement, it is an authoritative proof by consensus,
but if it is only in part, it is attributed to probability, and is called attaching the individual to what predominates."

Once you know this, and you know that complete induction in the Qur'an indicates what we have chosen, (p-328) and what Ibn Kathir chose, and it is the saying of al-Zarkashi that a command after a prohibition indicates the return of the ruling to what it was before the prohibition, then you know that this is the truth, and knowledge is with God, may He be exalted.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And let not the hatred of a people prevent you from transgressing﴾, to the end of the verse. In this noble verse God forbids the Muslims from allowing the hatred of the disbelievers, because they had prevented them from the Sacred Mosque during the 'Umrah of al-Hudaybiyah, to lead them to transgress against the polytheists in ways that are not lawful for them according to the Shari'ah.

As Ibn Abi Hatim related regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse, from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his Companions were at al-Hudaybiyah when the polytheists had prevented them from the House, and this had weighed heavily upon them. Then some polytheists from the people of the East passed by them intending 'Umrah. The Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'We shall prevent these as they prevented us.' So God revealed this verse." End of quotation from Ibn Kathir in his wording.

This is supported by his saying before it: ﴿Nor those who make for the Sacred House﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2], and he stated the like of this verse in his saying: ﴿And let not the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Ma'idah: 8]. God has mentioned in this verse that they actually prevented them from the Sacred Mosque, according to the reading of the majority: ﴿that they prevented you﴾, with the hamza pronounced with a fatha, because its meaning is: "because they prevented you." He did not clarify here the wisdom of this prevention, nor did He mention that they prevented with them the offering (hady) held back from reaching its place. He mentioned in Surah al-Fath that they prevented the offering with them, and that the wisdom in that was the protection of the believing men and women who were not yet distinguished from the disbelievers at that time, in his saying: ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and prevented you from the Sacred Mosque, and the offering held back from reaching its place. And if not for believing men and believing women whom you did not know, that you might trample them and thereby incur from them guilt without knowledge, [He would have permitted you to fight. But He admitted to His mercy whom He willed. If they had been separated, We would have punished those who disbelieved among them with a painful punishment]﴾ [al-Fath: 25]. In this verse there is clear evidence that a person must treat whoever disobeys God in regard to Him by obeying God in regard to that same matter.

And in the hadith: "Render the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you."

This is clear evidence of the perfection of the religion of Islam, and of the excellence of what it calls to of noble character, showing that it is a heavenly religion beyond doubt.

(p-329) As for his saying in this noble verse: "Let not ... prevent you," its meaning is: let not the hatred of a people lead you to transgress. A parallel from the speech of the Arabs is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed I stabbed Abu 'Uyayna with a stab, which made Fazara, after it, be angry."

That is, it impelled them to become angry.

Some scholars said: "Let not ... earn for you", that is: let not their hatred earn for you transgression against them. According to this, there is no implied preposition before "that you transgress," meaning: let not their hatred of you cause you to transgress against them.

Some of the seven readers read "shana'an" with a sukun on the nun. The meaning of "shana'an", whether with a fatha or sukun on the nun, is hatred, the verbal noun of "shana'ahu," meaning he hated him.

It was said that with the reading of the sukun on the nun it is an adjective like "ghadbaan" (angry). And on the reading "that they prevented you" with a kasra on the hamza, the meaning is: if their prevention of you from the Sacred Mosque occurs, then let that not lead you to transgress against them in ways that are not lawful for you.

The refutation of this reading, on the basis that the verse was revealed after the polytheists prevented the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions at al-Hudaybiyah, and that there is no basis for conditioning prevention after it has occurred, is rejected on two grounds:

The first: the reading "in case they prevent you" in the conditional form is a Sab'i (seven-canonical), mutawatir reading that cannot be rejected, and Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr among the seven read it so.

The second: there is no obstacle to the meaning of this reading being: "if they prevent you once more, as a supposition and an assumption," as the particle "in" indicates, for it indicates doubt about the occurrence of the condition. Thus the repetition of the evil act should not lead you to transgress against them in ways that are not lawful for you. And God knows best.

[p. 330] The words of the Exalted: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in faith, his deeds have become worthless, and he is in the Hereafter among the losers﴾. The apparent meaning of this noble verse is that the apostate nullifies all his deeds by his apostasy, without any additional condition. However, He indicated in another place that this applies when he dies upon disbelief, and that is His words: ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217].

The established principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl) require that this unrestricted (muṭlaq) statement be read in light of this restricted (muqayyad) one. So the nullification of deeds is restricted to dying upon disbelief. This is the view of al-Shafi'i and those who agree with him, in contrast to Malik, who held that apostasy nullifies deeds absolutely. [p. 330 continued] And Allah knows best.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in *Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab* (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book):

[p. 259] In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Sūrat al-Mā'idah

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you, and the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾, and so on.

This noble verse, by its generality, indicates the permissibility of the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book absolutely, even if they invoke other than Allah over them, or if they remain silent and do not mention Allah or anyone else, because all of this falls under "their food."

Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Umamah, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata', al-Hasan, Makhul, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, al-Suddi, and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: the intended meaning of "their food" is their slaughtered animals. This is as Ibn Kathir transmitted from them, and al-Bukhari transmitted it from Ibn 'Abbas. The inclusion of their slaughtered animals within "their food" is agreed upon by the Muslims. However, there are other verses indicating that what has been dedicated to other than Allah is not lawful to eat, and that what the name of Allah has not been mentioned over is also not lawful to eat.

As for those verses which indicate the prohibition of eating what has had the name of other than Allah mentioned over it, such as His words: ﴿And that which has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173] in Sūrat al-Baqarah.

And His words: ﴿And that which has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 3] in al-Mā'idah, and in al-Naḥl [al-Naḥl: 115].

And His words in al-An'am: ﴿Or a grave sin dedicated to other than Allah﴾ [al-An'ām: 145].

The meaning of *ihlāl* (dedication) is raising the voice with the name of other than Allah at the time of slaughter.

As for those verses which indicate the prohibition of eating what the name of Allah has not been mentioned over, such as His words: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾, and so on [al-An'ām: 121].

And His words, the Exalted: ﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, if you are believers in His verses﴾ and ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned﴾ [al-An'ām: 118–119]. From this it is understood that one should not eat what the name of Allah has not been mentioned over.

[p. 260] The answer to such matters includes two investigations:

The first investigation: on the manner of reconciling the generality of the verse ﴿and the food of those who were given the Scripture﴾ with the generality of the verses prohibiting what has been dedicated to other than Allah, in the case where the People of the Book mention other than Allah over their slaughtered animal, by dedicating it to the cross, or to Jesus, or the like.

The second investigation: on the manner of reconciling the verse ﴿and the food of those who were given the Scripture﴾ also with His words ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾, in the case where the People of the Book do not mention Allah or anyone else over their slaughtered animal.

As for the first investigation, its outcome is that between His words ﴿and the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾ and His words ﴿and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾ there is general and specific relationship from one aspect (ʿumūm wa-khuṣūs min wajh). The verse ﴿and the food of those who were given the Scripture﴾ stands alone regarding, for example, bread and cheese from their food; and the verse ﴿and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾ stands alone regarding the slaughter of an idolater for his idol. They overlap in the slaughtered animal of a People of the Book which was dedicated to other than Allah, such as to the cross or to Jesus. So the generality of His words ﴿and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾ requires its prohibition, while the generality of His words ﴿and the food of those who were given the Scripture﴾ requires its permissibility.

It has been established in the science of the principles of jurisprudence that two generals related from one aspect conflict in the case in which they overlap, so preference (tarjīḥ) must be made between them. The preferred one is given precedence, and the generality of the other is specified by it.

As we have already mentioned in Sūrat al-Nisā' in reconciling His words, the Exalted: ﴿And that you combine two sisters﴾ [al-Nisā': 23] with His words, the Exalted: ﴿or those their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minūn: 6], and as the author of *Marāqī al-Su'ūd* indicated with his words:

*"If a general related from one aspect appears, then the ruling by preference is an absolute binding requirement."*

Having understood this, know that the scholars differed regarding these two generals as to which of them is preferred. The majority holds the preference of the verses that prohibit. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, a narration from Malik, and a narration transmitted by Isma'il ibn Sa'id from Imam Ahmad.

It is also what the author of *al-Mughni* mentioned, and it is the view of Ibn 'Umar and Rabi'ah, as al-Baghawi transmitted it from them in his *Tafsir*. Al-Nawawi mentioned it in his *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab* from 'Ali and 'A'ishah. Some scholars preferred the generality of the verse of permission [p. 261], because Allah made their slaughtered animals lawful, and He knows best what they say. al-Sha'bi and 'Ata' also used it as evidence for the permissibility of what they dedicated to other than Allah.

The author of this commentary (may Allah pardon him) said: What appears to be correct, and Allah knows best, is that the generality of the verses of prohibition is preferred and more deserving of consideration, from several routes. Among them is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt." And his saying (ﷺ): "Sin is that which stirs unease in the soul," the hadith. And his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever avoids doubtful matters has cleared his religion and his honor."

Among them also is that averting harms takes precedence over securing benefits, as has been established in the principles. From this it follows that when a prohibition conflicts with a permission, as here, the prohibition is more deserving of precedence and consideration, because abandoning something permissible is easier than committing something forbidden.

Indeed, most of the usulis have stated explicitly that a text indicating permission ranks third among texts, after a text indicating a prohibition of forbiddance, because the prohibition of forbiddance takes precedence over a command indicating obligation, for the reason we mentioned: averting harms takes precedence over securing benefits. And a command indicating obligation takes precedence over that indicating permission, for the sake of caution in being free of the obligation of the demand.

The author of *Marāqī al-Su'ūd* indicated this in the section on preference by consideration of the indicated meaning, with his words:

*"The transmitter and the affirmer, and the commander after the prohibitions, then this last one, is for permissibility, etc."*

The meaning of his words, "the commander after the prohibitions," is that what indicates a command after what indicates a prohibition: the one indicating the prohibition is the one given precedence. And his words, "then this last one is for permissibility," mean that the text indicating a command takes precedence over the permission, as we have mentioned. So the outcome is that the first is the prohibition, then the command, then the permission. Thus the precedence of the prohibition regarding what has been dedicated to other than Allah over the permission of the food of the People of the Book becomes clear.

Know that the scholars differed concerning what was forbidden to the People of the Book, such as the inner fat of cattle and sheep, which was forbidden to the Jews. Is it permissible for a Muslim to eat from what a Jew slaughtered? The majority holds that it is permissible for a Muslim, because the slaughter (dhakāh) is not divisible. Malik disliked it, and some of his companions, such as Ibn al-Qasim and Ashhab, prohibited it. The majority argued against them with proofs that, as far as appears, do not stand as proof against them. The explanation is that Malik's companions argued with His words, the Exalted: ﴿and the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾, saying: [p. 262] what is forbidden to them is not part of their food, so it does not fall under what the verse permitted.

The majority argued against them with what is established in *Sahih al-Bukhari* concerning the Prophet's (ﷺ) approval of 'Abdullah ibn Mughaffal (may Allah be pleased with him) taking a waterskin of Jewish fat on the day of Khaybar.

And with what Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal transmitted from Anas: "that a Jew invited the Prophet (ﷺ) to barley bread and rancid fat," i.e., fat with a changed smell. And with the story of the poisoned sheep which the Jewish woman poisoned for him (ﷺ), and from whose foreleg he ate, and from which Bishr ibn al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur died. It is well known and authentic. They said: he (ﷺ) resolved to eat it, he and those with him, and did not ask them whether they had removed from it what they believed to be forbidden of its fat or not.

It has been established in the principles that leaving out inquiry (tark al-istifsal) has the status of generality in statements, as the author of *Marāqī al-Su'ūd* indicated with his words:

*"And let the omission of inquiry hold the position of generality in speech."*

What appears to me, may Allah pardon its writer: these proofs contain no argument against Malik's companions. As for the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mughaffal and the hadith of Anas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), neither of them contains an explicit text on the specific forbidden fat for them, and fat in general is not forbidden for them, by the proof of His words, the Exalted: ﴿except what their backs carry, or the entrails, or what is mixed with bone﴾ [al-An'ām: 146]. So what is in the two hadiths is more general than the point of dispute, and evidence for the more general is not evidence for the more specific, because the existence of the general does not necessitate the existence of the specific, by the consensus of rational people.

Like the refutation of this argument with what we have mentioned is what undermines the proof known among the usulis as *al-qawl bil-mūjib* (argument by the implication of the proof). The author of *Marāqī al-Su'ūd* indicated it with his words:

*"Argument by the implication is clearly undermined, and it is the granting of the proof as recorded."*

*"Among those preventing that the proof entails what the forms of contention concern."*

As for *al-qawl bil-mūjib* according to the rhetoricians (bayānīyūn), it is one of the categories of the figurative badi' (rhetorical ornamentation), and it has two well-known types in the science of rhetoric. Here we intend *al-qawl bil-mūjib* in the usuli technical sense, not the rhetorical one. As for [p. 263] his (ﷺ) leaving out inquiry regarding the Jewish woman's sheep, there is no doubt that it contains no proof, because he (ﷺ) looked with his own eye, and the inner fat, the fat of the entrails, and the fat mixed with bone were not hidden from him, as is self-evident. So there is no need to ask about a sensible thing that is present.

Among the opinions applied to principles in the case of the fat mentioned is that disliking it is a recommended disapproval (karāhah tanzīhīyyah), because there is no decisive proof for either permissibility or prohibition. For what a person believes to be forbidden to him is not part of his food, and the slaughter's divisibility does not clearly appear, so the ruling of the matter is uncertain. "And whoever abandons doubtful matters has cleared his religion and his honor."

As for the second investigation, which is reconciling His words, ﴿and the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾ with His words, ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾, in the case where the People of the Book do not mention Allah's name over their slaughtered animal, nor the name of anyone else.

Its outcome is that in His words ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾ there are two interpretations:

The first: and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, and Ibn Kathir in his *Tafsir* described it as strong, that the intended meaning of "that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned" is that which has been dedicated to other than Allah. According to this interpretation, the investigation of this verse is exactly the first investigation and nothing else.

The second interpretation: that it is on its apparent meaning. According to this, there is also a general and specific relationship from one aspect between the two verses. The verse ﴿and the food of those who were given the Scripture﴾ stands alone regarding what the People of the Book slaughtered while mentioning the name of Allah over it; this is lawful without dispute. And the verse ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾ stands alone regarding what an idolater or a Muslim slaughtered without mentioning the name of Allah over it. What the idolater slaughtered is forbidden without dispute, and what a Muslim slaughtered without invoking the name will have its ruling come, Allah willing. They overlap in what a People of the Book slaughtered without mentioning Allah over it, so they conflict regarding it.

So the generality of ﴿and the food of those who were given the Scripture﴾ indicates permissibility, and the generality of ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾ indicates prohibition, so recourse is made to preference, as we have mentioned.

Regarding these two generals too, it has been disputed which of them is preferred. The majority held the preference of the generality of ﴿and the food of those who were given the Scripture﴾, and so on.

And some of them held the preference of the generality of ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 5 (part 2 of 3):

(p-264) Al-Nawawi said in his commentary on al-Muhadhdhab: The slaughter of the People of the Book is permissible whether or not they mention the name of God over it, based on the apparent meaning of the Mighty Qur'an. This is our school's position and the position of the majority (al-jumhur).

Ibn al-Mundhir reported it from ʿAli, al-Lakhmi, Hammad ibn Sulayman, Abu Hanifa, Ahmad, Ishaq and others. But if they slaughter upon an idol or something else, it is not permissible. The point of his statement ends here, in his own words.

Al-Nawawi also reported the other view from ʿAli as well, and from Abu Thawr, ʿAʾisha and Ibn ʿUmar.

The one who writes these notes, may God pardon him, says: What appears, and God knows best, is that each of the two verses has a factor giving it preference, and that the factor for the verse of permission is stronger and more deserving of consideration. As for the verse of permission, its generality is given preference for two reasons:

The first: it is less in specification (takhsis), whereas the verse of prohibition is more specified. This is because al-Shafiʿi and those who agreed with him specified it by what was slaughtered for other than God, and the majority specified it by what was left without the basmala deliberately, saying that leaving it out by forgetfulness has no effect. The verse of permission contains no specification beyond the case under dispute, except one single specification, which is what we mentioned earlier: that it is specified by what has not had the name of other than God invoked over it, according to the correct view.

It has been established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that the less specified is given precedence over the more specified, just as what has not been subject to specification at all is given precedence over what has. This is the view of the majority of usuliyyun. Al-Subki and Safi al-Din al-Hindi dissented. The author of Nashr al-Bunud in his commentary on Maraqi al-Suʿud, in the section on preference by the condition of the transmitted report, explained in his commentary on the line:

"Giving precedence to what is specified over what is not specified, and the reverse—each has a text in its support."

that the less specified is given precedence over the more specified, and that what has not been subject to specification is given precedence over what has, according to the great majority of usuliyyun, and that only al-Subki and Safi al-Din al-Hindi dissented on this.

The second: what Ibn Jarir reported, and Ibn Kathir reported from him, from ʿIkrima, al-Hasan al-Basri and Makhul, that the verse "The food of those who were given the Book" abrogates the verse "And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned."

(p-265) Ibn Jarir and Ibn Kathir said: their intended meaning by abrogation is specification. But we have already noted that specification after acting on the general text is abrogation, because specification is an explanation (bayan), and an explanation may not be delayed beyond the time of action.

This is supported by the fact that the verse "And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned" is from surah al-Anʿam, which is Meccan by consensus, while the verse "The food of those who were given the Book" is from al-Ma'ida, which is among the last things revealed of the Qur'an in Medina. As for the verse of prohibition, its generality is given preference by the factors we mentioned earlier concerning the words of God: "And that over which other than God has been invoked," because both indicate a prohibition that appears to conflict with a permission.

The summary of this issue is that the slaughter of a People of the Book has five states, with no sixth:

The first: it is known that he mentioned God's name over it. In this case it is eaten without dispute, and the dissent of the Shiʿa on this carries no weight, because they are not counted in consensus.

The second: it is known that it was dedicated to other than God. Here there is disagreement, and we have already noted that the sound position is that it is not eaten, because of God's words: "And that over which other than God has been invoked."

The third: it is known that he combined God's name with the name of another. The apparent meaning of the texts is that it is also not eaten, because it falls under "that over which other than God has been invoked."

The fourth: it is known that he remained silent and mentioned neither God nor anyone else. The majority hold it permissible, which is the truth, and some hold it prohibited, as already mentioned.

The fifth: the matter is unknown because it was slaughtered while he was alone. It is eaten according to the position of the majority of scholars, and this is the truth, provided the People of the Book is not known for eating carrion, such as one who pulls the neck of a chicken with his hand. If he is known for eating carrion, what was slaughtered out of sight is not eaten according to some scholars, and this is the school of Malik. Others permit eating it. Indeed Ibn al-ʿArabi the Maliki said: if we witness him pulling the neck of a chicken with his hand, we say: eat from it, because it is with his food, and God has permitted us their food. Ibn ʿAbd al-Salam found this unlikely.

The one who writes these notes, may God pardon him, says: It is deserving of being considered unlikely. Just as their women may be married though intercourse with them during menstruation is not permitted, likewise their food is permitted to us without permitting carrion, because the furthest the matter goes is that the slaughter of the People of the Book is lawful as a slaughter like that of a Muslim.

(p-266) As for what we promised regarding the ruling on what a Muslim slaughters without mentioning God's name over it, its summary is that there are three views:

The most preferred, which is the view of the majority: if he deliberately left out the basmala, it is not eaten, because of the generality of God's words: "And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned." If he left it out by forgetfulness, it is eaten, because had he remembered, he would have mentioned God's name.

Ibn Jarir said: whoever prohibits the slaughter of one who forgot has departed from the word of the proof and opposed the established report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Ibn Kathir said: Ibn Jarir means by this what al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "A Muslim is sufficed by his name if he forgets to mention it when slaughtering; let him mention God's name and eat it."

Then Ibn Kathir said: raising this hadith to the Prophet is an error, in which Maʿqil ibn ʿUbayd Allah al-Jazari erred, and the correct form is that it stops at Ibn ʿAbbas (as a statement of his).

Sa'id ibn Mansur and ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr al-Humaydi narrated it in the same way.

Among what some scholars used as evidence for eating the slaughter of one who forgot the basmala is the indication of the Book, the Sunna and the consensus regarding excusing forgetfulness.

Among what some used for this is a hadith narrated by the memorizer Abu Ahmad ibn ʿAdi from Abu Hurayra, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of God, what about one of us who slaughters and forgets to mention the name? The Prophet (ﷺ) said: The name of God is upon every Muslim." Ibn Kathir mentioned this hadith and declared it weak, because its chain contains Marwan ibn Salim Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Shami, who is weak.

The second view: the slaughter of a Muslim is eaten even if he deliberately leaves out the basmala. This is the school of al-Shafiʿi, may God have mercy on him, as already mentioned, because he holds that "what God's name has not been mentioned over" refers only to what was dedicated to other than God, and nothing else. Some claimed that a consensus was formed before al-Shafiʿi that what was deliberately left without the basmala is not eaten, and for this reason Abu Yusuf and others said: if a judge ruled to permit its sale, the ruling would not be enforced, because it contradicts the consensus. Ibn Kathir found the claim of consensus on this strange, saying: the disagreement on it before al-Shafiʿi is well known.

(p-267) The third view: if a Muslim does not mention God's name over his slaughter, it is not eaten at all, whether he left it deliberately or by forgetfulness. This is the school of Dawud al-Zahiri.

Ibn Kathir said: Then Ibn Jarir and others reported from al-Shaʿbi and Muhammad ibn Sirin that both disliked what was left without the basmala by forgetfulness, and the early scholars often use "disliked" to mean "prohibited."

Then Ibn Kathir mentioned that Ibn Jarir does not regard the dissent of one or two against the majority as breaking a consensus, so he counts it as consensus despite the dissent of one or two. For this reason he reported a consensus on eating what was left without the basmala by forgetfulness, although he himself reported the contrary from al-Shaʿbi and Ibn Sirin.

**

Important issues related to these discussions

The first issue: know that many scholars among the Malikis, the Shafiʿis and others distinguish between what the People of the Book slaughter for an idol and what they slaughter for Jesus or Gabriel, or for their churches. They say the first is among what was dedicated to other than God, but the second is, in their view, disliked as a matter of reverence (karahat tanzih). They rely on God's words: "And what is slaughtered upon the stone altars" [al-Ma'ida: 3].

What appears to its writer, may God pardon him, is that this distinction is invalid, by the testimony of the Qur'an. The slaughter offered as an act of worship (qurba) is worship by consensus, and God said: "So pray to your Lord and sacrifice" [108].

God also said: "Say: Indeed my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for God" [al-An'am: 162].

So whoever directs any of that to other than God has made a partner with God in this act of worship, which is slaughter, whether it is a prophet, an angel, a building, a tree, a stone or anything else. There is no difference in this between the righteous and the wicked, as God stated by His words: "Nor would He order you to take the angels and the prophets as lords" [Al 'Imran: 80].

Then He explained that the doer of this is a disbeliever, by His words: "Would He order you to disbelieve after you have submitted?" [Al 'Imran: 80].

God said: "It is not for a human that God should give him the Book and judgment and prophethood, and then he would say to the people: Be servants to me rather than God" [Al 'Imran: 79].

(p-268) God said: "Say: O People of the Book, come to a word that is equitable between us and you: that we will not worship except God and not associate anything with Him and not take one another as lords other than God" [Al 'Imran: 64].

If it is said: Abu al-Darda', Abu Umama al-Bahili, al-ʿIrbad ibn Sariya, al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymira, Hamza ibn Habib, Abu Salama al-Khawlani, ʿUmar ibn al-Aswad, Makhul, al-Layth ibn Sa'd and others granted a concession to eat what they slaughtered for their churches.

The answer: this is the view of a group of scholars from among the Companions and those after them, and others have disagreed with them. Among those who disagreed with them was the Mother of the Believers ʿAʾisha, may God be pleased with her, and the Imam al-Shafiʿi, may God have mercy on him. God says: "If you dispute about anything, then refer it to God" [al-Nisa': 59]. So we refer this dispute to God, and we find that He prohibited what was dedicated to other than God.

His words "to other than God" include the angel and the prophet, just as they include the idol, the stone altar and the devil. They agreed with us in prohibiting what they slaughter in the name of an idol. The evidence indicates there is no difference between the prophet and the angel, and between the idol and the stone altar, so they are bound to the prohibition.

As for their citing God's words "And what is slaughtered upon the stone altars," there is no proof in it, because God's words "And what is slaughtered upon the stone altars" do not specify His words "And that over which other than God has been invoked," since it mentions only some of what the general wording of "And that over which other than God has been invoked" covers.

It has been established in the science of usul al-fiqh that mentioning some individual instances of a general ruling by a ruling of the general does not specify it, according to the correct view, which is the position of the majority, in contrast to Abu Thawr, who argued that mentioning it has no purpose except specification. The majority answered that the concept of a proper name (mafhum al-laqab) is not a proof, and the benefit of mentioning a part is to exclude the possibility of its being taken out of the general. Once you have verified this, know that mentioning a part does not specify the general, whether both are mentioned in one text, as in God's words: "Guard the prayers and the middle prayer" [al-Baqara: 238], or each is mentioned separately, as in the hadith of al-Tirmidhi and others: "Any hide that is tanned has become pure," and in the hadith of Muslim that he (ﷺ) passed by a dead sheep and said: "Why did you not take its hide?"

So the mention of the middle prayer in the first does not indicate neglect of the other prayers, (p-269) and the mention of the sheep's hide in the second does not indicate that benefit may not be taken from the hide of other than a sheep, because mentioning a part does not specify the general.

And likewise, the return of a pronoun to a part [of the general term] does not specify it either, according to the correct view, as in His saying, ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back during that [waiting period]﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 228]. The pronoun refers back to His saying, ﴿And divorced women shall wait [concerning themselves] for three periods﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 228], and it refers specifically to the revocable divorcees among the divorced women, even though the waiting of three periods (qurū', menstrual cycles) is general to all divorced women, both revocable and irrevocable (bawā'in). The author of Marāqī al-Su'ūd pointed to this, also stating together with it that the occasion of revelation (sabab al-wāqi'ah) does not specify the ruling, and that the view of the narrator (madhhab al-rāwī) does not specify what he narrated, according to the correct view in both cases, saying:

"Leave aside the pronoun of a part, and the occasions [of revelation],
and the mention of what agrees with a singular [case],
and the view of the narrator, according to the accepted position."

It is related from al-Shafi'i and most of the Hanafis that the specification is by the pronoun of a part, and according to this, the waiting of three qurū' for irrevocable divorcees is derived from another evidence.

As for the non-specification by mentioning a part, none disagreed about it except Abu Thawr, and the refutation of his view has already passed.

Even if we grant that the verse is opposed by His saying, ﴿And the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾, we find that the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded leaving such a matter in which the texts conflict, by his saying: "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt."

The second issue: The scholars differed concerning the slaughter (dhakāh) of the Christians of the Arabs, such as the Banū Taghlib, Tanūkh, Bahrā', Judhām, Lakhm, 'Āmilah and the like. The majority hold that their slaughtered animals are not eaten; this was said by Ibn Kathir, and it is the view of al-Shafi'i. Al-Nawawi in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab transmitted it from 'Ali, 'Ata' and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Al-Nawawi also transmitted the permissibility of their slaughter from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, 'Ata' al-Khurasani, al-Zuhri, al-Hakam, Hammad, Abu Hanifah, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh and Abu Thawr. Ibn Qudamah in al-Mughni affirmed this view, arguing from the generality of His saying: ﴿And the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾.

The evidence of the first view is what is related from 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Christians of the Arabs are not People of the Book; their slaughtered animals are not lawful for us."

And what is related from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "The slaughtered animals of the Banū Taghlib's Christians are not lawful, because they entered Christianity after the alteration (tabdīl), and it is not known whether they entered the religion of those among them who altered, or the religion of those who did not alter. So they became like the Magians, since their status in the Scripture became unclear, so their slaughtered animals are not eaten." This was mentioned by the author of al-Muhadhdhab, and al-Nawawi remained silent on it in the Sharh, saying: "It is the evidence of the Shafi'is for prohibiting their slaughtered animals." It is understood from this that the slaughter of all Jews and Christians today is not permitted because of their alteration, especially regarding those known to eat carrion, like the Christians.

The third issue: Is the slaughter of the Magians lawful for Muslims? Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: "It is forbidden according to us, and this was said by the majority of scholars." Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted it from most scholars, and he said: "Among those who said this were Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, al-Nakha'i, 'Ubayd Allah ibn Yazid, Murrah al-Hamdani, Malik, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah, Ahmad and Ishaq."

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir, regarding His saying: ﴿And the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾:

"As for the Magians, even though the jizyah is taken from them by extension and assimilation to the People of the Book, their slaughtered animals are not eaten and their women are not married, contrary to Abu Thawr Ibrahim ibn Khalid al-Kalbi, one of the jurists among the companions of al-Shafi'i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. When he said that and it became known from him, the jurists denounced him, until Imam Ahmad said of him: 'Abu Thawr is like his name' (meaning in this issue). It seems he held to the generality of a hadith related mursal from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: 'Treat them as you treat the People of the Book (sunnū bihim sunnata ahl al-kitab),' but this wording is not established. What is established in Sahih al-Bukhari is from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf that 'the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took the jizyah from the Magians of Hajar.' Even if the authenticity of this hadith is granted, its generality is specified by the mafhum (implied meaning) of this verse: ﴿And the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾. Its mafhum al-mukhalafah (implication by contrary) indicates that the food of all others among the followers of religions is not lawful." End of Ibn Kathir's words verbatim.

In the margin, Shaykh al-Sayyid Muhammad Rashid Rida objected to this, saying: "This is mafhum al-laqab (implication from a title), which is not a proof."

The author of this commentary (may Allah pardon him) says: The correct view is with the Hafiz Ibn Kathir (may Allah have mercy on him), and the Shaykh's objection to it is an oversight on his part, because the implication of His saying ﴿those who were given the Scripture﴾ is mafhum of cause ('illah), not mafhum of title (laqab), as the Shaykh supposed. The mafhum of title in the terminology of the usulis is that the ruling is attached to a fixed noun, whether it is a noun of kind, a proper noun or a collective noun, and its criterion is that it is what is mentioned only so that attribution to it is possible, because it does not include an attribute that requires specifying it by mention over others.

As for the attachment of this ruling, which is the permissibility of their food, to the attribute of being given the Scripture, this is attaching the ruling to its cause ('illah), because the attribute of being given the Scripture is suitable to be the basis (manat) of the ruling of the permissibility of their food.

The third path of the paths of causation known as indication and allusion (al-iymā' wa al-tanbīh) has shown that the basis for the permissibility of their food is their being given the Scripture, and that is precisely the basis for the permissibility of marrying their women, because if arranging the ruling of the permissibility of their food and women upon their being given the Scripture were not because it is its cause, there would be no benefit in specifying it by being given the Scripture, and it is known that arranging a ruling upon an attribute which is not its cause would be superfluous without benefit, from which it is understood that it is its cause by the path of indication and allusion.

The author of Marāqī al-Su'ūd said, enumerating the forms of indication:

"As when he hears an attribute and rules [on it],
and the mention of it in the ruling as an attribute has been inferred,
if it is not its cause, it would not benefit;
and its prevention from what would render it void, take [it as proof],
its arrangement of the ruling upon it, and let it be clear."

etc.

The point of evidence in it is his saying, "take [as proof] its arrangement of the ruling upon it," and his saying, "and the mention of it in the ruling as an attribute, if it is not its cause, would not benefit."

What further clarifies what we have mentioned is that His saying ﴿those who were given the Scripture﴾ is a relative clause (mawsul) with a verbal clause as its complement, and it has been established among the grammarians in the correct, well-known view that the explicit attribute such as the active participle and the passive participle occurring as the complement of al (ال) functions as the verb with the relative pronoun; that is why the attribute with al as a relative, in the past tense, governs, because it is in the position of the verb, as indicated in the Khulasah by his saying:

"If it is the complement of al, then in past and other tenses
its governing is approved."

When you have verified this, you know that "those who were given the Scripture" is in the position of what you would say as "the food of those who have given the Scripture" using the passive participle form, and no one has said that the mafhum of the passive participle is a mafhum of title, because it includes a matter, namely the verbal noun, that the one characterized by it may be intended by the speaker over others, as they mentioned regarding the mafhum of the attribute.

It thus becomes clear that being given the Scripture is an attribute specific to them over others, and it is the cause for the permissibility of their food and marrying their women; so the claim that it is mafhum of title is an obvious oversight.

It becomes clear from the verification that the mafhum in His saying ﴿those who were given the Scripture﴾ is mafhum of cause, and mafhum of cause is a type of the kinds of mafhum of attribute. So the attribute is more general than the cause. Its clarification, as al-Qarafi explained, is that an attribute may complete the cause without being the full cause, such as the obligation of zakah on pasturing livestock (sa'imah): its cause is not pasturing alone, for otherwise it would be obligatory on wild animals since they graze freely; rather the cause is possession of what achieves wealth, and that is more complete with grazing than with fodder. This is according to those who do not see zakah on fodder-fed animals.

It becomes clear that what the Hafiz Ibn Kathir (may Allah have mercy on him) said is the correct view.

It has been established in the science of usul that mafhum in both its kinds is among the specifiers of generality. As for specifying the general by mafhum al-muwafaqah in both its types, there is no disagreement about it. Among those who related the consensus on it are al-Amidi and al-Subki in Sharh al-Mukhtasar. The evidence for its permissibility is that acting upon two evidences is better than discarding one of them.

An example is the specification of the hadith: "The delay of the wealthy (in payment) makes his honour and his punishment lawful," meaning it makes his honour lawful by his saying "you have delayed me" and his punishment by imprisonment; it is specified by mafhum al-muwafaqah, which is the implication by a fortiori in His saying: ﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾ [Al-Isra': 23], because its implication is the prohibition of harming them, so a father is not imprisoned for his son's debt.

As for specifying it by mafhum al-mukhalafah, there is a disagreement about it, and the more preferred of it is what the Hafiz Ibn Kathir, may Allah cover him with His vast mercy, followed, which is specification by it. The evidence for it is what we previously presented, that acting upon two evidences is better than discarding one of them.

It was said: it is not permissible to specify by it, and al-Baji related this from most of the Malikis.

The argument for this view is that the general's indication of what the mafhum indicates is by the explicit statement, which takes precedence over the mafhum. It is answered that what takes precedence is a specific explicit statement, not something that is one of the individuals of the general; so the mafhum takes precedence over it, because acting upon two evidences is better than discarding one of them.

Sahib Marāqī al-Su'ūd adopted specification by it in his saying in the section on the specific, in discussing the separate specifiers:

"Most people regarded consensus as valid, and the two kinds of mafhum, like analogy."

An example of specification by mafhum al-mukhalafah is the specification of his saying (ﷺ): "In every forty sheep, one sheep," whose generality includes both pastured and fodder-fed animals, by the mafhum of his saying: "In pastured sheep there is zakah," according to those who do not see zakah on fodder-fed animals, and they are the majority, because it is understood from it that zakah is not due on non-pastured animals; so the generality of "In every forty sheep, one sheep" is specified by that. And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: What a People of the Book hunts with trained animals (jawarih) and weapons is lawful for a Muslim, because the wounding (al-'aqr) is the slaughter (dhakah) of game. The four imams hold this view, and it was said by 'Ata', al-Layth, al-Awza'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Dawud and the majority of scholars, as al-Nawawi related from them in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab.

The majority's evidence is clear, namely His saying: ﴿And the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾. Malik and Ibn al-Qasim disagreed and distinguished between the slaughter of a People of the Book and his hunting, relying on His saying: ﴿Your hands and your spears can reach﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 94], because He restricted the game to the hands and spears of Muslims, excluding non-Muslims.

The author of this commentary (may Allah pardon him) says: What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that this argument does not stand against the majority, and that the correct view is with the majority.

Ashhab, Ibn Harun, Ibn Yunus, al-Baji and al-Lakhmi agreed with the majority from the Malikis. Malik's view in al-Muwazanah was its disliking; Ibn Bashir said: "It is possible to interpret the Mudawwanah as reflecting disapproval."

The fifth issue: The slaughter of People of the Book in the land of war is like their slaughter in the land of Islam. Al-Nawawi said: "There is no disagreement about this," and Ibn al-Mundhir related the consensus on it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 6 (part 1 of 7):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And your feet, up to the ankles﴾. In His words "wa-arjulakum" (and your feet) there are three recitations: one is irregular (shadhdhah), and two are mutawatir (widely transmitted).

As for the irregular one: it is the reading with raf' (nominative, arjulukum), which is the reading of al-Hasan. As for the two mutawatir ones: the reading with nasb (accusative, arjulakum) and the reading with jarr (genitive, arjulikum).

As for nasb: it is the reading of Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs, from the Seven, and Ya'qub from the Three.

As for jarr: it is the reading of Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and in the transmission of Abu Bakr.

As for the reading with nasb: there is no difficulty in it, because the feet in it are conjoined (ma'tufah) to the faces, and the meaning según it is: "So wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, and your feet up to the ankles, and wipe over your heads."

The wiping of the head was placed between the washed members only to preserve the order (tartib), because the head is wiped between the washed members. From here a group of scholars derived that the order among the members of wudu' is obligatory, as indicated by the noble verse.

As for the reading with jarr: in the noble verse there is an ambiguity (ijmal), namely that it may be understood that wiping the two feet in wudu' suffices instead of washing them, like the head; and this is contrary to reality, given the sound and explicit ahadith on the obligation of washing the two feet in wudu' and the threat of Fire for whoever neglects that, such as his saying ﷺ: "Woe to the heels from the Fire."

Know first that when two readings appear to conflict in one verse, they have the ruling of two verses, as is known among the scholars. Having known this, know that the reading "wa-arjulakum" with nasb is explicit in the obligation of washing the two feet in wudu'. It indicates that the reading with khafd (jarr) is only for proximity to the word in genitive (mujawarat al-makhfud), although originally it is in the accusative, by the evidence of the reading with nasb. The Arabs give a word the genitive case because of its proximity to a genitive word, although its i'rab is nasb or raf'.

What some of them mentioned, that jarr by proximity (al-jarr bil-mujawarah) is counted among the solecisms (lahn) that are tolerated only for the necessity of poetry specifically, and that it is not heard in conjunction (al-'atf), and that it is permitted only when there is no risk of confusion, is rejected, because the imams of the Arabic language explicitly affirmed its permissibility.

Among those who explicitly affirmed it are al-Akhfash, Abu al-Baqa', and others.

Only al-Zajjaj denied it, and his denial of it, despite its establishment in the speech of the Arabs and in the Great Qur'an, indicates that he did not investigate the matter with sufficient thoroughness.

The verified position is that jarr by proximity is one of the styles of the Arabic language, and that it came in the Qur'an because it is in a clear Arabic tongue.

Among its examples in the adjective is the saying of Imru' al-Qays (al-Tawil):

"As if Thabir, at the tips of its rain-clouds, were a great man in a folded cloak."

Here "muzamмal" is in the genitive by proximity, although it is an adjective of "kabir" which is nominative as the predicate of "ka'anna."

And the saying of Dhu al-Rummah (al-Basit):

"It shows you the custom of a face, not blemished, smooth, in which there is no mole nor scar."

For the transmission is with the genitive of "ghayr," as many have said, by proximity, although it is an adjective of "sunnata," which is accusative as an object.

Among its examples in conjunction is the saying of al-Nabighah (al-Basit):

"None remained except a captive not escaping, and a bound one, tied in leather thongs, struck down."

Here "muwathaq" is in the genitive by proximity to the genitive word, although it is conjoined to "asir," which is nominative as subject.

And the saying of Imru' al-Qays (al-Tawil):

"The cooks of meat remained between one who cooks and one who places a dish of roasting, or a pot, hastened."

Here "qadir" is in the genitive by proximity to the genitive word, although it is conjoined to "safif," which is accusative as the object of the active participle "mundij." "Safif" is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, and it is the meat laid on the coals to be roasted; "qadir" is likewise fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, and it is the meat placed in the pot to be cooked by boiling.

This i'rab that we have mentioned is the truth, because the cooking applies to each of the safif and the qadir. What al-Sabban claimed in his gloss on al-Ashmuni, that his saying "aw qadir" is conjoined to "mundij" with an implied governed noun, meaning "and a cook of a pot..." etc., is clearly baseless; for "mundij" includes both the roaster of the safif and the cook of the qadir, so there is no need to conjoin the cook to the cooked, since it is included, nor any need to posit a deleted "tabikh."

What al-Ayni mentioned, that it is conjoined to "shiwa'," is also clearly baseless; al-Sabban has refuted him, for the meaning would become: "and a safif of qadir," and the qadir cannot be a safif.

The verified position is what we have mentioned of jarr by proximity, and Ibn Qudamah firmly affirmed it in al-Mughni.

Among jarr by proximity in conjunction is the saying of Zuhayr (al-Kamil):

"Time has played with them and changed them after me, the winds of dust and rain."

Here "al-qatr" is in the genitive by proximity to a genitive word, although it is conjoined to "sawafi," which is nominative, as the agent of "ghayyara."

Among it in emphasis is the saying of a poet (al-Basit):

"O companion, inform all of the owners of wives that there is no union when the knots of the bond are loosened."

Here "kulli-him" is in the genitive according to what al-Farra' related, by proximity to a genitive word, although it is an emphasis of "dhawi," which is accusative as an object.

Among its examples in the Great Qur'an in conjunction, like the verse we are dealing with, is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And houris, with wide, lovely eyes﴾ ﴿like hidden pearls﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 22], according to the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i.

And the transmission of al-Mufaddal from 'Asim with jarr is by proximity to "akwab" and "abariq," up to His saying: ﴿and the flesh of birds, of what they desire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 21], although the ruling on His saying "wa-hurun 'in" is nominative. It was said that it is conjoined to the subject of "yatufu," which is ﴿young boys made eternal﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17].

It was also said that it is nominative as a subject whose predicate is deleted, indicated by the context; that is: "and therein are houris with wide eyes," or "for them are houris with wide eyes."

Thus it is conjoined in terms of meaning.

Sibawayh recited, for conjunction according to meaning, the saying of al-Shammakh, or Dhu al-Rummah (al-Kamil):

"They perished, and the signs of them were changed by ruin, except for the stationary hearths, whose embers are ash."

"And a stake, whose face is smooth, then it appeared, and the goat hid its traces."

For the transmission is with nasb of "rawakida" as an exception, and raf' of "mushajjaj" conjoined to it; because the meaning is: "nothing remained of them except stationary hearths and a stake." By "rawakid" he means the stones of the cooking pot, and by "mushajjaj" the tent peg. By this you know that the reason for the jarr in the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i is proximity to the genitive word, as we have mentioned, contrary to whoever says that in the reading of jarr the conjunction is to "akwab," meaning they are served with cups, and with houris, and to whoever says it is conjoined to "jannat al-na'im," meaning they are in gardens of delight, and in houris, with an implied governed noun, meaning in the company of houris.

These two views are not hidden in their weakness: the first is refuted by the fact that houris are not served drinks, according to His saying: ﴿houris, restrained in pavilions﴾ [al-Rahman: 72]. The second is clearly baseless, as you see, for their being in gardens of delight and in houris, and positing what has no evidence has no basis.

The first has been answered with two responses. The first: the conjunction there is according to meaning, because the meaning is: they enjoy cups, and fruit, and flesh, and houris. This was said by al-Zajjaj and others.

The second response: houris are of two kinds:
1. houris restrained in pavilions;
2. and houris who are served to them.

This was said by Fakhr al-Din al-Razi and others, and it is a division for which there is no evidence, and it is not known from the attributes of the houris with wide eyes that they are served as drinks are. The most apparent is jarr by proximity, as we have mentioned.

The statements of al-Farra' and Qutrub indicate this. And what was used to refute the view of conjunction to "akwab," namely that houris are not served, is equally used to refute the view of conjunction to "wildanun mukhalladun" in the reading of raf', for it would imply that the houris circulate among them like the young boys, and restraint in pavilions contradicts that.

Among those who firmly held that the jarr of "wa-arjulikum" is by proximity to a genitive word is al-Bayhaqi in "al-Sunan al-Kubra," for he said verbatim: "Chapter on the reading of those who read 'wa-arjulakum' with nasb, and that the matter returns to washing; and that whoever read it with khafd, it is only by proximity." Then he cited his chains to Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata', al-A'raj, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn Ghaylan, Nafi' ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Nu'aym the reciter, and Abu Muhammad Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Yazid al-Hadrami, that they all read it: "wa-arjulakum," with nasb.

He said: It reached me from Ibrahim ibn Yazid al-Taymi that he read it with nasb, and from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amir al-Yahsubi, and from 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs, and from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash through the transmission of al-A'sha, and from al-Kisa'i; all of these read it with nasb.

And whoever read it with khafd, it is only by proximity. Al-A'mash said: They used to read it with khafd, and they used to wash. End of al-Bayhaqi's words.

Among examples of jarr by proximity in the Qur'an in adjectives is His saying: ﴿the punishment of a encompassing day﴾ [Hud: 84], with the jarr of "muhit," although it is an adjective of "'adhab." And His saying: ﴿the punishment of a painful day﴾ [Hud: 26]. What indicates that the adjective belongs to "'adhab," which was put in the genitive by proximity, is the frequency with which "alim" (painful) occurs in the Qur'an as an adjective of "'adhab." And His saying: ﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an﴾ ﴿on a preserved tablet﴾ [al-Buruj: 21-22], according to the reading of those who read "mahfuz" with jarr, as al-Qurtubi said. And from the speech of the Arabs: "This is the hole of a dhabb lizard, ruined" (kharib), with jarr of "kharib" by proximity to a genitive word, although it is an adjective of the predicate of the subject.

By this you know that the claim that jarr by proximity is a solecism tolerated only for the necessity of poetry is false. As for the answer to what they mentioned, that it is permitted only when there is no risk of confusion: the confusion here is removed by the limit "up to the ankles," since the limit of the wiped member is not stated, and it is removed by the reading with nasb, as we have mentioned. If it is said that the reading with jarr, which indicates wiping the two feet in wudu', is the one that clarifies the reading with nasb, by making the reading with nasb a conjunction to the place (al-mahall), since the heads are in the genitive by the particle "bi" in a place of nasb, according to the saying of Ibn Malik in the Khulasah:

"The genitive of what follows the genitive, and whoever considers the place in following, it is good."

Although Ibn Malik mentioned this in the chapter on the governing of the verbal noun, its ruling is general, that is, the same applies to the verb and the adjective, as he indicated for the adjective with his saying:

"Put in the genitive or the accusative the follower that was lowered, like 'seeking rank and wealth' whoever rises."

The answer is that clarifying the reading with nasb by the reading with jarr, as he mentioned, is refuted by the explicit, sound Sunnah, which speaks against it, and by its threat of the punishment of Fire for the one who commits it. This differs from clarifying the reading with khafd by the reading with nasb, which accords with the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, established from him in word and deed.

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded in their two Sahihs, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ lagged behind us on a journey we were travelling, and he caught up with us when the 'Asr prayer had come upon us while we were making wudu', and we began to wipe over our feet, so he called out in a loud voice: 'Perfect the wudu'; woe to the heels from the Fire.'" And it is likewise in the two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.

In Sahih Muslim, from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Perfect the wudu'; woe to the heels from the Fire." Al-Bayhaqi and al-Hakim related with a sound chain, from 'Abd Allah ibn Harith ibn Juz', that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Woe to the heels and the soles of the feet from the Fire." Imam Ahmad, Ibn Majah, and Ibn Jarir related from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Woe to the heels from the Fire."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 6 (part 2 of 7):

Imam Ahmad narrated from Mu'aygib that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Woe to the heels from the Fire." Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Woe to the heels from the Fire." He said: "No one remained in the mosque, noble or humble, except that I looked at him as he turned over his heels, looking at them."

It is established in the hadiths on wudu' (ablution, the ritual washing before prayer) from the Commander of the Faithful 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Mu'awiyah, 'Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn 'Asim, and al-Miqdad ibn Ma'di Karib: "That the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) washed his two feet in his wudu', once or twice or three times," according to the differences in their narrations.

In the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father from his grandfather: "That the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed wudu' and washed his two feet." Then he said: "This is the wudu' with which Allah does not accept the prayer except with it."

The hadiths on this subject are very numerous, and they are authentic and explicit in requiring the washing of the two feet in wudu', and in denying that wiping them suffices.

* *

Some scholars said: What is meant by wiping the two feet is washing them. The Arabs also use the word "wiping" (mash) for "washing" (ghasl), and they say "tamassahtu" meaning "I performed wudu'," and "masaha al-matar al-ard" meaning the rain washed the earth, and "masaha Allahu ma bika" meaning Allah washed away from you sins and harm. There is no obstacle to the view that "wiping" in the verse with regard to the feet means washing, while "wiping" with regard to the head means the wiping that is not washing. This is not a case of carrying a homonym (mushtarak) on both its meanings, nor of carrying a word on both its literal and metaphorical senses, since these are two separate questions, each independent of the other. Moreover, the verified view is that it is permissible to carry a homonym on both its meanings, as the Shaykh Taqi al-Din Abu al-'Abbas Ibn Taymiyyah verified in his treatise on the sciences of the Qur'an, and he established that this is the correct view in the schools of the four Imams, may Allah have mercy on them. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, in his tafsir, reconciled the reading in the accusative (nasb) and the reading in the genitive (jarr) by saying that the reading in the accusative means the washing of the two feet, because the conjunction in it links them with the faces and the hands up to the elbows, and these are among the washed parts without dispute, while the reading in the genitive means wiping together with washing, that is, rubbing with the hand or something else.

The apparent wisdom in this regarding the two feet, and not other limbs, is that the two feet are the limbs of a person most exposed to filth, because they make contact with the ground. It is therefore fitting that both be combined: washing with water and wiping, that is rubbing with the hand, so that this is more thorough in cleaning.

Some scholars said: What is meant by the genitive reading is wiping, but the Prophet (ﷺ) explained that this applies only to the khuff (leather socks).

Accordingly, the verse points to wiping over the khuff in the genitive reading. Wiping over the two khuffs, if one put them on in a state of purity, is mutawatir (transmitted by so many chains that it is certain) from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and none opposed it except one whose opinion has no weight. The claim that it was abrogated by the verse of al-Ma'idah (naskh, abrogation) is refuted by the hadith of Jarir: "That he urinated, then performed wudu', and wiped over his khuffs. It was said to him: 'Do you do this?' He said: 'Yes, I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) urinate, then perform wudu', and wipe over his khuffs.'" Ibrahim said: "This hadith used to impress them, because Jarir's conversion to Islam was after the revelation of al-Ma'idah." Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh).

What confirms that there is no abrogation is that the verse of al-Ma'idah was revealed on the expedition of al-Muraysi'.

There is no doubt that Jarir's conversion came after that. Also, al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah narrated wiping over the khuffs from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the expedition of Tabuk, which was the last of his expeditions (ﷺ).

Among those who explicitly stated that the verse of al-Ma'idah was revealed on the expedition of al-Muraysi' is Ibn Hajar in Fath al-Bari. Al-Badawi al-Shinqiti alluded to this in his Nazm al-Maghazi, with his saying concerning the expedition of al-Muraysi', in rajaz meter:

"The slander on their return, and it was transmitted that
Tayammum (dry ablution) was revealed with it."

Tayammum is in the verse of al-Ma'idah. The scholars agreed on the permissibility of wiping over the khuff made of leather, and they differed concerning what is not of leather, if it is thick and covers the place of the obligatory washing. Malik and his companions said: One does not wipe over anything other than leather. They therefore stipulated for wiping that the wiped item be a khuff of leather, or a thick sock (jawrab) layered with leather on its outside and inside, meaning what is above the foot and what is beneath it, not its inner side which touches the foot.

They argued that wiping over the khuff is a concession (rukhsah, dispensation), that concessions do not extend beyond their proper place, and they said: The Prophet (ﷺ) did not wipe over anything other than leather, so it is not permissible to extend it to something else. This is based on half of a disputed principle of legal theory (usul al-fiqh): Does what has the same meaning as a concession apply to it, or is it restricted to it and not extended beyond its place?

Among its branches is their disagreement over the sale of 'araya (a permitted sale of fresh dates on the tree in exchange for dried dates) of grapes for dried raisins: Is it permissible by analogy to fresh dates for dates, or not?

The majority of scholars, including al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah, Ahmad, and their companions, hold that leather is not a condition, because the cause of the concession is the need for it, and this need exists in wiping over non-leather. They also rely on what came from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he wiped over the jawrabayn (thick socks) and the mawqayn.

They said: The jawrab is a wrapping for the foot, and it is not leather. In the Qamus (dictionary): "al-jawrab is a wrapping for the foot." In the Lisan (dictionary): "al-jawrab is a wrapping for the foot; it is arabized, and in Persian it is 'kawrab'."

Those who stipulated leather answered that the jawrab is the large khuff, as some people of knowledge said. As for al-jurmuq and al-muwq, the apparent view is that they are types of khuff.

It was said that they are one and the same thing, and this is the apparent meaning of the words of the lexicographers. It was also said that they are different. In the Qamus: "al-Jurmuq, like 'usfur (sparrow), is what is worn over the khuff." Also in the Qamus: "al-Muwq is a thick khuff worn over the khuff." In the Lisan: "al-Jurmuq is a small khuff," and it was said: "a small khuff worn over the khuff." Also in the Lisan: "al-Muwq is what is worn over the khuff; it is Persian, arabized, and al-muwq is the khuff," end of quote.

They said: The tasakhin (warm coverings) are khuffs. There is nothing in the hadiths that specifies that the Prophet (ﷺ) wiped only over leather.

The majority said: Leather itself has no effect. Rather, every thick khuff that covers the place of the obligatory washing and in which continuous walking is possible may be wiped over, whether it is leather or something else.

* *

Issues related to wiping over the two khuffs.

The first: The scholars agreed on the permissibility of wiping over the two khuffs both while travelling and while resident. The Shi'ah and the Khawarij said it is not permissible. Al-Qadi Abu al-Tayyib narrated something similar from Abu Bakr ibn Dawud. The verified view from Malik and most of his companions is that wiping over the khuff is permissible both in residence and while travelling.

It has been narrated from him (Malik) that he prohibited it absolutely, and it has been narrated from him that it is permissible while travelling but not while resident.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: I know of no one who denied it except Malik in one narration, which most of his companions rejected. The authentic narrations from him explicitly affirm it. His Muwatta' bears witness to wiping both in residence and while travelling, and all his companions and all the People of the Sunnah hold this view.

Al-Baji said: The narration of denial in al-'Utbiyyah, and its apparent meaning is prohibition, but its real meaning is that washing is better than wiping. Ibn Wahb said: The last thing I parted from Malik on was wiping in residence and while travelling. This is the truth about which there is no doubt. Therefore what Ibn al-Hajib said about Malik, that it is permissible while travelling but not while resident, is incorrect, because wiping over the khuff is mutawatir from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Zurqani said in his commentary on the Muwatta': Someone gathered its narrators and they exceeded eighty, among them ten (of the Companions). Ibn Abi Shaybah and others narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri: "Seventy of the Companions narrated to me about wiping over the two khuffs," end of quote.

Al-Nawawi said in his commentary on al-Muhadhdhab: Ibn al-Mundhir in his book al-Ijma' (consensus) reported the consensus of the scholars on the permissibility of wiping over the khuff. The authentic and widely transmitted hadiths about the Prophet's (ﷺ) wiping in residence and while travelling, his commanding it, and his permitting it, as well as the agreement of the Companions and those after them, indicate this. The Hafiz Abu Bakr al-Bayhaqi said: We have narrated the permissibility of wiping over the two khuffs from 'Umar, 'Ali, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, 'Ammar ibn Yasir, Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, 'Amr ibn al-'As, Anas ibn Malik, Sahl ibn Sa'd, Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari, al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Jabir ibn Samurah, Abu Umamah al-Bahili, 'Abdullah ibn al-Harith ibn Juz', and Abu Zayd al-Ansari, may Allah be pleased with them all.

I say: Many more of the Companions than those mentioned by al-Bayhaqi narrated it, and their hadiths are well known in the books of the Sunan and others.

Al-Tirmidhi said: On this subject there are also narrations from 'Umar, Salman, Buraydah, 'Amr ibn Umayyah, Ya'la ibn Murrah, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Usamah ibn Sharik, Usamah ibn Zayd, Safwan ibn 'Assal, Abu Hurayrah, 'Awf ibn Malik, Ibn 'Umar, Abu Bakrah, Bilal, and Khuzaymah ibn Thabit.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: We have narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri, who said: "Seventy of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) narrated to me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to wipe over the two khuffs."

He said: We have also narrated from Ibn al-Mubarak, who said: "There is no disagreement concerning wiping over the two khuffs," end of quote.

It is established in the authentic collection that in the hadith of al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, the Prophet (ﷺ) wiped over the khuff on the expedition of Tabuk, which was the last of his expeditions (ﷺ). It is also established in the authentic collection, in the hadith of Jarir ibn 'Abdullah al-Bajali, that the Prophet (ﷺ) wiped over the khuff, and there is no doubt that this was after the revelation of the verse of al-Ma'idah, as already mentioned. In the Sunan of Abu Dawud, when they said to Jarir: "It was only before the revelation of al-Ma'idah," he said: "I did not embrace Islam except after the revelation of al-Ma'idah."

These authentic texts we have mentioned indicate that wiping over the two khuffs was not abrogated, and there is no doubt about its legislation (mashru'iyyah). Therefore, disagreement on it has no basis at all.

* *

The second issue: The scholars differed over which is better, washing the foot or wiping over the khuff.
