A group of the people of knowledge said: Washing the foot is better than wiping over the khuff, provided that one does not abandon wiping out of disinclination to the concession of wiping. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, Malik, Abu Hanifah, and their companions. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated it from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and his son, may Allah be pleased with them both. Al-Bayhaqi narrated it from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari.

The argument for this view is that washing the foot is what the Prophet (ﷺ) consistently did in most of the times, and because it is the original (asl), and because it involves more hardship.

Another group of the people of knowledge held that wiping is better. This is the most authentic narration from Imam Ahmad, and al-Sha'bi, al-Hakam, and Hammad said the same.

Those who held this view cited the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying in some narrations of the hadith of al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah: "My Lord commanded me with this."

Its wording in the Sunan of Abu Dawud from al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah is: "That the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wiped over the two khuffs. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, have you forgotten?' He said: 'Rather, you have forgotten; my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, commanded me with this.'"

They also cited the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying in the hadith of Safwan ibn 'Assal, which will come, if Allah the Exalted wills: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us to wipe over the two khuffs," the hadith.

They said: A command, if it is not for obligation, is at least for recommendation.

The author of this commentary (muqayyiduhu), may Allah pardon him, says: In my view, the most evident of what has been said on this question is what Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned and attributed to his teacher Taqi al-Din, namely that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not deliberately contrive a condition opposed to the state his feet were in. Rather, if they were in khuffs, he wiped over them and did not remove them, and if they were uncovered, he washed the two feet and did not put on khuffs in order to wipe over them. This is the most balanced of the views on this question, end of quote.

It is a condition regarding the leather sock (khuff) that it be sturdy enough to allow continuous walking in it at places of descent, during dismounting and travelling, in the needs that one repeatedly goes about in the dwelling, and for the resident likewise, as is the custom of those who wear khuffs.
* *
The third issue: if the khuff is torn, there is a difference of opinion among the scholars regarding the permissibility of wiping over it. Malik and his companions held that if the torn part reveals an amount equal to a third of the foot, wiping over it is not permitted, and if it is less than that, wiping over it is permitted. They argued that the Law indicates that a third is the final limit of what is minor and the first limit of what is major.

Some scholars said: wiping over a khuff in which there is a tear through which some part of the foot shows is not permitted. This was the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Shafi'i in his later view (al-Jadid), and Ma'mar ibn Rashid.

(p-341) The proponents of this view argued that the exposed part of the foot has the ruling of washing, while the covered part has the ruling of wiping, and combining wiping and washing is not permitted. Just as it is not permitted for a person to wash one foot and wipe over the khuff of the other, it is likewise not permitted to wash part of the foot while wiping the khuff over the remainder of it.

Abu Hanifa and his companions held that a large tear prevents wiping over the khuff, but a small one does not. They defined a large tear as the size of three fingers.
It was said: of the small fingers of the foot; and it was said: of the fingers of the hand.

Some scholars said: wiping is permitted over all khuffs, even if they are torn extensively, as long as continuous walking in them is possible. Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted this from Sufyan al-Thawri, Ishaq, Yazid ibn Harun, and Abu Thawr.

Al-Bayhaqi narrated in al-Sunan al-Kubra from Sufyan al-Thawri that he said: "Wipe over them so long as they hold onto the foot, even if they are torn." He said: "And the khuffs of the Muhajirun and the Ansar were thus, torn and split." End of quotation.

Al-Bayhaqi said: "Ma'mar ibn Rashid's view on this is more beloved to us. This view which we mentioned from al-Thawri and those who agree with him is the choice of Shaykh Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyyah."

Ibn al-Mundhir said: "I say in accordance with the words of al-Thawri, due to the apparent general permission of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to wipe over the two khuffs, a general statement that includes all khuffs." End of quotation. al-Nawawi and others transmitted this from him, and it is strong.

From al-Awza'i: if some part of the foot appears, he wipes over his khuffs and over what appears of his foot. This is the summary of the scholars' statements on this issue.

The closest view to me is wiping over the torn khuff so long as the tear does not become excessive to the point of preventing continuous walking in it, based on the unrestricted texts, together with the fact that the khuffs of travellers and warriors are generally not free from tearing. And Allah the Exalted knows best.
* *
The fourth issue: scholars differed regarding the permissibility of wiping over sandals (na'layn). One group said wiping over sandals is permitted, while the majority of scholars disagreed. Those who permit wiping over sandals relied on hadiths, among them what Abu Dawud narrated in his Sunan: Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, from Waki', from Sufyan al-Thawri, from Abu Qays al-Awdi, who is Abd al-Rahman ibn Tharwan, from Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil, from al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah: "that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed ablution and wiped over the stockings (jawrabayn) and the sandals (na'layn)." Abu Dawud said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi would not narrate this hadith, because what is known from al-Mughirah is that "the Prophet ﷺ wiped over the two khuffs." Al-Bayhaqi also narrated this hadith.

Then he said: Abu Muhammad said: I saw Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj weaken this report, and Abu Qays al-Awdi and Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil cannot bear it, given their opposition to the great scholars who narrated this report from al-Mughirah, saying: "He wiped over the khuffs." He said: "We do not abandon the apparent meaning of the Qur'an for the likes of Abu Qays and Hudhayl." I mentioned this account from Muslim to Abu al-Abbas Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Daghuli, and I heard him say: Ali ibn Shayban said: I heard Abu Qudamah al-Sarakhsi say: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi said: I said to Sufyan al-Thawri: "If you narrated to me the hadith of Abu Qays from Hudhayl, I would not accept it from you." Sufyan said: "The hadith is weak, or baseless," or a word similar to that. End of quotation.

Al-Bayhaqi also narrated from Abd Allah ibn Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal that he said: "I narrated this hadith to my father, and my father said: 'This is not narrated except from the hadith of Abu Qays.' My father said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi says it is munkar (rejected).'" Al-Bayhaqi also narrated from Ali ibn al-Madini that he said: "The hadith of al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah regarding wiping was narrated from al-Mughirah by the people of Madinah, the people of Kufah, and the people of Basrah, and Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil narrated it from al-Mughirah, except that he said: 'and he wiped over the stockings,' and he opposed the people."

It is also narrated from Yahya ibn Ma'in that he said regarding this hadith: "All the people narrate it as 'over the khuffs' except Abu Qays." Then he also mentioned what we have already cited from Abu Dawud, that Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi would not narrate this hadith, because what is known from al-Mughirah is "that the Prophet ﷺ wiped over the two khuffs." Abu Dawud said: This hadith is also narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari from the Prophet ﷺ, but it is neither strong nor connected. Al-Bayhaqi explained Abu Dawud's meaning in describing it as not connected and not strong: its disconnection is because its narrator from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari is al-Dahhak ibn Abd al-Rahman, and al-Bayhaqi said: "The hearing of al-Dahhak ibn Abd al-Rahman from Abu Musa is not established. Its weakness is because its chain includes Isa ibn Sinan, and al-Bayhaqi said: 'Isa ibn Sinan is weak.'" End of quotation.

Ibn Hajar said of him in al-Taqrib: "weak in hadith" (layyin al-hadith). The opponents objected to weakening the aforementioned hadith about wiping over the stockings and sandals. They said: Abu Dawud narrated it and remained silent about it, and what he remains silent about is, at its lowest level in his view, acceptable (hasan). They said: Ibn Hibban authenticated it, and al-Tirmidhi said: "hasan sahih." They said: Abu Qays was deemed trustworthy by Ibn Ma'in, and al-Ijli said: "trustworthy and firm." Hudhayl was deemed trustworthy by al-Ijli, and al-Bukhari narrated from both of them in his Sahih. Furthermore, they did not oppose the people in a manner of contradiction; rather, they narrated an additional matter through an independent chain that does not contradict others, so it is taken to be two separate hadiths. They said: We do not accept that Dahhak ibn Abd al-Rahman did not hear from Abu Musa, because contemporaneity is sufficient for that, as Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj established in the introduction to his Sahih; and because Abd al-Ghani said in al-Kamal: "Dahhak heard from Abu Musa." They said: As for Isa ibn Sinan, Ibn Ma'in deemed him trustworthy and others deemed him weak, and al-Tirmidhi narrated in "al-Janaiz" a hadith with Isa ibn Sinan in its chain and graded it hasan.

The aforementioned hadith is also strengthened by what came in some narrations of the hadith of Ibn Umar, which is established in the Sahih: that Ubayd ibn Jurayj said to him: "O Abu Abd al-Rahman, I see you do four things which I have not seen any of your companions do." He said: "What are they?" So he mentioned them, and among them he said: "I see you wear the sabtiyyah sandals." He said: "As for the sabtiyyah sandals, I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wear sandals that have no hair on them and perform ablution in them, so I love to wear them."

Al-Bayhaqi said, after citing this hadith with its chain: It was narrated by al-Bukhari in the Sahih from Abd Allah ibn Yusuf from Malik; it was narrated by Muslim from Yahya ibn Yahya; and a group narrated it from Sa'id al-Maqbari; and Ibn Uyaynah narrated it from Ibn Ajlan from al-Maqbari, adding in it: "and he wipes over them"; and this is the point of evidence. Al-Bayhaqi said: This addition, although it is preserved, does not contradict washing them, for he may wash them while in the sandal and wipe over them.

The aforementioned argument for wiping over sandals is also strengthened by what al-Bayhaqi narrated with his chain from Zayd ibn Wahb, who said: "Ali urinated while standing, then performed ablution and wiped over the sandals." Then he said: With his chain: Sufyan narrated to us from Salamah ibn Kuhayl, from Abu Zabyan, who said: "Ali urinated while standing, then performed ablution and wiped over the sandals, then went out and prayed Zuhr." Al-Bayhaqi also narrated something similar from Abu Zabyan by another chain. The aforementioned argument is also strengthened by what al-Bayhaqi narrated through the route of Rawwad ibn al-Jarrah, from Sufyan, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ata ibn Yasar, from Ibn Abbas: "that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed ablution once once, and wiped over his sandals."

Then he said: Thus narrated Rawwad ibn al-Jarrah, and he is alone in narrating from al-Thawri with rejected reports, this being one of them, while the trustworthy narrators narrated from al-Thawri without this wording. It was also narrated from Zayd ibn al-Hubab from al-Thawri in this manner, but it is not preserved. Then he said: Abu al-Hasan ibn Abdan informed us, Sulayman ibn Ahmad al-Tabarani informed us, Ibrahim ibn Ahmad ibn Umar al-Wakili narrated to us, my father narrated to me, Zayd ibn al-Hubab narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, and he mentioned it with its chain: "that the Prophet ﷺ wiped over the sandals." End of quotation.

Al-Bayhaqi said after citing it: The correct report is that of the group. Abd al-Aziz al-Darawardi and Hisham ibn Sa'd narrated it from Zayd ibn Aslam, and they both related in the hadith: "a sprinkling on the foot while the sandal was on it," and this may mean that he washed it while in the sandal. Sulayman ibn Bilal, Muhammad ibn Ajlan, Warqa' ibn Umar, and Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn Abi Kathir narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, and they related in the hadith his washing of his two feet, and the hadith is one hadith. A large number is more worthy of preservation than a small number, together with the superiority of the memory of one who preserved the washing after the sprinkling over one who did not preserve it. The aforementioned argument is also strengthened by what al-Bayhaqi also narrated: Abu Ali al-Rudhbari informed us, Abu Bakr ibn Dasah informed us, Abu Dawud narrated to us, Musaddad and Abbad ibn Musa narrated to us, both saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from Ya'la ibn Ata, from his father, Abbad said: he said: Aws ibn Abi Aws al-Thaqafi informed me, he said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ perform ablution and wipe over his sandals and feet."

Musaddad said: "that he saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." Hammad ibn Salamah narrated it from Ya'la ibn Ata, from Aws al-Thaqafi: "that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed ablution and wiped over his sandals," and it is mursal (disconnected). Abu Bakr ibn Furak informed us, Abd Allah ibn Ja'far informed us, Yunus ibn Habib narrated to us, Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, and he mentioned it.

This chain is not strong, and it bears the same possibility as the first hadith. End of al-Bayhaqi's statement.

It is not hidden that the summary of this is that among the hadiths on wiping over sandals, some are weak and cannot be used as evidence, (p-345) and others whose meaning, in his view, is: "that he ﷺ washed his feet in the sandals."

Then al-Bayhaqi argued that the intended meaning of "ablution in the sandals" is washing the two feet while in them, based on the hadith of Ibn Umar, established in the two Sahihs, that he said: "As for the sabtiyyah sandals, I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wear sandals that have no hair on them, and perform ablution in them, so I love to wear them." End of quotation.

Al-Bayhaqi's meaning is that the sense of Ibn Umar's words "and he performs ablution" in them is that he washes his feet in them. You have already learned that we cited the report of Ibn Uyaynah, which al-Bayhaqi mentioned from Ibn Ajlan, from al-Maqbari, and in it is the addition "and he wipes over them."

Al-Bayhaqi, may Allah have mercy on him, said regarding the prohibition of wiping over sandals and stockings: "The basic principle is the obligation of washing the two feet, except what is specified by an established Sunnah or a consensus about which there is no disagreement; and neither of them, sandals or stockings, has any such evidence." End of quotation.

And it is answered from the side of those who differ: the wiping over the *jawrabayn* (thick socks) and the *na'layn* (sandals) is established from the Prophet ﷺ. They say: al-Tirmidhi authenticated (*sahhaha*) wiping over the socks and sandals, and graded it *hasan* (good) through the narration of Hudhayl from al-Mughirah. He also graded it *hasan* through the narration of al-Dahhak from Abu Musa. Ibn Hibban authenticated wiping over the sandals through the narration of Aws. Ibn Khuzaymah authenticated the hadith of Ibn Umar concerning wiping over the *sabtiyyah* sandals (sandals of tanned leather).

They say: what al-Bayhaqi related through the narration of Zayd ibn al-Hubab, from al-Thawri, concerning wiping over the sandals, is a *jayyid* (sound) hadith. They say: al-Bazzar related from Ibn Umar that he used to perform ablution while his sandals were on his feet, and he would wipe over them, and he would say: "Thus the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to do." Ibn al-Qattan authenticated it.

Ibn Hazm said: the prohibition of wiping over the socks is an error, because it contradicts the established Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and contradicts the reports (*athar*). This is the summary of what has come concerning wiping over the sandals and the socks.

The author of this commentary (may Allah pardon him) says: If by wiping over the sandals and the socks is meant that the socks are attached to the sandals, such that the combined whole covers the place of the obligatory washing while it is still possible to walk continuously in it, and the socks are thick, then there is no difficulty.

But if what is meant is wiping over the sandals on their own, then there is something troubling in the soul about it, because in that case he has not washed his foot, nor has he wiped over a covering for it. So he has not performed the original (*asl*) nor the substitute (*badal*).

Wiping over the foot itself is rejected by the authentic hadiths that explicitly prohibit that in abundance, such as his ﷺ saying: "Woe to the heels from the Fire." And Allah the Most High knows best.

* *

The fifth issue: the scholars differed regarding the time limit (*tawqit*) for wiping over the leather socks (*khuffayn*).

The majority of scholars held that the time limit for wiping is one day and one night for the resident (*muqim*), and three days with their nights for the traveller (*musafir*).

To this view went the Four Imams: Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and their companions. It is also the view of al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Abu Thawr, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Dawud al-Zahiri, Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari, and al-Hasan ibn Salih ibn Husayn.

Among the Companions who held it: Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Hudhayfah, al-Mughirah, and Abu Zayd al-Ansari. It is also related from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and from all of them.

Among the Successors who held it: Shurayh the judge, Ata ibn Abi Rabah, al-Sha'bi, and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz.

Abu Umar ibn Abd al-Barr said: most of the Successors and jurists hold this.

Abu Isa al-Tirmidhi said: the time limit of three days for the traveller and one day and night for the resident is the view of the general body of scholars among the Companions, the Successors, and those after them.

al-Khattabi said: the time limit is the view of the general body of jurists, as al-Nawawi reported.

The proof of those who hold the time limit is the hadiths reported concerning it. Among them is the hadith of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "For the traveller three days and their nights, and for the resident one day and a night." It was related by Muslim, Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and Ibn (p-347) Hibban.

Among them also is the hadith of Abu Bakrah from the Prophet ﷺ: that he granted a concession to the traveller of three days and their nights, and to the resident one day and a night, when he has purified himself and put on his two khuffs, that he may wipe over them. It was related by Ibn Khuzaymah, al-Daraqutni, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Hibban, al-Bayhaqi, al-Tirmidhi in *al-'Ilal*, al-Shafi'i, Ibn al-Jarud, and al-Athram in his *Sunan*. al-Khattabi, Ibn Khuzaymah, and others authenticated it.

Among them also is the hadith of Safwan ibn Assal al-Muradi, who said: "He (meaning the Prophet ﷺ) commanded us to wipe over the khuffs when we have put them on in a state of purity: three days if we are travelling, and one day and a night if we are resident, and we are not to remove them because of defecation, urination, or sleep, and we are not to remove them except because of major impurity (*janabah*)." It was related by Imam Ahmad, Ibn Khuzaymah, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Shafi'i, Ibn Hibban, al-Daraqutni, and al-Bayhaqi, and al-Tirmidhi and others graded it sound.

Al-Shawkani said in *Nayl al-Awtar*: al-Tirmidhi related from al-Bukhari that it is a *hasan* hadith, and its transmission centres on Asim ibn Abi al-Nujud, who is truthful but weak in memory. A group has followed him, and more than forty persons related from him, as Ibn Mandah said. End of quotation.

A group of scholars held that there is no time limit for wiping, and they said: whoever puts on his khuffs while in a state of purity wipes over them as long as he wishes, and he is not obliged to remove them except because of major impurity.

Among those who held this view: Malik and his companions, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, and al-Hasan al-Basri.

It is related from Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman, al-Sha'bi, and Rabi'ah, and it is the old view (*qawl qadim*) of al-Shafi'i. It is also related from Umar ibn al-Khattab, his son Abd Allah, and Uqbah ibn Amir, may Allah be pleased with them all.

The proof of those who hold this view is what al-Hakim related with a sound chain from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ: "When one of you performs ablution and puts on his khuffs, let him wipe over them and pray in them, and let him not remove them, if he wishes, except because of major impurity or the like." al-Daraqutni also related it.

This sound hadith which al-Hakim and others related is strengthened by what al-Daraqutni related from Maymunah bint al-Harith al-Hilaliyyah, wife of the Prophet ﷺ, concerning the absence of a time limit.

(p-348) It is also supported by what Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, and Ibn Hibban related from Khuzaymah ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with him, that he added to the hadith of the time limit words whose wording is: "If we had asked him for more, he would have given us more." In another wording: "If the questioner had persisted in his question, he would have made it five," meaning the nights of the time limit for wiping.

The hadith of Khuzaymah in which this addition occurs was authenticated by Ibn Ma'in, Ibn Hibban, and others. By this you know that the claim of al-Nawawi in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab* that there is consensus on its weakness is not correct.

As for al-Bukhari's statement, may Allah have mercy on him, that it is not sound in his view because the transmission of al-Jadali from Khuzaymah is not known to have had direct hearing (*sama'*), it is based on his condition, which is the establishment of meeting (*liqa'*).

Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, may Allah have mercy on him, has clarified in the introduction to his *Sahih* that the truth is to be satisfied with the possibility of meeting, when contemporaneity is established, and this is the view of the majority of scholars.

If it is said: in the hadith of Khuzaymah in which the addition is found, he conjectured (*zanna*) that if the Prophet ﷺ had been asked for more, he would have given more; and others related it without making this conjecture; and there is no proof in a Companion's conjecture when another has differed from him in it.

The answer: Khuzaymah is the one of the two testimonies (*dhu al-shahadatayn*), whom the Prophet ﷺ made equal to two witnesses; his uprightness and truthfulness prevent him from affirming that if he had been asked for more, he would have given more, unless he knew that the matter was so, through other matters which he was aware of and which others were not aware of.

Among what supports the absence of a time limit is what Abu Dawud related, and he said: it is not strong, from Ubayy ibn Umarah, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall I wipe over the khuffs? He said: Yes. He said: For a day? He said: Yes. He said: And two days? He said: Yes. He said: And three days? He said: Yes, and as long as you wish."

This hadith, although it cannot serve as an independent proof, is fit to strengthen others among the hadiths we have mentioned.

So the hadith of Anas concerning the absence of a time limit is sound, and it is strengthened by the hadith of Khuzaymah in which the addition occurs, the hadith of Maymunah, the hadith of Ubayy ibn Umarah, and the reports stopping at Umar, his son, and Uqbah ibn Amir, may Allah be pleased with them.

Note (tanbih)

What appears to me, and Allah the Most High knows best, is that it is not possible to reconcile these hadiths by taking the absolute (*mutlaq*) to qualify the restricted (*muqayyad*), because the absolute here contains an explicit permission to wipe more than three days for the traveller and the resident, while the restricted contains an explicit prohibition of exceeding the three days for the traveller and the day and night for the resident. So they conflict regarding that excess: the absolute explicitly permits it, and the restricted explicitly prohibits it. Therefore it is necessary to weigh the evidences against each other. The evidences for the time limit are preferred on the grounds that they are more cautious, as Ibn Abd al-Barr preferred them on this basis; on the grounds that their transmitters among the Companions are more numerous; and on the grounds that among them is what is established in the *Sahih* of Muslim, namely the hadith of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned earlier.

The evidences for the absence of a time limit are preferred on the grounds that they contain an addition, and the addition of a trustworthy transmitter is accepted; and on the grounds that those who hold it affirm a matter, while those who prevent it negate it, and the affirmation takes precedence over the negation.

The author of this commentary (may Allah pardon him) says: The self inclines more toward preferring the time limit, because leaving the disagreement is more cautious, as some scholars have said:

*[Rajaz meter]*
"Indeed, the most scrupulous one is he who leaves their disagreement, even if it is weak, so discern this."

And another said:

*[Rajaz meter]*
"One who is cautious in the matters of religion flees from doubt into certainty."

The confirmation of this is in his ﷺ saying: "Leave what makes you doubtful for what does not make you doubtful."

So the one who acts on the evidences of the time limit has a valid purification by the agreement of both groups, unlike the other, for one of the two groups says that it is invalid after the stipulated period. And Allah the Most High knows best.

Know that those who hold the time limit differed concerning when the period of wiping begins.

Al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and his companions, Ahmad in the more sound of his two reports, Sufyan al-Thawri, Dawud in the more sound of his two reports, and others, held that the beginning of the time limit is from the first invalidator (*hadath*) that occurs after putting on the khuff. This is the view of the majority of scholars.

Those who hold this view took as evidence an addition which the memorizer (*al-hafiz*) al-Qasim ibn Zakariyya al-Mutarriz related in the hadith of Safwan: "from the invalidator to the invalidator."

Al-Nawawi said in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*: this is a strange addition and is not established.

They also argued by analogy (*qiyas*), that wiping is a time-bound act of worship, so the beginning of its time is from the moment its performance becomes permissible, by analogy with prayer.

(p-350) A group of scholars held that the period begins from the moment one wipes after the invalidator.

Among those who held this: al-Awza'i, Abu Thawr, one of the two reports from Ahmad, and Dawud. al-Nawawi preferred this view, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it. Something similar is related from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.

Those who hold this view argued from the hadiths of the time limit in wiping, which are sound hadiths.

The way they argue from them is that his ﷺ saying: "The traveller wipes for three days" is explicit that the three days are entirely a period (*zarf*) for the wiping.

This is not realised except if the beginning of the period is from the wiping. This is, as it appears to me, the view best supported by evidence, and Allah the Most High knows best.

There is a third view on the matter, namely that the beginning of the period is from the moment of putting on the khuff. It was reported by al-Mawardi and al-Shashi from al-Hasan al-Basri, as al-Nawawi said. And Allah the Most High knows best.

* *

The sixth issue: the scholars differed: is it sufficient to wipe the upper surface of the khuff, or must both its upper and under surfaces be wiped?

A group of scholars held that it is sufficient to wipe its upper surface.

Among those who held this: Abu Hanifah, Ahmad, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i. Ibn al-Mundhir related it from al-Hasan, Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Ata, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, and others.

The more sound of the reports from Ahmad is that what is obligatory is wiping most of the upper surface of the khuff. Abu Hanifah holds that wiping an amount equal to three fingers from the upper surface of the khuff is sufficient.

The proof of those who restricted themselves to wiping the upper surface of the khuff and not its underside is the hadith of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "Had religion been by opinion, the underside of the khuff would have been more deserving of wiping than its upper side. Indeed I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wiping over the upper surface of his two khuffs." It was related by Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni.

Ibn Hajar said in *Bulugh al-Maram*: its chain is *hasan*.

And in *al-Talkhis* he said: its chain is sound.

(p-351) Know that this hadith is not discredited by the fact that its chain includes ʿAbd Khayr ibn Yazid al-Hamdani, nor by al-Bayhaqi's statement: "The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) did not take as evidence ʿAbd Khayr mentioned," end quote. For ʿAbd Khayr mentioned is a trustworthy (thiqah) mukhadram, well known; it has been said that he was a Companion (sahabi).

The correct view is that he is a mukhadram (one who lived through both the Jahiliyyah and Islam). Yahya ibn Maʿin and al-ʿIjli declared him trustworthy. Ibn Hajar said of him in al-Taqrib: "A mukhadram, trustworthy, of the second tabaqah (generation), whose companionship (suhbah) is not authenticated."

As for the fact that the two Shaykhs did not record him, this is not a flaw in him by the consensus of the scholars. How many trustworthy and upright narrators have not been recorded by the two Shaykhs!

Imam al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, held that the obligatory requirement is to wipe the least part of the upper surface, and that wiping the lower surface is recommended.

Imam Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, held that it is required to wipe both the upper and lower surfaces together. If one suffices with the upper surface, he must repeat (the prayer) within the time, but does not repeat it permanently; if one suffices with the lower surface, he repeats it permanently.

It is also reported from Malik that wiping the upper surface is obligatory and wiping the lower surface is recommended (mandub).

Those who say that both the upper surface and the lower surface of the khuff must be wiped rely on what Thawr ibn Yazid narrated from Rajaʾ ibn Haywah, from Warrad, the scribe of al-Mughirah ibn Shuʿbah, from al-Mughirah ibn Shuʿbah: "The Prophet ﷺ wiped the upper surface of the khuff and its lower surface." It was recorded by Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni, al-Bayhaqi, and Ibn al-Jarud.

Al-Tirmidhi said: "This hadith is mu'allal (has a hidden defect). No one transmitted it from Thawr except al-Walid ibn Muslim. I asked Abu Zurʿah and Muhammad (al-Bukhari) about this hadith, and they both said: 'It is not authentic.'" There is no doubt that this hadith is weak.

Malik argued for wiping the lower surface of the khuff by the practice of ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.

* *

The seventh issue: The scholars have agreed that purification with water is a condition for wiping over the khuffs, and that whoever puts them on while in a state of minor impurity (muhdith), or after tayammum, is not permitted to wipe over them.

They differed regarding whether complete purification is a condition, as in the case of one who washed his right foot and put it into the khuff before washing his left foot, then washed his left foot and put it into the khuff too; is it permissible for him to wipe over the two khuffs if he becomes impure after that?

(p-352) A group of scholars held that complete purification is a condition, and they said in the aforementioned case: it is not permitted for him to wipe, because he put on one of the two khuffs before completing purification. Among those who said this are al-Shafiʿi and his companions, Malik and his companions, Ishaq, and it is the more sound of the two reports from Ahmad.

Those who held this view relied on the hadiths that stipulate purification as a condition for wiping over the two khuffs, such as the hadith of al-Mughirah ibn Shuʿbah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Leave them, for I put them on in a state of purity," and he wiped over them. Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim). And in Abu Dawud, from him, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Leave the two khuffs, for I put my feet into the khuffs while they were pure," and he wiped over them.

And from Abu Hurayrah in Ahmad, that he ﷺ said to him, when he alerted him that he had not washed his feet: "I put them in while they were pure."

And in the hadith of Safwan ibn ʿAssal mentioned earlier: "He commanded us to wipe over the khuffs when we put them on in a state of purity," and other hadiths besides these.

They also said: incomplete purification is like no purification.

A group of scholars held that complete purification is not a condition at the time of putting on the khuff, so they permitted putting on the khuff of the right foot before the left and wiping over it, if one becomes impure after that, because purification was completed after putting on the khuff.

They said: continuation is like initiation (al-dawam ka'l-ibtida'). Among those who said this view are Imam Abu Hanifah, Sufyan al-Thawri, Yahya ibn Adam, al-Muzani, and Dawud. Ibn al-Mundhir chose this view, as stated by al-Nawawi.

The author, may Allah pardon him, said: The source of disagreement in this issue is a disputed principle: "Does impurity (hadath) lift from each limb of the limbs of wudu' merely by washing it, or does impurity not lift from any of them except by completing wudu'?" The more apparent of the two, in my view, is that impurity is a meaning that does not divide or become partial, so no part of it is lifted; and that before completing wudu' one is still in a state of impurity, and the khuff, for wiping over it, must be put on while not in a state of impurity. And Allah the Exalted knows best. End quote.

* *

Notice
The majority of scholars hold that intention (niyyah) is a condition in wudu' and ghusl, because they are acts of worship (qurbah), and the Prophet ﷺ (p-353) said: "Actions are only by intentions." Abu Hanifah disagreed, saying that purification from minor impurity does not require intention, like purification from impurity (khabath).

The scholars also differed concerning the limit (ghayah) in His saying: ﴿to the elbows﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], whether it is included, so that washing the elbows is obligatory in wudu', which is the position of the majority; or whether it is excluded, so washing the elbows is not obligatory in it?

The truth is that intention is a condition and washing the elbows is obligatory, and Allah the Exalted knows best.

The scholars also differed concerning wiping the head in wudu', whether it is obligatory to wipe all of it. Malik, Ahmad, and a group said it is obligatory to wipe all of it, and there is no doubt that this is the more cautious way of discharging the obligation of wiping. Al-Shafiʿi and Abu Hanifah said that wiping all of it is not obligatory.

They differed on the sufficient amount. From al-Shafiʿi: the least that is called wiping suffices. From Abu Hanifah: a quarter. From some: a third. From some: two-thirds. It is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he wiped over the turban (ʿimamah), and the Malikis interpreted this as applying when removing it would cause harm, whereas the apparent evidence is general.

It is also established from him ﷺ that he wiped over the forelock (nasiyah) and the turban, but there is no basis for using this as evidence for sufficing with the forelock alone, because it is not reported that he ﷺ sufficed with it; rather he wiped over it together with the turban. Thus three states are established regarding wiping the head: wiping the head itself, wiping over the turban, and combining both by wiping the forelock and the turban.

The apparent indication of the evidence is the permissibility of all three states mentioned, and Allah the Exalted knows best.

What we have previously quoted regarding the consensus that wiping over the khuff does not suffice with tayammum, although there is some disagreement on it as will come, is because its weakness is, in our view, as nothing. Let us suffice with what we have mentioned of the rulings of this noble verse, lest the discussion become lengthy.

* *

His saying the Exalted: ﴿So perform tayammum with clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it﴾, the verse. Know that the particle "min" (from) in this noble verse is ambiguous: it may be partitive (lil-tab'id), in which case the earth used for tayammum must be dust that clings to the hand; and it may be for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), meaning the starting point of that wiping is from the clean earth, so it is not specified that it must have dust. The first was said by al-Shafiʿi (p-354) and Ahmad, and the second by Malik and Abu Hanifah, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on them all.

Having known this, know that in this noble verse there is an indication of this last view, namely in His saying the Exalted: ﴿Allah does not want to place upon you any hardship﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. His saying "min ḥaraj" (hardship) is an indefinite noun in a context of negation, with "min" added before it, and an indefinite noun in such a context is explicit in generality, as established in the principles of jurisprudence. In Marāqī al-Suʿūd, he said, coordinating with the forms of generality: [Rajaz]
"In a context of negation, among them is mentioned what is constructed or what has min added to an indefinite."

So the verse indicates the generality of negation over every kind of hardship, and what is appropriate to this is that "min" is for the beginning of the limit, because most lands contain nothing but sand or mountains, so obligating only what has dust clinging to the hand involves some hardship.

This is confirmed by what al-Shaykhan (Bukhari and Muslim) recorded in their two Sahihs from the hadith of Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I have been given five things that no one before me was given: I was made victorious through terror for a month's journey; the earth was made for me a place of prostration (masjid) and a means of purification (tahur); so whichever man of my nation the prayer reaches, let him pray." And in another wording: "Then his place of prostration and his purification are with him," the hadith.

This is an authentic and explicit text that whoever is reached by the prayer in a place where there is nothing but mountains or sand, that clean earth, which is stone or sand, is a means of purification (tahur) for him and a place of prostration. By this you know that what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, that it is necessarily partitive, is not correct. If it is said: the Sahih contains what indicates that the dust that clings to the hand is specified, to the exclusion of other kinds of earth, for Muslim recorded in his Sahih from the hadith of Hudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "We have been favored over people with three things: our rows were made like the rows of the angels, the whole earth was made a place of prostration for us, and its soil was made a means of purification for us when we do not find water," the hadith. So the restriction of purification to soil in a context of favor implies that other earth is not like that. The answer comes in three aspects:

First: that a matter mentioned in the context of favor prevents the consideration of the concept of opposition (mafhum al-mukhalafah), as established in the principles. In Marāqī al-Suʿūd, among the impediments to considering mafhum al-mukhalafah: [Rajaz] (p-355)
"Or a favor, or conformity to reality, or ignorance, or emphasis in the hearer's view."

For this reason the scholars agreed on the permissibility of eating dried fish (qadid min al-hut), although Allah specified fresh flesh from it in His saying: ﴿And it is He who subjected the sea that you might eat from it fresh flesh﴾ [al-Nahl: 14]; because He mentioned fresh flesh in the context of favor, so there is no opposition-concept for it, and thus eating dried fish from what is in the sea is permitted.

Second: that the concept of "soil" is a concept of title (mafhum laqab), and it is not considered by the majority of scholars, and this is the truth, as is well known in the principles.

Third: that soil is one individual of the kinds of clean earth (sa'id), and mentioning some individuals of a general term with the general ruling does not specify it according to the majority, whether both are mentioned in a single text, like His saying: ﴿Guard the prayers and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238], or mentioned in two texts, like the hadith "Any hide that is tanned has become pure," according to Ahmad, Muslim, Ibn Majah, al-Tirmidhi and others, together with the hadith "Why did you not benefit from its hide?" referring to a dead sheep, according to the two Shaykhs, both from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas. Thus the mention of the middle prayer in the first, and the hide of the sheep in the second, does not imply that other prayers in the first, or other hides in the second, are not like that. Said in Marāqī al-Suʿūd, coordinating with what generality is not specified by: [Rajaz]
"The mention of what agrees with it from a single instance, and the view of the narrator according to the relied-upon opinion."

None dissented on the non-specification by mentioning some individuals of a general term with its ruling except Abu Thawr, who argued that there is no benefit in mentioning it except specification. It was answered by the majority that the concept of title is not a proof, and the benefit of mentioning a part is to negate the possibility of its exclusion from the general term.

The word "al-sa'id" (ṣaʿīd) linguistically means the surface of the earth, whether or not it has soil on it, as said by al-Khalil, Ibn al-A'rabi, and al-Zajjaj. Al-Zajjaj said: I know of no disagreement among the people of language about it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed We will make what is upon it a barren, dry ṣaʿīd﴾ [al-Kahf: 8], meaning hard earth that produces nothing; and He said: ﴿So it becomes a slippery ṣaʿīd﴾ [al-Kahf: 40]. From it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah: [Basit]
"As if, in the forenoon, the ṣaʿīd casts at it a beetle-like creature, a proboscis in the bones of the head."

(p-356) It is called ṣaʿīd only because it is the extremity to which one ascends from the earth. Its plural is ṣuʿudāt by irregular analogy, and from it is the hadith: "Beware of sitting in the ṣuʿudāt (roadside/open ground)," as al-Qurtubi and others reported from him.

The scholars differed concerning it because of the restriction to "good" (ṭayyib). One group said: "ṭayyib" means pure (ṭāhir), so tayammum (dry ablution) is permissible with the entire surface of the earth, whether it is dust, sand, stones, a mineral, or saline soil, provided that it is pure. This is the position of Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Thawrī, and others.

Another group said: ṭayyib means lawful (ḥalāl), so tayammum is not permissible with dust that has been usurped. al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Yūsuf said: aṣ-ṣaʿīd aṭ-ṭayyib (the good surface) is fertile dust (at-turāb al-munbit), based on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And the good land, its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 58].

Having understood this, know that the matter has a middle ground and two extremes. One extreme is that all Muslims agreed on the permissibility of tayammum with it, namely pure fertile dust that is not moved from its place and is not usurped. The other extreme is that all Muslims agreed on the prohibition of tayammum with it, namely pure gold and silver, rubies and emeralds, foods such as bread and meat and others, and impurities. What lies between these is the middle ground on which the scholars differed. Among these is minerals (maʿādin).

Some permit tayammum upon them, like Mālik, and some prohibit it, like al-Shāfiʿī. Among them is grass (ḥashīsh). Ibn Khuwayz Mindād transmitted from Mālik that he permits tayammum upon grass when it is growing from the earth, whereas the well-known position of Mālik is prohibition. Among them is tayammum upon snow. It is transmitted from Mālik in al-Mudawwana and al-Mabsūṭ that its use is permissible. It was said: unrestrictedly; and it was said: only when no earth is available. In other works he prohibited it.

It has also been reported from him concerning tayammum upon wood, and the majority are of the view of prohibition. In Mukhtaṣar al-Waqqār it is stated that it is permissible. It was said: it is permissible with wood attached to the ground, but not with wood detached from it. al-Thaʿlabī mentioned that Mālik said: "If he strikes his hand upon a tree, then wipes with it, it suffices him." He said: al-Awzāʿī and al-Thawrī said: it is permissible with the earth and everything upon it of trees, stones, clods, and others, to the extent that they said: "If he strikes his hand upon ice or frozen snow, it suffices him."

al-Thaʿlabī mentioned from Abū Ḥanīfa that he permits it with kohl, orpiment, depilatory lime (nūra), plaster, and powdered gems, and prohibits it with the filings of gold, silver, copper, and lead, because (p-357) that is not of the same kind as earth.

an-Naqqāsh mentioned from Ibn ʿUlayya and Ibn Kaysān that both of them permitted it with musk and saffron. Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejected this view. Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh prohibited it with saline soil (sibākh). The same is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās. It is also reported from him concerning one who finds himself in mud, that he smears part of his body with it, and when it dries he performs tayammum with it. al-Qurṭubī reported this.

As for dust transported in a tray or other container, tayammum with it is permissible according to the well-known position of Mālik, which is the view of the majority of the Mālikīs, and the position of al-Shāfiʿī and his companions. Some Mālikīs and a group of scholars prohibit it.

Whatever has been fired, such as plaster and bricks, there is also a difference of opinion among the Mālikīs concerning it, and prohibition is more well known.

They also differed concerning tayammum upon a wall. It was said: it is permissible unrestrictedly. It was said: it is prohibited unrestrictedly. It was said: it is permissible for the sick only and not for others. The hadith of Abū Juhaym, which is coming, indicates permissibility unrestrictedly.

The apparent meaning is that its place is where the outer surface of the wall is of the types of the surface (ṣaʿīd). The well-known position of Mālik is the permissibility of tayammum upon minerals other than gold and silver, as long as they are not moved; its permissibility upon unprocessed salt; and its prohibition upon trees, reeds, and the like. Aḥmad, al-Shāfiʿī, and al-Thawrī permitted it upon felt, cushions, and the like, when there is dust upon them.

Tayammum linguistically means intention (al-qaṣd). One says "tayammamtu ash-shay'" meaning "I intended it," and "tayammamtu aṣ-ṣaʿīd" meaning "I deliberately aimed at it." al-Khalīl cited the verse of ʿĀmir ibn Mālik, the one who plays with spear-points:

"I aimed the spear at him sideways, then I said to him: 'This is bravery, not the play of the playful.'"

And from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"She aimed for the spring near Ḍārij, over which shade falls, and its moss is thick."

And the saying of Aʿshā Bāhila:

"I aimed for Qays, and how many a land lies beyond him, of a desert with a dangerous stretch."

And the saying of Ḥumayd ibn Thawr:

"Ask the campsite where Umm Ṭāriq aimed, and is it the habit of a campsite to speak?"

(p-358) In the sharīʿa, tayammum is the intention toward pure ṣaʿīd to wipe the face and both hands with it, with the intention of making the prayer permissible, when water is absent or one is unable to use it. That tayammum means intention indicates that intention is a condition of tayammum, and this is the truth.

* *

Issues concerning the rulings of tayammum

First issue: None of all the Muslims has disagreed about tayammum for the minor ritual impurity (ḥadath aṣghar), and likewise for the major ritual impurity (ḥadath akbar), except what is reported from ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿūd, and Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī among the Successors, that they prohibited it for the major impurity.

an-Nawawī, in Sharḥ al-Muhadhdhab, transmitted from Ibn aṣ-Ṣabbāgh and others the view that ʿUmar and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd returned from that position. The one who prohibited tayammum for the major impurity argued that the verse on women does not permit it except for one with the minor impurity, where Allah says: ﴿Or if any of you comes from the toilet, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then perform tayammum with clean earth﴾ [an-Nisāʾ: 43]. The rejection of this argument is from three aspects:

First: We do not concede that the major impurity is not mentioned in the verse on women, because His saying: ﴿or you have touched women﴾ [an-Nisāʾ: 43] was explained by the interpreter of the Qur'an, Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, as meaning intercourse. Accordingly, mentioning tayammum after intercourse, expressed by "touching" or "contact" depending on the two readings, and "coming from the toilet," is evidence that tayammum includes both states, the major and the minor impurity.

Second: In Sūrat al-Māʾida, Allah explicitly mentioned janāba (major impurity) without expressing it by "contact," and then mentioned tayammum after it. This indicates that it applies to it as well, where He says: ﴿O you who believe, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, and wipe your heads and your feet up to the ankles, and if you are in janāba, then purify yourselves﴾ [al-Māʾida: 6], then He said: ﴿and if you find no water, then perform tayammum﴾ [al-Māʾida: 6]. So it refers to the one with minor impurity and the one in janāba together, as is evident.

Third: His ﷺ statement to that effect, which is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ. The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhārī and Muslim) recorded in their two Ṣaḥīḥs from ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "I became junub and did not find water, so I rolled myself in the earth and prayed. I mentioned that to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: 'It would have sufficed you to do just this,' and the Prophet ﷺ struck the earth with his palms, blew into them, then wiped with them his face and his hands."

And both of them also recorded in their two Ṣaḥīḥs from the hadith of ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a journey, and he led the people in prayer. Then they saw a man standing apart, and he said: 'What prevented you from praying?' He said: 'I have become junub and there is no water.' He said: 'Upon you is the earth, for it will suffice you.'"

The hadiths on this subject are numerous.

* *

Second issue: The scholars differed on whether one strike suffices for tayammum or not. A group said: one strike suffices for both palms and the face. Among those who held this view were Imam Aḥmad, ʿAṭāʾ, Makḥūl, al-Awzāʿī, and Isḥāq. Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted it from the majority of scholars and chose it, and it is the view of the general body of the people of ḥadīth. Its evidence is the hadith of ʿAmmār, agreed upon, mentioned above.

Most jurists went to the view that two strikes are necessary: one for the face and the other for the two palms. Some of them said the second is obligatory, and some said it is recommended (sunna), as Mālik held. Ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Shihāb, and Ibn Sīrīn held that the obligatory is three strikes: one for the face, one for the two hands, and one for the two forearms.

The one who compiled this work, may Allah pardon him, says: The apparent position from the standpoint of the evidence is sufficiency with one strike, because nothing has been authentically established from the hadiths on this subject as a marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ) except the hadith of ʿAmmār mentioned earlier, and the hadith of Abū Juhaym ibn al-Ḥārith ibn aṣ-Ṣimma al-Anṣārī, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came from the direction of Biʾr Jamal, and a man met him, and greeted him with salam, but the Prophet ﷺ did not return the greeting until he turned toward a wall, wiped his face and his hands, then returned the salam to him." It was recorded by al-Bukhārī as a connected (mawṣūl) hadith and by Muslim as a suspended (taʿlīq) report. Neither of them contains anything indicating that these are two strikes, as you have seen. The hadith of ʿAmmār has shown that it is one.

* *

Third issue: Is it obligatory in tayammum to wipe anything other than the two palms? The scholars differed on this. Some made it obligatory to wipe up to the elbows in tayammum. Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī and their companions, ath-Thawrī, Ibn Abī Salama, and al-Layth said so; all of them hold that reaching the elbows in tayammum is an obligatory duty. Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam, Ibn Nāfiʿ, and Ismāʿīl al-Qāḍī also held this.

(p-360) Ibn Nāfiʿ said: "Whoever performs tayammum only to the two wrist-joints must repeat the prayer forever." Mālik said in al-Mudawwana: "He repeats it within the time." It was transmitted as a marfūʿ report that tayammum is to the elbows, from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, Ibn ʿUmar, Abū Umāma, ʿĀ'isha, ʿAmmār, and al-Aslaʿ. The critical remarks on the chains of their narrations will come, if Allah the Exalted wills. Ibn ʿUmar used to act accordingly. Ibn Shihāb said: one wipes up to the armpits in tayammum.

Those who held tayammum to the elbows argued with what was reported from those we mentioned concerning the elbows, and that Ibn ʿUmar used to do it, and by analogy to ablution, in which Allah said: ﴿and your hands up to the elbows﴾.

The one who compiled this work, may Allah pardon him, says: What appears from the evidences, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is that what is obligatory in tayammum is wiping the two palms only, because of what we have previously stated: that none of the hadiths describing the manner of tayammum has been established as authentically attributed to the Prophet ﷺ except the hadith of ʿAmmār and the hadith of Abū Juhaym, mentioned above.

As for the hadith of Abū Juhaym, it mentions the two hands only in general terms, as you have seen. As for the hadith of ʿAmmār, it mentions the two palms in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, as we have stated. It came in other than them with mention of the elbows, and in one narration up to half the forearm, and in another narration up to the armpits. As for the narration of the elbows and half the forearm, there is criticism of them that will come. As for the narration of the armpits, ash-Shāfiʿī and others said: If that occurred by the command of the Prophet ﷺ, then every tayammum performed by the Prophet ﷺ after it abrogates (nāsikh) it; and if it occurred without his command, then the proof is in what he commanded. What strengthens the narration of the two Ṣaḥīḥs in limiting it to the face and the two palms is that ʿAmmār used to give this ruling after the Prophet ﷺ, and the narrator of a hadith knows its meaning better than others, especially a companion who is a mujtahid. Ibn Ḥajar said this in al-Fatḥ.

As for the action of Ibn ʿUmar, it has not been established as attributed (marfūʿ) to the Prophet ﷺ, and a mawqūf report (one ending with a companion) cannot be set against an agreed-upon marfūʿ hadith, which is the hadith of ʿAmmār.

Abū Dāwūd recorded from Ibn ʿUmar, with a weak chain, that he said: "A man passed by the Prophet ﷺ in one of the lanes, having just come out from defecating or urinating, and he greeted him with salam, but he did not return it until the man was nearly hidden in the lanes. Then he struck the wall with his hand, wiped his face with it, then struck a second strike and wiped his forearms with it." The hadith turns on Muḥammad ibn Thābit, and Ibn Maʿīn, Aḥmad, al-Bukhārī, and Abū Ḥātim declared him weak. Aḥmad and al-Bukhārī said: "The hadith of tayammum is criticized from him." That is, this (p-361) hadith. al-Bukhārī added: "Ayyūb, ʿUbayd Allāh, and the people opposed him, and they said, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, that he did it."

Abu Dawud said: No one else narrated this story from Muhammad ibn Thabit in the form of two strikes from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Rather, they narrated it as the action of Ibn Umar. Al-Khattabi said: It is not authentic, because Muhammad ibn Thabit is extremely weak. This Muhammad ibn Thabit is al-Abdi, Abu Abdullah al-Basri. Concerning him, Ibn Hajar said in *al-Taqrib* (a book of hadith criticism): Truthful, weak in narration.

Know that the narration of al-Dahhak ibn Uthman and of Ibn al-Had for this hadith, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, contains no corroboration of Muhammad ibn Thabit regarding the two strikes or the two forearms. This is because al-Dahhak did not mention tayammum (dry ablution) in his narration, and Ibn al-Had said in his narration: "He wiped his face and his hands." This was stated by Ibn Hajar and al-Bayhaqi.

Al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi narrated, through the route of Ali ibn Zabyan, from Ubayd Allah ibn Umar, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Tayammum is two strikes: one strike for the face, and one strike for the two hands up to the two elbows."

Al-Daraqutni said: Yahya al-Qattan, Hushaym and others made it a statement of Ibn Umar (mawquf), and this is the correct view. He then narrated it through the route of Malik, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, as a statement of Ibn Umar only. This was stated by Ibn Hajar. Moreover, al-Qattan, Ibn Ma'in and others declared Ali ibn Zabyan weak.

He is Ibn Zabyan ibn Hilal al-Absi al-Kufi, judge of Baghdad. Concerning him, Ibn Hajar said in *al-Taqrib*: Weak.

Al-Daraqutni narrated through the route of Salim, from Ibn Umar, as a prophetic report (marfu'), with the wording: "We performed tayammum with the Prophet (ﷺ). We struck our hands on the good earth, then we shook off our hands, and wiped with them our faces. Then we struck another strike and wiped from the elbows to the palms," and so on. However, its chain contains Sulayman ibn Arqam, who is abandoned (matruk) in narration.

Al-Bayhaqi said: Ma'mar and others narrated it from al-Zuhri as a statement of a Companion (mawquf), and this is the sound version. Al-Daraqutni also narrated it through the route of Sulayman ibn Abi Dawud al-Harrani, who is also abandoned, from Salim and Nafi' together, from Ibn Umar, as a prophetic report, with the wording: "In tayammum there are two strikes: one strike for the face, and one strike for the two hands up to the two elbows."

Abu Zur'ah said: It is a false hadith (batil).

Al-Daraqutni and al-Hakim narrated through the route of Uthman ibn [p. 362] Muhammad al-Anmati, from Azrah ibn Thabit, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Tayammum is one strike for the face, and one strike for the forearms up to the elbows." And through the route of Abu Nu'aym, from Azrah with the same chain, he said: "A man came and said: I have become junub (in a state of major impurity), and I rolled in the dust. He said: Strike. So he struck the earth with his hand and wiped his face, then he struck with his hands and wiped with them up to the elbows."

Ibn al-Jawzi declared this hadith weak, because of Uthman ibn Muhammad in its chain. It was answered against Ibn al-Jawzi that no one has criticized Uthman ibn Muhammad, as Ibn Daqiq al-Id stated. However, his narration mentioned above is shadh (anomalous), because Abu Nu'aym narrated it from Azrah as a statement of a Companion (mawquf). Al-Daraqutni and al-Hakim also recorded it.

Al-Daraqutni said in *Hashiyat al-Sunan* (marginal notes on the Sunan), following the hadith of Uthman ibn Muhammad: All of them are trustworthy (thiqat), and the correct version is mawquf. Ibn Hajar stated all of this in *al-Talkhis* (a summary of hadith sources). In *al-Taqrib*, he said regarding Uthman ibn Muhammad mentioned: Acceptable (maqbul). He also said in *al-Talkhis*: On this topic, there is also a narration from al-Asla', who said: "I used to serve the Prophet (ﷺ), and Jibril came to him with the verse of al-Sa'id (the clean earth). He showed me tayammum, so I struck the earth once with my hands and wiped my face with them, then I struck the earth with them and wiped my hands up to the elbows." Al-Daraqutni and al-Tabarani narrated it, and in its chain is al-Rabi' ibn Badr, who is weak. Also from Abu Umamah, narrated by al-Tabarani, whose chain is also weak.

Al-Bazzar and Ibn Adi narrated from the hadith of A'ishah, as a prophetic report: "Tayammum is two strikes: one strike for the face, and one strike for the two hands up to the two elbows." Al-Harish ibn al-Kharrit alone narrated it, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from her. Abu Hatim said: It is a munkar (rejected) hadith, and al-Harish is a shaykh who is not used as proof.

As for the hadith: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ammar ibn Yasir: It suffices you to strike once for the face and once for the two palms," narrated by al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* and *al-Kabir*, in its chain is Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Yahya, who is weak. However, it is a proof according to al-Shafi'i.

And the hadith of Ammar: "I was among the people when the concession was revealed, and he commanded us, so we struck once for the face, then another strike for the two hands up to the two elbows." Al-Bazzar narrated it. There is no doubt that the agreed-upon narration from Ammar is more preferable than it.

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: Most of the prophetic reports from Ammar mention one strike. What is narrated from him regarding two strikes is all mudtarib (confused in its chain or text). End of quotation from him. From all of this, you know that nothing in this topic is authentic except the hadith of Ammar and Abu Juhaym, which were mentioned earlier, as we have noted. [p. 363]

Now that you know the textual evidences from the Sunnah on this question, know that what is obligatory in wiping is the two palms only. What Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said is not far from the truth: that the two palms are obligatory, while the forearms up to the elbows are recommended (sunnah, the practice of the Prophet, which is rewarded but not obligatory), because the obligation is indicated by the agreed-upon hadith concerning the two palms.

As for these narrations that mention the two hands up to the elbows, they indicate recommendation (sunniyyah), although none of them is free from criticism. Some of them strengthen others, because it is established in the sciences of hadith that weak chains which are considered (al-mu'tabar bihi) strengthen one another until their combined body becomes fit for use as evidence. There is a saying: Do not contend with one man of a household, for two weak ones can overcome one strong one. It is also reinforced by the aforementioned mawquf reports.

The principle is to apply both pieces of evidence, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

* * *

The fourth issue: Is the sequence (tartib) obligatory in tayammum or not? A group of scholars, including al-Shafi'i and his companions, held that giving precedence to the face over the hands is a pillar (rukn) of tayammum. Al-Nawawi reported that the Shafi'is agreed on this. A group, including Malik and most of his companions, held that giving precedence to the face over the hands is a sunnah.

The evidence for giving precedence to the face over the hands is that Allah the Exalted mentioned it first in the verse of al-Nisa' and the verse of al-Ma'idah, where He said in both: ﴿So wipe your faces and your hands﴾.

The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "I begin with what Allah began with," referring to His saying: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:158). In some of his narrations, the wording is "Begin" in the imperative form. Imam Ahmad and those who agreed with him held that the two hands should be given precedence, citing what is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, in the chapter "Tayammum is one strike," from the hadith of Ammar ibn Yasir, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "It was sufficient for you to do this," so he struck the earth once with his palms, then shook them off, then wiped with them the back of his right palm with his left hand, or the back of his left hand with his right palm, then wiped with them his face. (The hadith continues.)

It is known that "then" (thumma) implies sequence, while "and" (waw) does not imply sequence according to the majority, but only indicates general conjunction. This does not preclude that there may be a separate piece of evidence showing that what is joined by "and" comes after what precedes it, as the aforementioned hadith indicates in the verse: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah﴾, and as in the line of Hassan:

*You satirized Muhammad, and I answered on his behalf* (the wording with "waw" in this reading).

Therefore, this hadith of al-Bukhari is an explicit text on giving precedence to the two hands over the face. In al-Isma'ili's narration, through the route of Harun al-Hammal, from Abu Mu'awiyah, the wording is: "It suffices you to strike the earth with your two hands, then shake them off, then wipe with your right hand over your left, and your left over your right, then wipe over your face." Ibn Hajar stated this in *al-Fath* (his commentary on Sahih al-Bukhari). Most scholars hold that the face should be given precedence, although they differ on whether this is obligatory or recommended.

[The author's words have been abridged due to their great length.]

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 15:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O People of the Scripture, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture﴾ [etc., the verse], he did not clarify here any of that great deal which the Messenger (ﷺ) clarifies for them, from what they used to conceal of the Scripture, meaning the Torah and the Gospel. And he clarified much of it in other places.

From what they used to conceal of the rulings of the Torah is the stoning of the married adulterer. The Qur'an clarified it in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, being invited to the Book of Allah so that it may judge between them, and then a faction of them turns away while they are refusing?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 23].

That is, they were invited to the Torah so that it might judge between them concerning the legal punishment of the married adulterer by stoning, and they turned away from that and denied it. Among that is also what they concealed of the attributes of the Messenger (ﷺ) in their book, and their denial that they recognize that he is the Messenger, as He, exalted is He, clarified by His saying: ﴿And previously they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved, but when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it. So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 89].

Among that is their denial that Allah prohibited for them some of the good things because of their wrongdoing and their sins, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them﴾ [An-Nisa: 160], and His saying: ﴿And to those who were Jews We made unlawful every animal with claws; and of the cattle and sheep We made unlawful to them their fat, except what their backs or intestines carry or what is mixed with bone. That We repaid them for their rebellion, and indeed We are truthful﴾ [Al-An'am: 146].

They denied this and said: "Nothing was prohibited to us except what was prohibited to Israel." The Qur'an refuted them in that, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel, except what Israel had made unlawful for himself before the Torah was revealed. Say: "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 93].

Among that is the concealment by the Christians of the glad tidings of Jesus, son of Mary, to them concerning Muhammad (ﷺ). He, exalted is He, clarified it by His saying: ﴿And when Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O Children of Israel, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you, confirming what is before me of the Torah and giving glad tidings of a Messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad"﴾ [As-Saff: 6], among other verses that clarify what they concealed of their books.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam in truth﴾ — the verse.

The majority of scholars said: they are the two sons of Adam from his own loins, and they are Habil (Abel) and Qabil (Cain).

Al-Hasan al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him) said: they are two men from the Children of Israel. However, the Qur'an supports the view of the majority and indicates that al-Hasan's view is not correct. This is evident in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then Allah sent a crow scratching in the earth to show him how to conceal the dead body of his brother﴾ [al-Hijr: 31]. It is not hidden from anyone that there was no man among the Children of Israel who was ignorant of burial until a crow guided him to it. The story of learning burial by imitating the crow and gaining knowledge of it from it indicates that the event occurred at the very beginning of matters, before people had become accustomed to burying the dead, as is clear. Several scholars have also drawn attention to this. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 32 (part 1 of 7):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, other than for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had killed all of mankind﴾ [the verse]. In this noble verse He explicitly states that He prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, other than for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had killed all of mankind. He did not address here the ruling for one who kills a soul in retaliation for a soul, or for corruption in the land, but He clarified that in other places. So He clarified that killing a soul in retribution for a soul is permissible, in His saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life﴾ [the verse] [Al-Ma'idah: 45], and in His saying: ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾ [the verse] [Al-Baqarah: 178], and His saying: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority﴾ [the verse] [Al-Isra': 33].

Know that the verses on retaliation for life contain generality that the Sunnah (the prophetic tradition) has clarified. The summary of the detailed discussion on this is that a free Muslim man is killed for a free Muslim man, by consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement); that a free Muslim woman is likewise killed for a free Muslim woman, by consensus; and that a slave is likewise killed for a slave, by consensus. We do not take into account the view of 'Ata' that it is conditional upon the equality of the value of the two slaves, which is also a narration from Ahmad, nor the view of Ibn 'Abbas: "There is no retaliation among slaves, because they are property," because all of that is refuted by the explicit statement of His saying: ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain: the free for the free, and the slave for the slave﴾ [the verse].

And a woman is killed for a man, because if she is killed for a woman, then killing her for a man is more fitting. And a man is killed for a woman according to the majority of scholars regarding both.

It is narrated from a group including 'Ali, al-Hasan, and 'Uthman al-Batti, and Ahmad in one narration from him, that he is not killed for her unless her heirs commit to the amount by which his blood money exceeds her blood money; if they do not commit to it, they take her blood money.

It is narrated from 'Ali and al-Hasan that if she kills a man, she is killed for him, and his heirs also take the excess of his blood money over hers, or they take the blood money of the slain and spare her.

Al-Qurtubi said, after mentioning this statement from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and al-Hasan al-Basri, and it has also been denied from them: "al-Sha'bi narrated this from 'Ali, but it is not authentic, because al-Sha'bi did not meet 'Ali."

Al-Hakam narrated from 'Ali and 'Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) that they both said: "If a man intentionally kills a woman, then he is subject to retaliation (qawad) for her." (p-373) This contradicts the narration of al-Sha'bi from 'Ali. Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari, in the chapter "Questioning the killer until he confesses," and confession in the hudud (fixed punishments), after mentioning the aforementioned statement from 'Ali and al-Hasan: "It is not established from 'Ali, but it is the statement of 'Uthman al-Batti, one of the jurists of Basra. What refutes this view is that it states that if a woman kills a man, his heirs are given both retaliation and half the blood money. This is a view that the Book and the Sunnah show to be false, and that it is either retaliation alone or blood money alone, because He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾, then He said: ﴿But whoever is pardoned by his brother, let there be a follow-up with fairness﴾ [the verse] [Al-Baqarah: 178], so He made the pursuit of blood money a consequence of pardon, not of retaliation."

And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has a slain relative, he has the choice of one of two options" [the hadith], and it is explicit in the impossibility of combining the two, as is clear to the general body of scholars. It is related from Ahmad in one narration from him, and from 'Uthman al-Batti, and 'Ata', that a man is not killed for a woman, but rather blood money is due. This is what Ibn Kathir stated. It is also narrated from al-Layth and al-Zuhri that if she was his wife he is not killed for her, and if she was not his wife he is killed for her.

The verified position is that he is killed for her absolutely, as you will see from its evidences. Among the evidences for killing a man for a woman is the consensus of scholars that if a healthy, intact person kills a one-eyed man or a paralyzed man, or the like, intentionally, retaliation is due upon him, and nothing is due to his heirs in exchange for the excess of the healthy limbs that he has over the slain.

Among the evidences for killing a man for a woman is what is established in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from the Prophet (ﷺ), from the hadith of Anas: "that he (ﷺ) crushed the head of a Jew with stones as retaliation for a slave girl whom he had done the same to," and scholars have used this hadith as evidence for killing a male for a female, and for the obligation of retaliation for killing by means other than a sharp weapon or a blade.

Al-Bayhaqi said in al-Sunan al-Kubra, in the chapter "Killing a man for a woman": "Abu 'Abdullah al-Hafiz informed us, Abu Zakariyya Yahya ibn Muhammad al-'Anbari narrated to us, Abu 'Abdullah Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-'Abdi narrated to us, al-Hakam ibn Musa al-Qanṭari narrated to us, Yahya ibn Hamzah narrated to us, from Sulayman ibn Dawud, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to the people of Yemen a letter containing the obligatory duties, the Sunan, and the blood money, and sent it with 'Amr ibn Hazm, and it contained: 'and that a man is killed for a woman.'"

(p-374) This hadith was also narrated with a continuous chain (mawsul) by al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim. In the tafsir of Ibn Kathir there is the following text: "In the hadith narrated by al-Nasa'i and others: 'That the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote in the letter to 'Amr ibn Hazm that a man is killed for a woman.' The letter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to 'Amr ibn Hazm, which contains that a man is killed for a woman, was narrated by Malik, al-Shafi'i, and also narrated by al-Daraqutni, Abu Dawud, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, and al-Darimi. The statements of the scholars of hadith regarding this letter of 'Amr ibn Hazm are well known, between one who authenticates it and one who declares it weak. Among those who authenticated it are Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi. From Ahmad it is reported that he said: 'I hope it is authentic.' It was also authenticated, in terms of its fame, not in terms of its chain, by a group including al-Shafi'i, for he said: 'They did not accept this hadith until it was established with them that it was the letter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).'"

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "It is a letter well known among the people of biographies (siyar), and its contents are known among the people of knowledge; its fame makes it independent of a chain, because it resembles mutawatir (widely transmitted) reports in the way people have received it with acceptance." He said: "What indicates its fame is what Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik, from al-Layth ibn Sa'd, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: 'A letter was found with the family of Hazm, and they mention that it is the letter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).'" Al-'Uqayli said: "This is a established, preserved hadith." Ya'qub ibn Sufyan said: "I know of no letter among all the transmitted books more authentic than this letter of 'Amr ibn Hazm, for the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Successors would refer to it and abandon their own opinions."

Al-Hakim said: "'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and the imam of his age, al-Zuhri, bore witness to the authenticity of this letter," and then he traced that with his chain back to both of them. A group weakened the letter of Ibn Hazm, and Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm defended its weakness in his al-Muhalla.

The verified position is the validity of using it as evidence, because it is established that it is the letter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which he wrote to explain the rulings on blood money, zakat, and other matters, and its copy is well known in the books of fiqh.

The hadith, especially according to those who use mursal (a report whose chain omits a Companion) as evidence, such as Malik, Abu Hanifa, and Ahmad in the most well-known narrations.

Among the evidences for killing him for her is the general meaning of the hadith: "The Muslims' blood is equal (tatakafa'u dima'uhum)" [the hadith], and it will come the discussion of it, God willing.
