And among the clearest evidences for killing a man for a woman is His saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life﴾ [the verse] [Al-Ma'idah: 45], and His saying (ﷺ): "The blood of a Muslim man (p-375) who testifies that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah is not lawful, except in one of three cases: the married adulterer, and a life for a life" [the hadith]. It was recorded by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and the rest of the compilers, from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him).

So the general meaning of this noble verse and this sound hadith requires killing a man for a woman, because she is a soul for a soul, and nothing exits from this generality except what is brought out by evidence suitable to specify the text. Yes, two questions arise against this argument:

The first: What is the basis for citing His saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life﴾ [the verse], when it is a narration about the people of Moses, while Allah says: ﴿For each of you We have appointed a law and a method﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 48].

The second question: Why is the general meaning of killing a soul for a soul in the verse and hadith mentioned not specified by His saying: ﴿The free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 178]? Because this verse is more specific than that, since it details what was stated generally in the first, and because this Ummah is explicitly addressed by it in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain: the free for the free﴾ [the verse].

The answer to the first question: The verified position on which the majority agree, and which the texts of the Shari'ah indicate, is that everything mentioned to us in our Book and the Sunnah of our Prophet (ﷺ) that was a law for those before us is a law for us, from the standpoint that it is present in our Book or the Sunnah of our Prophet (ﷺ), not from the standpoint that it was a law for those before us. This is because He only related it to us in our law so that we would take lesson from it and act upon what it contains.

The texts indicating this are very numerous, and for this reason Allah commanded in many verses of the Mighty Qur'an to take lesson from their circumstances, and He rebuked the one who does not understand that, as in His saying regarding the people of Lot: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning﴾ ﴿and at night. Will you not reason?﴾ [As-Saffat: 137-138].

In His saying "Will you not reason?" there is a rebuke for whoever passes by their dwellings and does not take lesson from what happened to them, and does not reason about it so as to avoid falling into the like of it. Likewise His saying: ﴿Have they not traveled through the earth and observed how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them﴾, then He threatened the disbelievers with the like of that, saying: ﴿And for the disbelievers are the like thereof﴾ [Muhammad: 10].

(p-376) And He said regarding the stones of the people of Lot by which they were destroyed, or their dwellings in which they were destroyed: ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud: 83], and this is a great threat from Him, may He be exalted, to whoever does not take lesson from their state, so that he avoids committing what they perished because of. Similar examples are numerous in the Qur'an.

And He said: ﴿There was certainly in their stories a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Yusuf: 111]. So He explicitly stated that He relates their stories in the Qur'an for the sake of the lesson, and this is clear evidence for what we have mentioned. When Allah mentioned those prophets He mentioned in Surat al-An'am, He said to our Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [Al-An'am: 90]. His command (ﷺ) is a command for us, because he is our exemplar, and because Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern﴾ [the verse] [Al-Ahzab: 21], and He says: ﴿Say, if you should love Allah, then follow me﴾ [the verse] [Al 'Imran: 31], and He says: ﴿And whatever the Messenger has given you, take it﴾ [the verse] [Al-Hashr: 7].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 32 (part 2 of 7):

And He says: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾ [an-Nisa: 80], and part of obeying him is following him in everything he commanded, except what is established by evidence as specific to him (ﷺ). And the law of those before us that is established in our law is a law for us, unless there is evidence of abrogation. This is the view of the majority (al-jumhur), including Malik, Abu Hanifa, and Ahmad in the more well-known of his two narrations. Imam al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) disagreed in the most sound of the reports from him, and said: the law of those before us that is established in our law is not a law for us unless there is a text from our law that it is prescribed for us. He also disagreed, in the sound report from him, regarding whether a address specific to the Messenger (ﷺ) includes his community in its ruling. He cited for the first position the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿For each of you We have appointed a law and a way﴾. For the second, he argued that the form specific to the Messenger does not by its linguistic convention include the community, so including them in it is diverting the wording from its apparent meaning, and that requires a separate evidence. He also argued that interpreting "guidance" in His saying ﴿so follow their guidance﴾, and "religion" in His saying ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion...﴾ [ash-Shura: 13], as referring specifically to the fundamentals (usul), which is monotheism, and not to the practical rulings (furu'), is correct, because He the Exalted said regarding creed: ﴿We did not send any messenger before you except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ [al-Anbiya: 25], and said: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah and avoid the Taghut"﴾ [an-Nahl: 36], and said: ﴿Ask those We sent before you of Our messengers: Did We appoint deities other than the Most Merciful to be worshipped?﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 45].

And regarding the practical rulings He said: ﴿For each of you We have appointed a law and a way﴾, which indicates agreement in the fundamentals and difference in the practical rulings, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We, the company of the prophets, are brothers by different mothers; our religion is one." Al-Bukhari recorded it in his Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: As for interpreting the guidance in the verse ﴿so follow their guidance﴾, and the religion in the verse ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion﴾, as referring to monotheism to the exclusion of practical rulings, this is not accepted. As for the first, it is because al-Bukhari recorded in his Sahih, in the chapter on the tafsir of Surah "Sad", from Mujahid: "He asked Ibn Abbas: From where did you take the prostration in 'Sad'? He said: Do you not read: ﴿And of his offspring, Dawud﴾, up to His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 84 and 90]? So Dawud prostrated for it, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prostrated for it."

This is a sound and explicit text from Ibn Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) included the prostration of recitation within the guidance in His saying ﴿so follow their guidance﴾. It is known that the prostration of recitation is a branch of the practical rulings, not one of the fundamentals.

As for the second: the Prophet (ﷺ) stated, in the sound and well-known hadith of Jibril, that the name "religion" encompasses Islam, faith, and excellence (ihsan), when he said: "This is Jibril; he came to teach you your religion." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19], and said: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85].

In the same hadith the Prophet (ﷺ) stated that Islam includes practical matters, such as prayer, zakat, fasting, and hajj. In the hadith of Ibn Umar agreed upon by the scholars: "Islam is built upon five," and no one has said that Islam refers only to creed to the exclusion of practical matters. This shows that religion is not restricted to that in His saying ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Nuh﴾, and this is very clear, because the best way to interpret the Qur'an is by the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ).

As for the address specific to the Prophet (ﷺ) in such verses as His saying ﴿so follow their guidance﴾, the texts have shown that his ruling extends to the community, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed there has been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21], and other verses already mentioned. We know this from surveying the Noble Qur'an, where it frequently expresses itself with the form specific to him (ﷺ) and then indicates that the intended meaning is the general applicability of the address to the community. For example, at the beginning of Surah at-Talaq: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [at-Talaq: 1], and then He said: ﴿When you divorce women...﴾, which shows that all are included in the ruling under His saying "O Prophet." And in Surah at-Tahrim He said: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit...﴾ [at-Tahrim: 1], then He said: ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾ [at-Tahrim: 2]; this shows the general applicability of the address through His saying "O Prophet." A similar example is in Surah al-Ahzab, in His saying: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 1], then He said: ﴿Indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾ [an-Nisa: 94]; His saying "of what you do" indicates the general applicability of the address "O Prophet." Likewise His saying: ﴿And you are not in any matter﴾ [Yunus: 61], then He said: ﴿Nor do you do any deed except that We are witnesses over you﴾, the verse.

Among the clearest proofs on this point are the verse of ar-Rum and the verse of al-Ahzab. As for the verse of ar-Rum, it is His saying: ﴿So direct your face toward the religion, inclining (hanifan)﴾ [ar-Rum: 30], then He said: ﴿turning back (munibina) to Him﴾ [ar-Rum: 31], which is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the hidden pronoun of the subject addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) in His saying ﴿So direct your face﴾, the verse.

The meaning is established as: "So direct your face, O Prophet of Allah, while you are turning back [to Him]." Had the community not been included in the ruling of the address specific to him (ﷺ), He would have said "muniban ilayhi" in the singular. This is because the people of the Arabic language agree that a true circumstantial clause, meaning one that is not causal, must agree with its subject in number, gender, and person: singular, dual, plural, masculine, and feminine. So one may not say "Zayd came laughing" in the plural form, nor "Hind came laughing" in the feminine plural form.

As for the verse of al-Ahzab, it is His saying, in the story of Zaynab bint Jahsh al-Asadiyya (may Allah be pleased with her): ﴿So when Zayd had no longer any need for her, We married her to you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. This address is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ).

* *

Allah the Exalted has explicitly stated that His wisdom extends to all believers in His saying: ﴿so that there will not be upon the believers any discomfort﴾, the verse. He also pointed to this in al-Ahzab with His saying: ﴿exclusively for you, to the exclusion of the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50], because the address specific to him (ﷺ) in His saying ﴿and a believing woman if she gives herself to the Prophet﴾, the verse, had its ruling been specific to him (ﷺ), would have made His saying ﴿exclusively for you, to the exclusion of the believers﴾ unnecessary, as is evident.

'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) refuted those who claimed that giving a wife the choice is a divorce, by saying that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave his wives the choice and they chose him, and he did not count it as a divorce. Yet the address in that matter is specific to him (ﷺ) in His saying the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, say to your wives: If you should desire the worldly life...﴾ [al-Ahzab: 28], the two verses.

Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) took the irrevocable separation of a wife upon apostasy from His saying: ﴿If you should associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely become worthless﴾ [az-Zumar: 65], and that is an address specific to him (ﷺ).

(p-379) The summary of the discussion on the question "the law of those before us" is that it has an intermediate category and two extremes. One extreme is that which is unanimously a law for us: what is established in our law as having been a law for those before us, and then our law clarifies that it is a law for us, such as retaliation (qisas). It is established in our law that it was a law for those before us, in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And We ordained for them therein that a life is for a life﴾, the verse, and it is clarified in our law that it is prescribed for us in His saying: ﴿Retribution is prescribed for you concerning those who are killed﴾.

The other extreme, which is unanimously not a law for us, consists of two matters:

The first: what is not established in our law at all as having been a law for those before us, such as what is taken from the Israelite narrations (isra'iliyyat), because the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade us from believing them or disbelieving them concerning them. What the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade us from believing is unanimously not a law for us.

The second: what is established in our law as having been a law for those before us, and our law clarifies that it is not prescribed for us, such as the burdens and shackles that were upon those before us, because Allah removed them from us, as He the Exalted said: ﴿And He relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾ [al-A'raf: 157]. It is established in Sahih Muslim that when the Prophet (ﷺ) recited ﴿Our Lord, do not impose upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], Allah said: "Yes, I have done so."

Among those burdens that Allah removed from us, through the tongue of our Prophet (ﷺ), is what happened to the worshippers of the calf, when their repentance was accepted only by their offering themselves for killing, as He the Exalted said: ﴿So repent to your Creator and kill yourselves; that is better for you in the sight of your Creator. Then He accepted your repentance; indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54].

The intermediate category is the point of scholarly disagreement. It is what is established in our law as having been a law for those before us, and our law has not clarified whether it is prescribed for us or not prescribed for us. This is the category we previously said the verified position holds to be a law for us, and this is the view of the majority. You have seen their evidence for it. By this you know that the verse ﴿And We ordained for them therein that a life is for a life﴾, the verse, obligates us to act upon the rulings it contains.

Moreover, the Qur'an has explicitly stated this in general terms in His saying: ﴿Retribution is prescribed for you concerning those who are killed﴾, and His saying: ﴿And whoever is killed unjustly, We have given his heir authority﴾ [al-Isra: 33]. And in the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, agreed upon and mentioned earlier, there is an explicit statement that the taking of a life for a life contained in it is prescribed for us (p-380), where the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The blood of a Muslim man who testifies that there is no deity except Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah may not be shed except in one of three cases: the married adulterer, a life for a life," the hadith.

Al-Bukhari pointed to this in his Sahih when he said: "Chapter: the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿that a life is for a life﴾, up to His saying: ﴿then it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾," and then he mentioned the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud already cited. Ibn Hajar said: "The purpose of mentioning this verse is its correspondence with the wording of the hadith. Perhaps he intended to show that although it was revealed concerning the People of the Book, the ruling it indicates remains in effect in the law of Islam. It is therefore a basis for retaliation for intentional killing. This is supported by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: 'The Book of Allah is retaliation,' recorded by the two Shaykhs from the hadith of Anas, on the basis that the intended 'Book of Allah' is His saying: ﴿and the tooth for a tooth﴾ in this verse which we are discussing. According to the other opinions, there is no evidence in the hadith."

The scholars have continued to derive rulings from the stories of past nations, as we have clarified its evidence. Among that is the saying of the Malikis and others: a decisive circumstantial evidence (qarina) may sometimes take the place of proof, citing as evidence the making of Yusuf's witness's tearing of the shirt from behind as a sign of his truthfulness and the woman's lying, in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And a witness from her family testified: If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is of the liars. But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied and he is of the truthful.﴾ ﴿So when he saw his shirt torn from the back, he said: Indeed, it is of your plotting. Indeed, your plotting is great.﴾ [Yusuf: 26, 27, 28], the verse. His mentioning this and affirming it indicates the permissibility of acting upon it. From here Malik made the hadd punishment for wine obligatory upon one who is smelled and the smell of wine is detected on his breath, because the smell of it in his mouth is a circumstantial evidence of his drinking it.

The scholars also permitted, for a man who marries a woman without having seen her, when the women escorting her to him bring her and no proof is available regarding her identity that she is the daughter of so-and-so with whom the contract was made, that he may consummate with her, relying on the circumstantial evidence and treating it as equivalent to proof.

Similarly, a guest who arrives at a people's courtyard, and a child or a servant girl brings him food: it is permitted for him to eat it without a proof that the people of the food have given him permission to eat, relying on the circumstantial evidence.

[p. 381] The Malikis and others adopted the rejection of one presumptive indicator (qarina) by a stronger one. This is the case of Joseph's brothers: when they put Joseph in the bottom of the well, they put on his shirt the blood of a young goat, so that the blood on his shirt would be an indicator of the truth of their claim that a wolf had eaten him. Jacob rejected this with a stronger indicator, which is the absence of a tear in the shirt. He said: "Glory be to God! When did a wolf become gentle and clever, killing Joseph and not tearing his shirt?" This is what God explained in His saying: ﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood. He said, "Rather, your souls have enticed you to something. So patience is most fitting. And God is the one sought for help against what you describe."﴾ [Yusuf: 18]

The Malikis also took from His saying, in the story of Joseph and his brothers, the obligation of guarantee for loss (ḍamān al-ghurm): ﴿And for whoever brings it, there is a camel's load, and I am its guarantor.﴾ [Yusuf: 72]

Some of the Shafi'is took from His saying, in the story of Jacob and his sons, the guarantee known as kafala (surety for a person): ﴿I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn covenant from God that you will surely bring him back to me, unless you are surrounded.﴾ [Yusuf: 66]

The Malikis also took from His saying, in the story of Salih, the rebuke by the judge of the litigants three days after the terms have expired: ﴿So he said, "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days."﴾ [Hud: 65]

They also derived the obligation of giving warning (i'dhar) to the opponent to whom a ruling is directed, by saying, "Is there any proof remaining for you?" and similar, from His saying in the story of Solomon with the hoopoe: ﴿I will surely punish him with severe punishment, or I will slaughter him, or he must bring me a clear authority.﴾ [al-Naml: 21]

The Hanbalis took the permissibility of a long period of hire (ijara) from His saying in the story of Moses and his father-in-law Shu'ayb, or another: ﴿Indeed, I want to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine on the condition that you serve me for eight years; but if you complete ten, it is from you, and I do not intend to make it difficult for you.﴾ (the verse) [al-Qasas: 27]. Similar examples are very numerous.

As for His saying: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a method﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 48], it does not contradict what we have mentioned, because what is meant by it is that in some laws, rulings that were prescribed before them are abrogated (naskh), and new legislation of rulings that were not prescribed before is renewed.

In this respect, each law and method is for each community without contradicting what we have mentioned, and this is evident. Thus the answer to the first question becomes clear to you, and you know that what is contained in the verse ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that a life is for a life﴾ (the verse) is legislated for this community, and that a man is killed for a woman and vice versa, according to the verified position about which there is no doubt. The one who says there is no retaliation between them seems to hold on to the implication (mafhum) of His saying: ﴿and a female for a female﴾ [al-Baqara: 178], and you will see the verification of this matter soon, God willing.

As for the answer to the second question, which is: why does He not restrict the generality of "a life for a life" by the detailed statement in His saying: ﴿The free for the free, and the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾? It is [p. 382] what has been established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul), that the implication of opposition (mafhum al-mukhalafa), when it is capable of another meaning other than its contradiction of the ruling of the explicit statement (manṭuq), is prevented by that from being considered.

The author of Jam' al-Jawami' (a work on legal theory) said, in discussing the implication of opposition: "Its condition is that the unmentioned matter was not omitted out of fear or the like," until he said: "or other than that, which requires the specification by mention." When you know this, know that His saying: ﴿The free for the free, and the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾ indicates the killing of a free person for a free person, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female, but it did not address the killing of a female for a male, or a slave for a free person, nor the reverse, by explicit statement.

The implication of opposition here is not valid, because the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of the verse was that two tribes of the Arabs fought, and one of them said: "We will kill for our slave So-and-so the son of So-and-so, and for our slave-woman So-and-so the daughter of So-and-so," showing arrogance over them, and they claimed that their slave was equal to the free man of the others, and that their female was equal to the man of the others, showing arrogance over them and displaying their nobility over them. Al-Qurtubi mentioned the meaning of this from al-Sha'bi and Qatada.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, which Ibn Kathir transmitted from him in his tafsir, and al-Suyuti in Asbab al-Nuzul. Ibn Kathir also mentioned that it was revealed concerning Qurayza and al-Nadir, because there was fighting between them, and the Banu al-Nadir acted arrogantly toward the Banu Qurayza.

All of them agree that the occasion of its revelation was that one people acted arrogantly toward another, saying: "The slave from us is not equal to the slave from you; rather, the free man from you is equal to him. And the woman from us is not equal to the woman from you; rather, the man from you is equal to her." So the Qur'an came down explaining that they are equal, and the one who acts arrogantly toward the other is not more noble than him. For this reason, the implication of opposition is not considered here.

* *

As for killing a free person for a slave, there is disagreement about it. The majority of scholars hold that a free person is not killed for a slave, including Malik, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad.

Among those who said this were Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Ali, Zayd, and Ibn al-Zubayr, may God be pleased with them, as well as 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, 'Ata', al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, and 'Amr ibn Dinar, as Ibn Qudama transmitted from them in al-Mughni, and others.

Abu Hanifa said: a free person is killed for a slave. This is also narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Nakha'i, Qatada, and al-Thawri. These people argued for killing a free person for a slave with the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The believers' blood is equal, and they are one hand against whoever is other than them, and the least of them may give protection on their behalf," the hadith, which was narrated by Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, Abu Dawud, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it.

So the generality of "believers" includes slaves, and likewise the generality of "a life" in His saying: ﴿that a life is for a life﴾ (the verse), and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "and a life for a life" in the hadith mentioned above. They also argued with what Qatada narrated from al-Hasan, from Samura, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever kills his slave, we will kill him; and whoever mutilates his slave, we will mutilate him." Imam Ahmad narrated it, and the authors of the four Sunan; al-Tirmidhi said: "hasan gharib." In a narration of Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i: "And whoever castrates his slave, we will castrate him." These are the evidences of those who say a free person is killed for a slave.

The majority answered them with what you will see now, God willing. As for the inclusion of killing a free person for a slave in the generality of "believers" in the hadith "The believers' blood is equal," and the generality of "a life for a life" in the verse and the aforementioned hadith, know first that the inclusion of slaves in the general texts of the Book and the Sunna has been disputed among the scholars of usul, on three opinions:

The first, held by most scholars: slaves are included in the generality of the texts, because they are among those addressed by them.

The second, adopted by some scholars among the Malikis, Shafi'is, and others: they are not included in them except by a separate evidence. They argued for this view by the frequency of their non-inclusion, as in their not being included in the address of jihad and hajj, and His saying: ﴿And divorced women await [by themselves] for three periods﴾ (the verse) [al-Baqara: 228], where slave-women are not included.

The third, adopted by al-Razi of the Hanafis: if the general text is about acts of worship, they are included in it; if it is about transactions, they are not included. Also, in Maraqi al-Su'ud, he indicated that their inclusion in the general address is the correct view which the evidence requires, by his saying:

[Rajaz]
"The slave, the existent, and the disbeliever are all covered by it, according to those who reflect."

Upon the disagreement about their inclusion in the generalities of the texts depends the obligation of the Friday prayer for slaves: if they are included in the generality, it is obligatory for them; if they are not included except by a separate evidence, it is not obligatory for them. Likewise, a slave's confession to a punishment on his body is also based on the aforementioned disagreement, as said by the author of Nashr al-Bunud, a commentary on Maraqi al-Su'ud, in explaining the verse just mentioned. When you know this, know that according to the view that slaves are not included in the generality of the texts of the Book and the Sunna, there is no difficulty.

According to the view that they are included, the answer to their non-inclusion in the general texts we have mentioned is known from the arguments of the majority that follow, God willing, for the non-killing of a free person for a slave. As for the hadith of Samura, it is answered in several ways:

First: most scholars of hadith abandoned the narration of al-Hasan from Samura, because he did not hear from him. Some said he heard from him only the hadith of the 'aqiqa. 'Ali ibn al-Madini and al-Bukhari affirmed his hearing from him.

Al-Bayhaqi said in al-Sunan al-Kubra, in the Book of Crimes (Jinayat), the following text: "Most people of knowledge of hadith turned away from the narration of al-Hasan from Samura."

Some of them held that he did not hear from him except the hadith of the 'aqiqa. He also said, in the chapter on "the prohibition of selling animals for animals": "Most of the memorizers (huffaz) do not affirm al-Hasan's hearing from Samura except in the hadith of the 'aqiqa."

Second: al-Hasan used to give the ruling that a free person is not killed for a slave, and his opposition to what he narrated indicates its weakness in his view. Al-Bayhaqi also said: Qatada said: "Then al-Hasan forgot this hadith, and he said: a free person is not killed for a slave." The Shaykh (al-Bayhaqi) said: "It seems that al-Hasan did not forget the hadith, but he turned away from it because of its weakness."

Third: what the author of Muntaqa al-Akhbar mentioned, that most scholars said a free person is not killed for a slave, and they interpreted the report to mean one whose slave he is, lest it be thought that prior ownership prevents retaliation.

Fourth: it is opposed by the evidences the majority relied upon for the non-killing of a free person for a slave, which will come in detail, God willing. They indicate a prohibition against killing a free person for a slave, and a prohibition takes precedence over a command, as established in usul.

Fifth: what Ibn al-'Arabi claimed as evidence for the invalidity of this view, from His saying: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority﴾ [al-Isra': 33], and the heir of the slave is his master. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir of His saying: ﴿The free for the free and the slave for the slave﴾ (the verse), the following text: Ibn al-'Arabi said: "Ignorance has reached such people that they said: a free person is killed for his own slave." They narrated a hadith about this from al-Hasan, from Samura, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever kills his slave, we will kill him," and it is a weak hadith.

Our evidence is His saying: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority, so let him not commit excess in killing﴾, and "the heir" here is the master. How then can authority be given to him over himself? All agree that if a master kills his slave by mistake, nothing is taken from him as the slave's value for the public treasury. End of quote.

Al-Qurtubi responded to Ibn al-'Arabi's weakening of al-Hasan's hadith from Samura, by saying that al-Bukhari and Ibn al-Madini authenticated his hearing from him. You have already learned that most scholars weakened al-Hasan's narration from Samura, as mentioned before; and al-Hasan's own opposition to it indicates its weakness.

Sixth: the hadith comes out in the form of a warning and emphasis in deterrence.

Seventh: what has been said, that it is abrogated (mansukh).

Al-Shawkani said: "The abrogation is supported by al-Hasan's fatwa contrary to it."

Eighth: the implication (mafhum) of His saying: ﴿and the slave for the slave﴾. But we have already mentioned that this implication is not considered, as the occasion of revelation indicates.

The scholars who held that a free person is not killed for a slave, and they are the majority, cited several pieces of evidence. Among them is what al-Daraqutni narrated with his chain from Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash, from al-Awza'i, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather: "A man killed his slave deliberately, so the Prophet (ﷺ) flogged him, banished him for a year, erased his name from among the Muslims, did not impose retaliation (qisas) on him for it, and ordered him to free a slave." The narration of Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash from the Syrians is strong and sound.

It is known that al-Awza'i was a Syrian from Damascus. In *Nayl al-Awtar*, he said: "But before him in the chain of this hadith is Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz al-Shami. Ibn Abi Hatim said of him: 'He was not praised among them, and he has strange (gharib) narrations.'"

Al-Bayhaqi also narrated this hadith, saying: "Abu Bakr ibn al-Harith al-Faqih informed us; 'Ali ibn 'Umar al-Hafiz told us; al-Husayn ibn al-Husayn al-Sabuni al-Antaki, judge of the frontier regions, told us; Muhammad ibn al-Hakam al-Ramli told us; Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz al-Ramli told us; Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash told us, from al-Awza'i," through to the end of the earlier chain, with the wording of the text (p-386). Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz al-Ramli is among the narrators of al-Bukhari. Ibn Hajar said of him in *al-Taqrib*: "Truthful, but he makes mistakes." Therefore, weakening this hadith on account of him is open to question.

Apparently, al-Bayhaqi's weakening of it comes from the side of Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash. You already know that the correct view is that his narrations are strong when they come from Syrians, not from the people of the Hijaz, as the imams of hadith, such as Imam Ahmad and al-Bukhari, have stated.

This hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb has a supporting report from the hadith of 'Ali, narrated by al-Bayhaqi and others, through Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash, from Ishaq ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Farwa, from Ibrahim ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Hunayn, from his father, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "A man was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who had deliberately killed his slave, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) flogged him one hundred lashes, banished him for a year, erased his name from among the Muslims, and did not impose retaliation on him for it." However, Ishaq ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Farwa is matruk (abandoned as a narrator).

Among their evidence that a free person is not killed for a slave is what al-Bayhaqi and others narrated: "From 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: a slave girl came to him whom her master accused (of fornication), so he seated her in a fire, and her private part was burned. 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: 'By Him in whose hand my soul is, if I had not heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "A slave is not retaliated against by his owner, nor a child by his father," I would have retaliated against you for her.' So he (the master) was made to stand, struck him one hundred lashes, and said to the slave girl: 'Go, for you are free for the sake of Allah, and you are a client (mawlah) of Allah and His Messenger.'"

Abu Salih said, and al-Layth said: "This view is acted upon." In the chain of this hadith is 'Umar ibn 'Isa al-Qurashi al-Asadi. Al-Bayhaqi reported from Abu Ahmad that he heard Ibn Hammad mention from al-Bukhari that he is munkar al-hadith (a narrator of rejected narrations).

Al-Shawkani also said of him: "He is munkar al-hadith, as al-Bukhari said."

Among their evidence that a free person is not killed for a slave is what al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A free person is not killed for a slave." After quoting this hadith, al-Bayhaqi said: "There is weakness in this chain, and the narrator in its chain is Juwaybir, who is very weak."

Al-Shawkani said regarding the chain of this hadith: "It includes Juwaybir and others among the abandoned narrators."

Among their evidence that a free person is not killed for a slave is what al-Bayhaqi and others narrated through the route of Jabir ibn Zayd al-Ju'fi, from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), that he said: "It is part of the Sunnah that a free person not be killed for a slave." Only Jabir, mentioned above, narrated this hadith alone, and most scholars have declared him weak. Ibn Hajar said of him in *al-Taqrib*: "Weak, a Rafidi (extreme Shi'i)."

Al-Nasa'i said of him: "Matruk." Some people, including al-Thawri, regarded him as trustworthy. Al-Bayhaqi, in *al-Sunan al-Kubra*, in the chapter "On the prohibition of leading the prayer while seated," reported from al-Daraqutni that he is matruk.

Among their evidence also is what al-Bayhaqi narrated in *al-Sunan al-Kubra* through the route of al-Muthanna ibn al-Sabbah, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As (may Allah be pleased with both of them), who said: "Zinba' had a slave called Sandar, or the son of Sandar. He found him kissing a slave girl of his, so he seized him, castrated him, and cut off his ears and nose. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'Whoever mutilates his slave or burns him with fire, he is free, and he is a client of Allah and His Messenger.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) freed him and did not impose retaliation on him for it. He (the slave) said: 'O Messenger of Allah, give me a recommendation.' He said: 'I recommend you to every Muslim.'"

After quoting this hadith, al-Bayhaqi said: "Al-Muthanna ibn al-Sabbah is weak and cannot be used as evidence. It has been narrated from al-Hajjaj ibn Arta'ah, from 'Amr, in abridged form, and it cannot be used as evidence either. We have already mentioned in the verse on tayammum the weakness of al-Hajjaj ibn Arta'ah."

It has also been narrated from Sawwar ibn Abi Hamza, but he is not strong, and Allah knows best. Thus said al-Bayhaqi.

The author of this commentary (may Allah pardon him) says: Sawwar ibn Abi Hamza is among the narrators of Muslim. Ibn Hajar said of him in *al-Taqrib*: "Truthful, but he has errors."

Among their evidence also is what Abu Dawud transmitted from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "A man came seeking help (mustasrikh) to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'An incident has befallen him, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Woe to you, what is wrong with you?' He said: 'Evil. He saw a slave girl belonging to his master, became jealous, and castrated him.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Bring the man to me.' He was sought but could not be found. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Go, for you are free.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, from whom shall I seek help?' He said: 'From every believer,' or he said: 'From every Muslim.'"

Among their evidence also is what al-Bayhaqi transmitted in *al-Sunan al-Kubra* from Abu Ja'far, from Bukayr, who said: "The Sunnah has passed that a free Muslim is not killed for a slave, even if he kills him deliberately, but he owes the blood money (al-'aql)."

Among their evidence also is what al-Bayhaqi likewise transmitted from al-Hasan, 'Ata', al-Zuhri, and others, in their statement that a free person is not killed for a slave. Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather: "Abu Bakr and 'Umar did not kill a free person for a slave."

Although these numerous reports are not free from some criticism, some of them strengthen others and reinforce them, until the collection becomes fit to be used as evidence.

Al-Shawkani said in *Nayl al-Awtar*, and his exact words are: "Secondly, by the hadiths that decree that a free person is not killed for a slave. They have been narrated through multiple routes, some of which strengthen others, so they are fit to be used as evidence."

The author of this commentary (may Allah pardon him) says: These pieces of evidence are reinforced by the consensus of the scholars that there is no retaliation for a slave against a free person for injuries short of death. If no retaliation is imposed on him for injuries, then the absence of retaliation for killing is a fortiori. No one disagreed that a slave has no retaliation against a free person for injuries short of death except Dawud and Ibn Abi Layla. It is also reinforced by the scholarly consensus that if a slave is killed by mistake, what is due is his value (qimah), not the blood money (diyah). Some scholars restricted this to cases where his value does not exceed the blood money of a free person. It is also reinforced by the fact that the slave's resemblance to property is stronger than his resemblance to a free person, in that what applies to property applies to him: sale, purchase, inheritance, gifts, charity, and other kinds of disposal. Also, if a free person slanders him, the hadd (prescribed punishment) is not due on him according to the general body of scholars, except what is reported from Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, and the Zahiris, that it is due for slandering an umm walad (a slave mother of a child by her master) specifically.

What indicates that a free person is not subjected to the hadd for slandering a slave is what al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "I heard Abu al-Qasim (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever slanders his slave while the slave is innocent of what he says, he will be flogged on the Day of Resurrection, unless it was as he said.'" This indicates that he is not flogged in this world, as is clear.

This is a summary of the scholars' discussion on the ruling concerning the killing of a free person for a slave.

* *

As for the killing of a Muslim for a disbeliever, the majority of scholars prohibit it, including Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad. This was reported from 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Zayd ibn Thabit, and Mu'awiyah (may Allah be pleased with them). Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Ibn Shubrumah, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Ishaq, Abu 'Ubayd, Abu Thawr, and Ibn al-Mundhir also held this view, as Ibn Qudamah reported from them in *al-Mughni* and elsewhere. Al-Bayhaqi narrated it from 'Umar, 'Ali, 'Uthman, and others.

Abu Hanifah, al-Nakha'i, and al-Sha'bi held that a Muslim is killed for a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection). They based this on the general wording "a life for a life" in the verse and the hadith mentioned above, and on the hadith narrated by Rabi'ah ibn Abi 'Abd al-Rahman, from Ibn al-Baylamani, from Ibn 'Umar: "The Prophet (ﷺ) killed a Muslim for a mu'ahad (a non-Muslim under a treaty)." (p-389) This is a mursal (a narration whose chain omits the Companion) from the Companions and is weak. Ibn al-Baylamani cannot be used as evidence even if he had connected it, so how much more so when he has omitted a link. Al-Bayhaqi, in *al-Sunan al-Kubra*, titled a chapter for this hadith with the words: "Chapter: explaining the weakness of the report that was narrated concerning the killing of a believer for a disbeliever, and what came from the Companions on this matter," and he mentioned its routes and showed that all of them are weak.

Among what he said: "Abu Bakr ibn al-Harith al-Faqih informed us, saying: Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn 'Umar al-Daraqutni, the hafiz, said: 'Ibn al-Baylamani is weak; no proof can be established by him if he connects a hadith, so how much more so when he omits a link.' And Allah knows best."

Al-Qurtubi said, in his tafsir of the words of the Exalted: ﴿The free for the free, and the slave for the slave﴾ (the verse), and his exact words are: "What they narrated from the hadith of Rabi'ah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) killed a Muslim for a disbeliever on the day of Khaybar, cannot be authenticated, because it is cut off (munqati'); and from the hadith of Ibn al-Baylamani, who is weak, from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet), al-Daraqutni said: 'No one transmitted it with a chain except Ibrahim ibn Abi Yahya, who is matruk al-hadith (abandoned in hadith).' The correct version is from Rabi'ah, from Ibn al-Baylamani, as a mursal from the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn al-Baylamani is weak in hadith, and no proof can be established by him even if he connects the hadith, so how much more so when he omits a link."

So when you know the weakness of the evidence for killing a Muslim for a disbeliever, know that the ruling that he is not killed for him is established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with an authenticity free from any flaw, which clarifies the invalidity of those pieces of evidence that cannot be relied upon.

Al-Bukhari transmitted in his Sahih, in the chapter "Writing knowledge" and in the chapter "A Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever," that "Abu Juhayfah asked 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): 'Do you have anything that is not in the Qur'an?' He said: 'No, by Him who split the grain and created the soul, except an understanding that Allah gives a man in His Book, and what is in this sheet.' I said: 'What is in the sheet?' He said: 'The diyah (blood money), the ransom of captives, and that a Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever.'"

This is a sound, decisive text that ends the dispute. It specifies the general wording of "a life for a life," and it shows that the reports narrated to the contrary are not valid. Nothing sound in this matter contradicts it. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir, after quoting this hadith of 'Ali: "No hadith or interpretation that contradicts this is sound." Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir: "I say: in this matter, there is no sound report except the hadith of al-Bukhari, and it specifies the general wording of the Exalted's words: ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾ (the verse), and the general wording of His words: ﴿that a life is for a life﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]."

This, which we have mentioned in this discussion, is the verification of the ruling on qisas for lives among males and females, free persons and slaves, and Muslims and disbelievers.

And as for the law of retaliation (qisas) between them concerning limbs and body parts, the majority of scholars hold that it follows the qisas for lives. So every two persons between whom qisas for life applies, qisas for limbs also applies between them. Thus a free Muslim is amputated for a free Muslim, a slave for a slave, a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection) for a dhimmi, a male for a female, and a female for a male. A deficient person is also amputated for a complete one, such as a slave for a free person, and a disbeliever for a Muslim.

The well-known position of the school of Malik is that a deficient person is not subjected to qisas for a complete person in injuries. So no retaliation is taken from a slave who injured a free person, nor from a disbeliever who injured a Muslim. This is what Khalil ibn Ishaq al-Maliki meant in his *Mukhtasar* when he said: "Injury is like killing in the act, the doer and the victim, except that a deficient person who injures a complete person" (meaning, no retaliation is taken from him for that). The narration of Ibn al-Qassar from Malik is that qisas is obligatory, in agreement with the majority. Whoever is not killed for killing is not amputated for a body part, so a Muslim is not amputated for a disbeliever, nor a free person for a slave. Among those who said this are Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, al-Thawri, Abu Thawr, Ishaq and Ibn al-Mundhir, as transmitted from them by the author of *al-Mughni* and others.

Abu Hanifa said: there is no qisas for limbs between those whose blood-money (badal) differs. So a complete person is not amputated for a deficient person, nor a deficient person for a complete person, nor a man for a woman, nor a woman for a man, nor a free person for a slave, nor a slave for a free person.

A Muslim is amputated for a disbeliever, and a disbeliever for a Muslim, because equality (takafu') is considered in limbs. The evidence is that a healthy limb is not taken for a paralysed one, nor a complete limb for a deficient one. Likewise, a man's limb is not taken for a woman's limb, nor her limb for his, just as the left is not taken for the right.

The majority answered: whoever has qisas for life between them has qisas for limbs between them, like two free persons. What the opponent mentioned is refuted by qisas for life, for equality is considered there too. The evidence is that a Muslim is not killed for a person under safe-conduct (musta'man). Moreover, it would follow that a deficient woman's limb is taken for a complete woman's limb, since equality exists and there is an additional surplus. So it is obligatory to take it for that when the claimant agrees, just as the fingers of one with fewer fingers are taken for the fingers of one with a full set.

As for the left and right, they are treated as life is treated, because their places differ. For this reason their blood-money is equal. So it is known that they are not deficient relative to each other in the law, and that the reason for them is not as the opponent stated. This is what Ibn Qudama said in *al-Mughni*.

(p-391) Among the evidence that qisas applies to limbs between those among whom it applies to lives is the Most High's saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life, and the eye for the eye, and the nose for the nose, and the ear for the ear, and the tooth for the tooth, and for wounds is retaliation.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 45].

As for what is narrated from Imam Ahmad, that there is no qisas between slaves for what is less than life, this is also the view of al-Sha'bi, al-Thawri and al-Nakha'i, and agrees with Abu Hanifa. They reasoned that the limbs of slaves are property, like livestock, which must be returned to the owner, based on the majority's evidence mentioned above; and that the lives of slaves are also property, like livestock, although Allah the Most High explicitly mentioned qisas for them in His saying: ﴿and the slave for the slave﴾.

Know that for qisas in matters less than life, three conditions are required:

The first: that it be intentional. This is also required for life-for-life qisas.

The second: that qisas for life applies between the two.

The third: that retaliation can be carried out without excess (haif) or surplus. Allah the Most High says: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾, the verse [al-Nahl: 126], and He says: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqara: 194]. If it cannot be carried out without surplus, qisas falls away and blood-money (diya) becomes obligatory. For this reason the scholars agreed that whatever can be carried out without excess or surplus is subject to the qisas mentioned in the verse, in His saying: ﴿and the eye for the eye, and the nose for the nose, and the ear for the ear, and the tooth for the tooth﴾, and like injuries at a joint, such as cutting off the hand or foot at their joints.

They differed over cutting a limb not at a joint but from within the bone itself. Some made qisas obligatory in it, seeing that it can be done without surplus. Among those who said this is Malik, who made qisas obligatory for cutting a bone not at a joint, except where death is feared, such as cutting the thigh and the like.

Al-Shafi'i said: qisas is not obligatory for any bone absolutely. This is also narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn Abbas. Ata', al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Zuhri, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz also held this, and Sufyan al-Thawri and al-Layth ibn Sa'd followed it. It is the well-known position of Imam Ahmad, as transmitted from them by Ibn Kathir and others.

Abu Hanifa and his two companions said: qisas is not obligatory for any bone except the tooth.

(p-392) Those who said there is no qisas for cutting a bone not at a joint argued by what Ibn Majah narrated through Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash, from Dahtham ibn Qaran, from Nimran ibn Jariya, from his father Jariya ibn Zafar al-Hanafi: "that a man struck another man on his forearm with a sword, not at a joint, and cut it off. He sought the Prophet (ﷺ) for justice, and he ordered blood-money for him. The man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I want qisas.' He said: 'Take the blood-money; may Allah bless you in it,' and he did not decide qisas for him."

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: this hadith does not have any chain other than this one. Dahtham ibn Qaran al-Ukli is weak, a Bedouin, and his narrations are not used as evidence. Nimran ibn Jariya is also weak, a Bedouin, and his father Jariya ibn Zafar is mentioned among the Companions. End of quotation from Ibn Kathir.

Ibn Hajar said in *al-Taqrib* about the aforementioned Dahtham: "abandoned" (matruk), and about the aforementioned Nimran: "unknown" (majhul). The scholars' disagreement on this is only from their disagreement over the realization of the point (manat) of the question. Those who say there is qisas say it can be carried out without excess. Those who say there is not say it cannot be carried out without surplus or deficiency. They are the majority.

From here the scholars prohibited qisas where death is feared, such as after the *mudiha* (a wound exposing the bone) of a *munaqqila* (a wound that displaces bone fragments and removes some of the skull bones), or a *ma'mouma* (a head wound reaching the membrane covering the brain), or a *damigha* (a wound that pierces the membrane of the brain), and like the *jaifa* (a wound penetrating into the body cavity), and similar, out of fear of destruction.

People objected to Ibn al-Zubayr's (ruling of) qisas for the *ma'mouma*. They said: "We have not heard of anyone saying this before him." Know that a healthy eye is not taken for a blind eye, and a healthy hand is not taken for a paralysed one, and similar, as is clear.

* *

Note (tanbih)

If the injured party takes qisas from the one who injured him, for something less than life, and he dies from the qisas, then nothing is owed by the one who took qisas from him, according to Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and this is the view of the majority of the Companions, the Successors and others.

Abu Hanifa said: the blood-money is owed from the property of the one who took qisas. Al-Sha'bi, Ata', Tawus, Amr ibn Dinar, al-Harith al-Ukli, Ibn Abi Layla, Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, al-Zuhri and al-Thawri said: the blood-money is owed from the 'aqila (the paternal kin who bear blood-money) of the one who took qisas.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, al-Hakam ibn Utayba and Uthman al-Batti said: the portion of that wound is dropped from the one who took qisas, and the remainder is owed from his property. This is what Ibn Kathir said.

The truth is that the spread (sirayat) of retaliatory qisas is not liable, because the one killed by qisas was killed by right (al-haqq), as is narrated from Abu Bakr, Umar and others. This differs from the spread of a wrongful injury (jinaya), which is liable. The difference between them is very clear.

Know that an eye, an ear, or a left hand is not taken for a right hand, nor the reverse, because the place must be the same in qisas. It is reported from Ibn Sirin and Shurayk that they said one of them may be taken for the other. The first is the view of most people of knowledge.

Know that qisas for injuries must be delayed until the wound of the injured party heals. If he takes qisas before healing, and then his wound worsens, nothing is owed to him.

The evidence for this is what Imam Ahmad narrated from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather: "that a man stabbed another man with a horn in his knee, and came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Retaliate against me.' He said: 'Wait until you are healed.' Then he came to him and said: 'Retaliate against me,' and he retaliated against him. Then the man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have become lame.' He said: 'I forbade you, but you disobeyed me; may Allah keep you far away, and your lameness be nullified.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade that qisas be taken for a wound before its owner has healed." Ahmad alone narrated it. This is what Ibn Kathir said.

Some scholars permitted hastening qisas before healing. You have learned from the hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb mentioned above that the spread of the injury after qisas is wasted (hadar). Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said: it is not wasted, but is liable. The hadith is a proof against both of them, may Allah have mercy on them both. Its meaning is clear, because he hastened what was not his to hasten, so the Lawgiver nullified his right.

* *

When you have understood from what we mentioned the detail of the meaning of His saying: ﴿that whoever kills a soul, without a soul...﴾ the verse, then know that the implication of His saying: ﴿or corruption in the land﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 32] is what is mentioned in His saying: ﴿The only recompense for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption is that they be killed or crucified or have their hands and feet cut off from opposite sides, or be exiled from the land﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 33].

Ibn Kathir said in his *tafsir* (Qur'anic commentary): *muharaba* (waging war) is opposition and hostility, and it applies to disbelief, to highway robbery, and to terrorizing the road. Likewise corruption in the land applies to various kinds of evil. Allah the Most High says: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and livestock, and Allah does not like corruption﴾ [al-Baqara: 205].

Knowing this, understand that the one who wages war, who cuts the road and terrorizes the way, Allah mentioned that his recompense is one of four things: that they be killed, or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off from opposite sides, or be exiled from the land. The apparent meaning of this noble verse is that the imam has the choice among these, doing whatever he wills with the fighter, as the wording indicates, or because it indicates choice.

Its parallel in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿So the expiation is feeding ten needy persons, from the average of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 89], and His saying: ﴿So the recompense is the like of what he killed of livestock, judged by two just men among you, as an offering reaching the Ka'ba, or an expiation of feeding the needy, or the equivalent of that in fasting﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 95], and His saying: ﴿So a ransom of fasting or charity or sacrifice﴾ [al-Baqara: 196].

That the imam has the choice between them absolutely, without detail, is the view of Malik. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Mujahid, Ata', al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and al-Dahhak also said this, as transmitted from them by Ibn Jarir and others. It is also a narration from Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas. al-Qurtubi transmitted it from Abu Thawr, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i and Malik, and said: "It is also narrated from Ibn Abbas."

The Malikis preferred this view because the wording in it is self-standing, not requiring an omitted supposition. When wording is between being self-standing and requiring an omitted supposition, self-standing takes precedence, because it is the original state, unless there is a separate proof for the necessity of the supposition. Alluding to this, in *Maraqi al-Su'ud* he said, in *rajaz* meter:

"Likewise what opposes the defect of a flaw, from being original and self-standing..."

to his saying:

"Likewise the sequence for obligating action, by what has the preponderance among what is possible."

(p-395) The well-known report from Ibn 'Abbas is that this verse was revealed concerning several circumstances, and that it contains restrictions that are implied. Its explanation is that the meaning is: they are to be killed if they killed and did not take property; or they are to be crucified if they killed and took property; or their hands and feet are to be cut off from opposite sides if they took property and did not kill anyone; or they are to be banished from the land if they spread terror on the road, without killing anyone or taking property. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Abu Mijlaz, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Suddi, Ata al-Khurasani, and many others of the early scholars (al-salaf) and the Imams.

This is what Ibn Kathir said. al-Qurtubi and Ibn Jarir [al-Tabari] also transmitted it from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Mijlaz, Ata al-Khurasani, and others.

al-Qurtubi also reported from Abu Hanifa: if he kills, he is killed; if he takes property without killing, his hand and foot are cut off from opposite sides; and if he takes property and kills, the ruler has the choice: if he wishes, he cuts off his hand and foot, and if he wishes, he does not cut them off, and kills him and crucifies him.

It is not hidden that the apparent and immediate meaning of the verse is the first view, because adding restrictions to the apparent sense of the Qur'an requires a text from the Book or the Sunnah. And a Companion's (sahabi) explanation of this with such details does not have the ruling of a attributed-to-the-Prophet report (hukm al-raf'), since it may be from his own ijtihad (independent reasoning). We do not know of anyone who narrated, in explaining this verse with the mentioned restrictions, a report traced to the Prophet, except what Ibn Jarir reported in his Tafsir from Anas:

Ali ibn Sahl narrated to us, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, from Ibn Lahi'a, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, that 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan wrote to Anas ibn Malik, asking him about this verse. Anas wrote back to him informing him that this verse was revealed concerning those men of 'Urayna, and [the narration continues until] Anas said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked Jibril about the judgment regarding those who wage war (man harab), and he said: 'Whoever steals and spreads terror on the road, cut off his hand for his theft and his foot for his terrorizing; and whoever kills, kill him; and whoever kills and spreads terror on the road and makes lawful the forbidden private parts (al-farj al-haram), crucify him.'"

If this hadith were established, it would be decisive in the dispute. But in its chain is Ibn Lahi'a, and it is known that he became confused after his books were burned, so he is not to be used as proof. Also, the one who narrated it from him is not Ibn al-Mubarak nor Ibn Wahb, because their narration from him is more reliable than the narration of others. And Ibn Jarir himself does not consider this hadith he cited to be sound, for he said when citing it: "It has been reported from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, confirming what we have said on this, with a chain of narration about which there is scrutiny (nazar), and that is what 'Ali ibn Sahl narrated to us: al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us," up to the end of the chain we mentioned earlier, and we mentioned along with it the point of relevance from the text. However, this hadith, even if weak, strengthens this view upon which most of the scholars agree, and Ibn Kathir attributed it to the majority.

Know that the crucifixion mentioned in His saying ﴿or they be crucified﴾ has been disputed among the scholars. It has been said: he is crucified alive and prevented from drink and food until he dies. It has been said: he is crucified alive and then killed with a spear or the like while crucified. It has been said: he is killed first and then crucified after the killing. It has been said: he is taken down after three days. It has been said: he is left until his pus flows. The apparent view is that he is crucified after being killed for a period in which this becomes well known, because his crucifixion is a deterrent to others.

Likewise, His saying ﴿or they be banished from the land﴾: the scholars have also disputed what is meant by banishment. Some said its meaning is that they are pursued until they are overpowered, and the prescribed punishment (hadd) is enforced upon them, or they flee from the abode of Islam. This view was transmitted by Ibn Jarir from Ibn 'Abbas, Anas ibn Malik, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, al-Zuhri, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, and Malik ibn Anas.

Others said: it means that they are banished from their town to another town, or the ruler, or his deputy, expels them from his jurisdiction entirely. Ata al-Khurasani, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-Sha'tha', al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said that they are banished and are not expelled from the land of Islam.

A group went to the view that what is meant by banishment in the verse is imprisonment, because it is a banishment from the wideness of the world to the narrowness of the prison, so the imprisoned man becomes as if he were banished from the land, except from the place where he is held. They argued with the words of one of the prisoners on this:

*We went out from the world while we were of its people,*
*so we are not among the dead in it, nor among the living.*

*When the jailer comes to us one day for some need,*
*we are astonished and say: "This one has come from the world!"*

This is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions, and its lack of clear support is not hidden.

Ibn Jarir chose that what is meant by banishment in this verse is that he is taken out of his town to another town, and imprisoned there. A similar view is also reported from Malik. It has a sound basis, because exile from one's homeland is a kind of punishment, as is done to the unmarried fornicator (al-zani al-bikr). This is the closest of the views to the apparent meaning of the verse, because it is known that they are not meant to be banished from the entire earth to the heavens; so it is understood that what is meant by "the land" is their homelands, the leaving of which is hard upon them. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

* *

Issues on the rulings concerning those who wage war (muharibin)

The first issue: know that the majority of scholars establish the ruling of hirabah (armed brigandage) equally in cities (amsar) and on roads, due to the generality of His saying, ﴿and they strive upon the earth in corruption﴾. Among those who said this are al-Awza'i, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, and it is the school of al-Shafi'i and Malik. Malik even said regarding one who lures a man, deceives him until he brings him into a house, kills him, and takes what he has: this is hirabah, and his blood belongs to the ruler, not to the victim's heir, so his pardon of him does not carry weight in dropping the killing.

Al-Qadi Ibn al-'Arabi al-Maliki said: "During my days of judging among people, if someone brought me a thief who had entered a house with a knife, holding it to the heart of the owner of the house while he was asleep, and his companions were taking the man's property, I ruled concerning them with the ruling for those who wage war." Imam Ahmad hesitated on this. The apparent statement of al-Khiraqi is that there is no hirabah except on roads; so one is not a muharib in a city, because help reaches him there.

Many of the Hanbalis went to the view that one is a muharib in a city too, due to the generality of the evidence.

Abu Hanifa and his companions said: hirabah occurs only on roads, and not in cities, because help reaches a person there when he calls for it, unlike the road, where help is far from him and no one can come to his aid.

Ibn Kathir said: the ruling of hirabah does not apply to them unless they have weapons.

Among the weapons, according to most scholars, are sticks and stones, because lives and limbs are destroyed by them just as by weapons; Abu Hanifa disagreed.

The second issue: if the property that the muharib destroyed is less than the minimum value (nisab) of theft for which the hand is cut, or the person he killed was not an equal (ghayr mukafi'a) to him, such as if he kills a slave, or a disbeliever while he is a free Muslim, is the hand cut off for less than the nisab? And is he killed for killing one who is not equal to him or not?

The scholars differed on this. Some said: the hand is not cut off unless he takes a quarter dinar, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, and Ahmad. Malik said: the hand is cut off even if he did not take the nisab, because he is judged by the ruling of a muharib.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is the correct view, because Allah the Exalted set, through the tongue of His Prophet ﷺ, a quarter dinar as the threshold for the obligation of cutting the hand for theft, but He did not set any amount for the cutting in hirabah. He mentioned the recompense of the muharib; so this requires that their recompense be fulfilled in accordance with the hirabah, regardless of a grain. Furthermore, this is analogy of one principle upon another principle, which is itself disputed, and it is analogy of the higher upon the lower, which is the reverse of analogy. And how is it right to analogize the muharib upon the thief, when the muharib seeks to snatch property? If he is noticed, he flees; but if the thief enters with a weapon seeking property, and he is prevented from it, or people shout at him, and he fights against them, then he is a muharib, and he is judged by the ruling of those who wage war." End of Ibn al-'Arabi's words.

What supports this view is that taking from a secured place (hirz) is not a condition for what the muharib takes in order for his hand to be cut off. As for killing the muharib for one who is not equal to him, this is the view of most scholars; from al-Shafi'i and Ahmad there are two reports on it. The verified position is that equality is not a condition for killing in hirabah, because the killing in it is not merely for killing; rather, it is for general corruption, from terrorizing the road and seizing property.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption is only that they be killed﴾. So He commanded the enforcement of the prescribed punishments upon the muharib when he combines two things: hirabah and striving upon the earth in corruption. And He did not specify a noble person from a lowly one, nor an exalted one from a base one. End of al-Qurtubi.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: Among what indicates that equality is not considered in killing in hirabah is the consensus of the scholars that the pardon of the victim's heir in hirabah is void, having no effect, and the ruler must kill the muharib who killed. This is evidence that it is not a matter of pure retaliation (qisas), but rather there is an added severity from the aspect of hirabah.

The third issue: if the muharibun attacked a caravan, for example, and some of them killed some of the caravan, while some of the muharibun did not directly kill anyone, is everyone killed, or is only the one who directly killed killed? There is a difference of opinion on this. The verified position is that all are killed, because hirabah is based on achieving protection, support, and backing, so the one who directly does the act cannot carry it out except by the strength of the other who is a supporter to him and an aid in his hirabah. And if some of them killed and some of them took property, it is permissible to kill them all and crucify them all, because they are all partners in all of that. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, disagreed on this, saying: the prescribed punishment is due only on the one who committed the sin, and it does not extend to one who helped him in it, as with all the prescribed punishments; and upon the helper there is only discretionary punishment (ta'zir).

The fourth issue: if among the muharibun there is a child, or an insane person, or the father of the one against whom the crime was committed, does the prescribed punishment fall from all of them, so that the killing becomes for the heirs, who may kill if they wish or pardon if they wish, based on the view that the ruling for all is one, and so doubt concerning one act is doubt concerning all? This is the view of Abu Hanifa. Or does the prescribed punishment not fall from the others mentioned (other than the child, insane person, or father), and this is the view of most scholars, and it is the apparent view?

The fifth issue: if the muharibun repent after they have been overpowered, their repentance then does not change anything regarding the enforcement of the mentioned prescribed punishments upon them. But if they come repentant before they are overpowered, then the imam has no authority over them at that point, because the Divine prescribed punishments (hudud Allah) fall from them, and the rights of human beings (huquq al-adamiyyin) remain upon them. So retaliation is taken from them for lives and wounds, and they are obliged to make good what they destroyed of property, and the heir of the blood has the right to pardon if he wishes, and the owner of the property may waive it for them.

This is the view of most scholars, together with the consensus that the Divine prescribed punishments fall from them by their repentance before they are overpowered, as is the explicit statement of His saying: ﴿except those who repent before you gain power over them﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 34]. The taking of what is in their hands of property, and their being made to compensate for what they consumed, is required because that is usurpation (ghasb), so it is not permissible for them to own it. A group among the Companions and the Successors (tabi'un) said: the muharib who comes repentant before being overpowered is not pursued except for what property is found with him; as for what he consumed, he is not pursued for it. al-Tabari mentioned this from Malik through a narration of al-Walid ibn Muslim from him.

Al-Qurtubi said: This is the apparent position in the action of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him) regarding Ḥārithah ibn Badr al-Ghudānī. He was a *muḥārib* (one who wages war against God and His Messenger), but he repented before he was captured, so ʿAlī wrote him a public decree (*kitāban manshūran*) that the property and blood penalties were dropped from him. Ibn Jarīr mentioned something similar.

Ibn Khuwayz Mindād said: The reports from Mālik differ concerning the *muḥārib* when the prescribed punishment (*ḥadd*) has been carried out on him and no property is found with him. Is he pursued for the value of what he took as a debt, or is it dropped from him, as it is dropped from the thief? According to Mālik, the Muslim and the *dhimmī* are equal in this. As for the meaning of His words: ﴿Whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had slain mankind entirely; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved mankind entirely﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 32], the scholars differed about it. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: its meaning is that whoever kills a prophet or a just ruler (*imām ʿadl*), it is as if he had slain mankind entirely, and whoever supports him and strengthens his arm, it is as if he had saved mankind entirely. This was transmitted by al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Jarīr and others. Its distance from the apparent sense of the Qur'an is not hidden.

(p-400) Also from Ibn ʿAbbās: its meaning is that whoever violates the sanctity of a single soul by killing it, it is as if he had killed mankind entirely, because violating the sanctity of souls is equal in its sanctity and sin. Whoever refrains from killing one soul and spares it out of fear of Allah, it is as if he had saved mankind entirely, because souls are equal in this.

Also from Ibn ʿAbbās: ﴿it is as if he had slain mankind entirely﴾, meaning in the eyes of the one slain, since he has no interest in anyone's life after his own death. Whoever saves it and rescues it from destruction, it is as if he had saved mankind entirely in the eyes of the one rescued.

Mujāhid said: the meaning is that the one who kills a believing soul deliberately, Allah has made his recompense Hell, and He is angry with him, curses him, and prepares for him a great punishment. Even if he had slain all mankind, it would not add to that. And whoever does not kill, mankind is preserved from him.

Ibn Jarīr chose this view. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is that whoever kills a soul incurs the retaliation (*qiṣāṣ*) that is incurred by one who kills all mankind. He said: "and whoever saves it" means he pardons the one against whom killing has become obligatory. Al-Ḥasan also said: it is pardoning after having the power to punish. It was also said: the meaning is that whoever kills a soul, all believers are his opponents, because he has wronged them all, and whoever saves it, thanks to him is obligatory upon everyone. It was also said: this was specific to the Children of Israel. It was also said: the meaning is that whoever permits the killing of one person has permitted the killing of all, because he has denied the Sharīʿah, and whoever forbids the blood of one Muslim, it is as if he has forbidden the blood of all mankind.

Al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn Jarīr and others mentioned these views. Ibn Kathīr favoured the last view and attributed it to Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

Al-Bukhārī said in his Ṣaḥīḥ, a chapter titled "The words of Allah Most High: ﴿and whoever saves it﴾." Ibn ʿAbbās said: whoever forbids its killing except by right, mankind is preserved from him entirely.

Al-Qurṭubī said: its "saving" is an expression for abstaining and rescuing from destruction. Otherwise, the true giving of life, which is origination (*al-ikhtirāʿ*), belongs only to Allah Most High. This "giving of life" is like the words of Nimrod, may Allah curse him: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258], where he called abstention "giving life."

Likewise Ibn Jarīr said: the words of Allah Most High: ﴿The recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption is only that...﴾, the verse. Know that the reason for its revelation has been disputed. It was said: it was revealed concerning a group of polytheists. It was said: it was revealed concerning a group of People of the Book. It was said: it was revealed concerning the Ḥarūriyyah.

(p-401) The most famous of the views is what the reports in the authentic collections and others have attested to: that it was revealed concerning the people of ʿUrayna and ʿUkl, who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and found Medina unhealthy. So the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded that they be given milch camels, and commanded them to drink from their urine and milk. They set out, and when they became healthy and fat, they killed the Prophet's (ﷺ) shepherd and drove off the camels. News of them reached him (ﷺ), so he sent a detachment after them and they brought them back. He ordered that their hands and feet be cut off, their eyes branded with hot iron, and they were thrown into the lava field (*al-Ḥarrah*) asking for water, but they were not given water until they died.

According to this view, it was revealed concerning people who stole, killed, and disbelieved after their faith. These are the views of the scholars on the reason for its revelation. What the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates is that it concerns Muslim highway robbers, as a group of jurists said, based on His words: ﴿except those who repent before you have power over them﴾, the verse. For it is certainly not about disbelievers, because the repentance of a disbeliever is accepted after one has power over him, just as it is accepted before, by consensus (*ijmāʿ*), based on His words: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾ [al-Anfāl: 38].
