Nor is it about apostates, because the apostate is killed for his apostasy and disbelief and is not having his hand and foot cut off, based on the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) connecting it to what requires killing: "the one who abandons his religion and separates from the community," and his words: "Whoever changes his religion, kill him." So it is specifically about Muslim combatants. If it is asked: is it correct to describe a Muslim as one who wages war against Allah and His Messenger? The answer is: yes.

The evidence is His words: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and give up what remains of interest, if you are believers﴾ ﴿But if you do not, then be informed of war from Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 278–279].

Note:
Some scholars were troubled by his (ﷺ) treatment of the people of ʿUrayna, since he branded their eyes along with cutting off their hands and feet, whereas the apostate is killed and is not mutilated.

The answer has been disputed. It was said, as al-Ṭabarī related from some scholars, that this verse abrogated the Prophet's (ﷺ) action toward them. Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn said that this happened before the prescribed punishments (*ḥudūd*) were revealed. Abū al-Zinād said that this verse was a rebuke to him (ﷺ) for what he did to them, and after that rebuke he did not repeat it. This was stated by Abū Dāwūd.

The verified answer is that he (ﷺ) did this to them as retaliation (*qiṣāṣ*). It is established in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim and elsewhere that he (ﷺ) branded their eyes only as retaliation, because they had branded the eyes of the herders of the milch camels. Al-Badawī al-Shinqīṭī put this in his poem on the *Maghāzī* with these words (in *rajaz* meter):

Afterward, those who had gone to extremes plundered them, and they, with the severity of hunger, found Ṭaybah (Medina) unhealthy.
So they went out and drank their milk, and when they became fat, they broke their covenant of safety.
So the Prophet (ﷺ) took retaliation against them, because they mutilated his servant, and they branded his eyes.

The commentator of the poem, Ḥammād, objected to the poet's wording "his servant," because it is established that they mutilated the herders. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and seek the means (wasilah) to Him⦆ — the verse.

Know that the majority of scholars hold that what is meant by al-wasilah (means, a means of nearness) here is drawing near to Allah, the Exalted, by carrying out His commands and avoiding His prohibitions in accordance with what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought, sincerely for Allah, the Exalted, in that; for this alone is the path that leads to the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted, and attaining what He has of the good of this world and the Hereafter.

The root meaning of al-wasilah is the path that brings one close to a thing and conveys one to it, and it is, by the consensus of the scholars, righteous deeds; for there is no means to Allah, the Exalted, except by following His Messenger (ﷺ). On this basis, the verses that clarify the meaning of al-wasilah are very numerous, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7], and His saying: ﴿Say: If you should love Allah, then follow me﴾ [Al 'Imran: 31], and His saying: ﴿Say: Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ [al-Nur: 54], and other verses besides these.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that what is meant by al-wasilah is need (hajah). When Nafi' al-Azraq asked him, "Do the Arabs know that?", he recited to him the verse of 'Antarah:

"Indeed, men have a wasilah to you; if they take you, then adorn yourself with kohl and dye (your hands)."

He said: it means that they have a need of you. In accordance with this statement narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, the meaning is: ﴿and seek to Him the wasilah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 35], i.e., seek your need from Allah, for He alone is the One who is able to grant it. Among what clarifies the meaning of this view is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those you worship besides Allah do not possess for you any provision; so seek provision from Allah and worship Him﴾ — the verse [al-'Ankabut: 17], and His saying: ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty﴾ — the verse [al-Nisa': 32], and in the hadith: "If you ask, then ask Allah."

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The verified meaning of al-wasilah is what the majority of scholars have held, namely that it is drawing near to Allah, the Exalted, by sincerity toward Him in worship, in accordance with what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought. The interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas falls within this; for calling upon Allah and turning to Him in supplication for needs is among the greatest forms of His worship, which is the means to attaining His good pleasure and mercy.

By this verification you know that what many of the heretics, the followers of ignorant people who claim Sufism, assert, namely that what is meant by al-wasilah in the verse is the shaykh who serves as an intermediary between a person and his Lord, is a stumbling in ignorance and blindness, a manifest error, and a trifling with the Book of Allah, the Exalted. Taking intermediaries other than Allah is among the roots of the disbelief of the disbelievers, as He, exalted is He, explicitly stated about them: ﴿We do not worship them except that they bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], and His saying: ﴿And they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah." Say: Do you inform Allah of what He does not know in the heavens or on the earth? Glory be to Him and exalted is He above what they associate﴾ [Yunus: 18]. Therefore it is obligatory upon every accountable person to know that the path that leads to the pleasure of Allah, His Paradise and His mercy is following His Messenger (ﷺ), and whoever deviates from that has strayed from the right way: ﴿It is not by your wishful thinking, nor the wishful thinking of the People of the Scripture; whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ — the verse [al-Nisa': 123].

Apparently, the meaning of al-wasilah in the verse of 'Antarah is also drawing near to the beloved, because it is a means to attaining what is intended from him. For this reason Ibn Jarir, al-Qurtubi and others cited the verse of 'Antarah mentioned above for this meaning which we have mentioned. The plural of wasilah is wasa'il, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"When the slanderers become heedless, we return to our union, and the purity between us and the means (wasa'il) return."

This which we have explained wasilah by here is also its meaning in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those whom they call upon seek a means to their Lord, which of them is nearest﴾ — the verse [al-Isra': 57]. Nor is the meaning of wasilah here the rank in Paradise which we were commanded by the Prophet (ﷺ) to ask Allah to give him; we hope that Allah grants it to him, for it is not fitting except for one servant, and he hopes that he will be that one.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 41:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿They say: "If you are given this, then accept it; but if you are not given it, then beware."﴾ In this noble verse there is brevity (ijmal), because what is pointed to by His words "this" (hadha) explains the pronoun in His words "then accept it" (fakhudhuhu), and His words "if you are not given it" (lam tu'tawhu). It was not stated explicitly in the verse, but Allah alluded to it here and mentioned it in another place.

Know first that this verse was revealed concerning the Jewish man and the Jewish woman who committed adultery after having been married (ihsan). The Jews had altered the ruling on stoning (rajm) in the Torah, and they deliberately distorted the Book of Allah. They agreed among themselves that the adulterer who was married, whose punishment they knew to be in the Book of Allah, the Torah, was stoning, would instead be flogged and disgraced by blackening the face and being mounted on a donkey. When the two mentioned had committed adultery, they said among themselves: "Come, let us refer the matter of their punishment to Muhammad (ﷺ). If he rules for flogging and blackening the face, then take that from him and make it a proof between you and Allah the Exalted, and it will be that a prophet of the prophets of Allah has ruled concerning them with that. But if he rules for stoning, then do not follow him." When you know this, know that what is meant by His words "this" (hadha), His words "then accept it" (fakhudhuhu), and His words "but if you are not given it" (wa in lam tu'tawhu) is the distorted ruling, which is flogging and blackening the face, as we have explained. Allah alluded to this here with His words: ﴿They distort words from their places, saying: "If you are given this"﴾, meaning the distorted and altered ruling which is flogging and blackening the face, "then accept it"; ﴿"but if you are not given it"﴾, meaning if he rules with the truth, which is stoning, "then beware of accepting it."

He, exalted is He, also mentioned this in His words: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book, being called to the Book of Allah﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 23], meaning the Torah, ﴿that it may judge between them﴾, meaning concerning the two adulterers mentioned, ﴿then a party of them turns away while they are refusing﴾, that is, from what is in the Torah of the ruling on stoning the married adulterer. His words here: ﴿then a party of them turns away while they are refusing﴾ are the meaning of His words about them: ﴿but if you are not given it, then beware﴾. And Allah, the Exalted, knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 42:

The author said in (Dafʿ Iham al-Idtirab ʿan Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them﴾, and so on, to the end of the verse.

This noble verse indicates that the Prophet (ﷺ), when the People of the Book came to him for judgment, was given a choice between judging between them and turning away from them. But another verse has come which indicates the opposite of this, namely His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Ma'idah: 49].

The answer is that His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And judge between them﴾ abrogates (naskh) His saying ﴿or turn away from them﴾. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Zayd ibn Aslam (p-274) and ʿAta' al-Khurasani, and others besides them. This is what Ibn Kathir stated.

It has also been said: the meaning of ﴿And that you judge﴾ is: if you judge between them, then judge by what Allah has revealed and not by following whims. On this basis the first verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated), and Allah knows best.

He (Exalted is He) said in this noble verse that the rabbis and the monks were entrusted with the Book of God, meaning they were made its custodians, and He required them to preserve it. Here He does not state whether they complied and preserved it, or failed to comply and lost it. But He made clear in other passages that they did not comply, and did not preserve what they were entrusted with. Rather, they deliberately distorted and altered it, as in His saying: ﴿They distort words from their places﴾ [an-Nisa: 46], and His saying: ﴿They distort words after their (proper) places﴾, and His saying: ﴿You make it into scattered pages, showing some and concealing much﴾ [al-An'am: 91], and His saying: ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands, then say, "This is from God"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79], and His saying, Majestic and Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed among them is a group who twist their tongues with the Book, so that you may think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 78], along with other verses.

**Note**

If it is said: what is the difference between the Torah and the Qur'an? Both are the speech of God, which He sent down to one of His messengers (may the blessings and peace of God be upon them). The Torah was distorted and altered, as we have explained above, whereas the Qur'an is protected from distortion and alteration. Were anyone to distort a single letter of it, replacing it with another, or adding a letter to it, or removing another, the thousands of young children among the Muslims would refute him, not to mention their adults.

The answer is that God entrusted them with the Torah and made them its custodians, but they betrayed the trust, did not preserve it, and deliberately lost it. As for the Mighty Qur'an, God did not leave its preservation to anyone, such that it would be possible for them to lose it. Rather, He Himself, Majestic and Exalted, undertook its preservation with His own noble and holy Self, as He clarified in His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [al-Hijr: 9], and His saying: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it﴾ [Fussilat: 42], along with other verses. The "ba'" in His saying ﴿by what they were entrusted with﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44] is connected to "the monks and the rabbis," because they only attained that rank by means of what they were entrusted with from the Book of God.

It has also been said that it is connected to "judges" (yahkumu). The meaning is close.

* *

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾. The scholars differed concerning this noble verse: is it about the Muslims, or about the disbelievers? It is related from ash-Sha'bi that it refers to the Muslims, and it is also related from him that it refers to the Jews. It is also related from Tawus that it refers to the Muslims, and that the meaning of "disbelief" in it is a lesser disbelief, not the disbelief that removes one from the religious community. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning this verse that he said: "It is not the disbelief you think it to be." This was narrated from him by Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who said it is sound according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), though they did not record it. This was stated by Ibn Kathir.

Some scholars said: The Mighty Qur'an indicates that it refers to the Jews, because He, Exalted, mentioned before it that they ﴿distort words from their places﴾, and that they say ﴿If you are given this, take it﴾, meaning the distorted ruling which is other than the ruling of God; ﴿but if you are not given it﴾, that is, the distorted one, but rather you are given the true ruling of God, then beware. So they command caution against the ruling of God, which they know to be true.

And He, Exalted, said after it: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the soul is for the soul﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]. This indicates that the discourse is about them. Among those who said that the verse concerns the People of the Book is what was mentioned by al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Mijlaz, Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi, 'Ikrimah, 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah, al-Hasan al-Basri, and others. al-Hasan added: "And it is obligatory upon us." Ibn Kathir transmitted this from them, and he transmitted something similar to al-Hasan's view from Ibrahim an-Nakha'i.

al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾, and ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ and ﴿the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44, 45, 47], all of them were revealed concerning the disbelievers. This is established in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of al-Bara', which has already been mentioned. According to this majority view, a Muslim does not become a disbeliever even if he commits a major sin. It has also been said that there is an omission in it, meaning: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed﴾, rejecting the Qur'an and denying the words of the Messenger (ﷺ), so he is a disbeliever. This was stated by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

On this view the verse is general. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan said: it is general to everyone who does not judge by what God has revealed, from among the Muslims, the Jews, and the disbelievers, that is, one who holds that belief and considers it lawful.

As for one who does this while believing that he is committing a forbidden act, he is among the defiantly disobedient Muslims, and his affair is up to God, Exalted: if He wills, He punishes him, and if He wills, He forgives him.

Ibn 'Abbas said in one narration: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed﴾ has done an act resembling the acts of the disbelievers. It has also been said: that is, whoever does not judge by all that God has revealed is a disbeliever. But whoever judges by monotheism and does not judge by some of the laws is not included in this verse. The first view is the correct one, except that ash-Sha'bi said: it refers specifically to the Jews. an-Nahhas chose this view, and he said: three things show this:

Among them: the Jews were mentioned before this in His saying: ﴿for those who became Jews﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44], so the pronoun returns to them.

Among them: the context of the discourse indicates this. Do you not see that after it is ﴿And We prescribed for them﴾? This pronoun refers to the Jews by consensus. Also, the Jews are the ones who denied stoning and retaliation (qisas). If someone says: "man" (whoever), when it is conditional, is general unless there is evidence specifying it, it is said to him: "man" here means "alladhi" (those who), along with the evidence and explanation we have mentioned. The Jews who did not judge by what God revealed: ﴿those are the disbelievers﴾. This is among the best of what has been said on this matter.

It is narrated that Hudhayfah was asked about these verses: "Are they about the Children of Israel?" He said: "Yes, they are about them, and you will surely follow their path step by step (hadhw an-na'l bi-n-na'l)." It has also been said: "the disbelievers" refers to the Muslims, "the wrongdoers" to the Jews, and "the defiantly disobedient" to the Christians. This is the choice of Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi, who said: because this is the apparent meaning of the verses. It is also the choice of Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir ibn Zayd, Ibn Abi Za'idah, Ibn Shubrumah, and also ash-Sha'bi. Tawus and others said: it is not a disbelief that removes one from the religious community, but it is a disbelief short of disbelief.

This differs: if he judges by what he has, claiming it is from God, then it is an alteration of it that necessitates disbelief. If he judges by it out of desire and disobedience, then it is a sin which forgiveness can reach, according to the principle of Ahl as-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) regarding the forgiveness of sinners. al-Qushayri said: the doctrine of the Kharijites is that whoever accepts a bribe and judges by a ruling other than God's is a disbeliever. He attributed this to al-Hasan and as-Suddi. al-Hasan also said: God took three things from the rulers: that they not follow desire, that they fear God and not fear people, and that they not trade His verses for a small price. The words of al-Qurtubi end here.

The author of this commentary, may God pardon him, says: The apparent and immediate meaning from the context of the verses is that the verse ﴿then those are the disbelievers﴾ was revealed concerning the Muslims, because He, Exalted, said before it, addressing the Muslims of this nation: ﴿So do not fear the people, but fear Me, and do not trade My verses for a small price﴾, then He said: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾. So the address is to the Muslims, as is apparent and immediate from the context of the verse. Accordingly, the disbelief is either a disbelief short of disbelief, or he did it considering it lawful, or he intended by it the denial of God's rulings and rejecting them while knowing them.

As for one who judges by other than God's ruling while knowing that he is committing a sin, doing an ugly act, and desire led him to it, he is among the other disobedient Muslims. The context of the Qur'an also clearly shows that the verse ﴿then those are the wrongdoers﴾ concerns the Jews, because He said before it: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the soul is for the soul, and the eye for the eye, and the nose for the nose, and the ear for the ear, and the tooth for the tooth, and for wounds is retaliation. But whoever gives it as charity, it is expiation for him. And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the wrongdoers﴾.

So the address is to them, because the context clearly indicates this. It is likewise apparent that the verse ﴿then those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ concerns the Christians, because He said before it: ﴿And let the People of the Gospel judge by what God revealed therein. And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the defiantly disobedient﴾.

Know that the precise determination of the matter in this discussion is that each of disbelief (kufr), wrongdoing (zulm), and defiance (fisq) is sometimes used in the Sacred Law to mean sin, and at other times to mean disbelief that removes one from the religious community. "And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed," in opposition to the messengers and nullifying the rulings of God, then his wrongdoing, his defiance, and his disbelief are all disbelief that removes one from the religious community. And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed while believing that he is committing a forbidden act and doing an ugly deed, then his disbelief, his wrongdoing, and his defiance do not remove him from the religious community. You have come to know that the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that the first is about the Muslims, the second about the Jews, and the third about the Christians. What matters is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the causes. The verification of the rulings of all of them is what you have seen, and God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 45:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the soul is for the soul﴾, the verse. We have already presented the argument of Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) from the generality of this verse for the killing of a Muslim for a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection). The verse itself contains an indication that the disbeliever does not fall within the generality of the verse, as the majority of scholars (jumhur al-'ulama') have held. This is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever gives it as charity, it is an expiation for him﴾, the verse.

It is known that the disbeliever is not among those who give charity whose charity serves as an expiation for them, because disbelief is an evil deed with which no good deed benefits. Isma'il al-Qadi (Isma'il ibn Ishaq al-Qadi) drew attention to this in *Ahkam al-Qur'an*, as Ibn Hajar transmitted it in *Fath al-Bari*. What Isma'il al-Qadi mentioned, that the verse also indicates the exclusion of the slave, is based on the view that he cannot validly give his wound as charity, because the right belongs to his master, which is not accepted. For among the scholars there are those who say that matters relating to the slave's body, such as retaliation (qisas), he may pardon in them without his master. On this basis there is no obstacle to his giving his wound as charity. As for the view of the one who says that the meaning of ﴿it is an expiation for him﴾ is that giving the offence as charity is an expiation for the offender, not for the victim, there is likewise no obstacle to the aforementioned argument from the verse. This is because Allah does not mention of the disbeliever that he gives charity, since the disbeliever has no charity due to his disbelief. And what is false and has no benefit in it, Allah, exalted is He, does not mention in the context of affirmation and establishment. Moreover, this view is weak in the meaning of the verse.

The majority of scholars, from the Companions and those after them, hold that its meaning is that it is an expiation for the one who gives charity. This is the more apparent view, because the pronoun in it refers back to a previously mentioned party, and that is definitely the believer, not the disbeliever. Thus the argument from the verse is very clear.

**Caution (tanbih)**

Some scholars have used this noble verse as proof that two persons are not killed for one. For if they were both killed for him, this would go outside His saying: ﴿that the soul is for the soul﴾, since they would be two souls for one soul.

Among those who said this, relying on this proof, were Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Zuhri, Ibn Sirin, Habib ibn Abi Thabit, Abd al-Malik, Rabi'a, Dawud, and Ibn al-Mundhir. Ibn Abi Musa related it from Ibn Abbas. It was also narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Sirin, and al-Zuhri that only one of them is killed, and the shares of the rest of the blood money (diyah) are taken from the others, because each of them is equivalent to the victim, so substitutes are not exacted for one substituted party, just as blood money is not owed for a single victim. Ibn Qudamah transmitted this from those we have mentioned in *al-Mughni*.

They said: the requirement of His saying: ﴿the free for the free﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178], and His saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the soul is for the soul﴾, is that no more than one soul is taken for a soul. They said: and because the difference in attributes prevents retaliation, as shown by the fact that a free man is not killed for a slave, and difference in number is more fitting for that.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: there is no proof for the one who requires the killing of a group for one person. The view that a group is not killed for one is a narration from Imam Ahmad.

The well-known narration from Imam Ahmad, and the position of the three other Imams, is that a group is killed for one person. It is established from Umar ibn al-Khattab that he killed seven for one and said: "If the people of San'a' had colluded against him, I would have killed them all for him." Something similar was related from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him). He held back from fighting the Harurites until they committed aggression. When they slaughtered Abd Allah ibn Khabbab as a sheep is slaughtered, and Ali was informed of this, he said: "Allah is greatest. Call out to them: bring out to us the killer of Abd Allah ibn Khabbab." They said: "We all killed him," three times. Ali then said to his companions: "Take the people." He had not stayed long before Ali and his companions killed them. Al-Qurtubi transmitted this from al-Daraqutni in his *Sunan*.

What strengthens the killing of a group for one is what al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurayra, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If the people of the heavens and the people of the earth shared in the blood of a believer, Allah would throw them all into the Fire." al-Tirmidhi said of it: "It is a gharib hadith." Al-Qurtubi transmitted it from him.

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Sunan al-Kubra* narrated something similar from Ibn Abbas, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he added: "except if He wills." Al-Bayhaqi also narrated from Abu Hurayra, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever helps in the killing of a Muslim with half a word will meet Allah, mighty and majestic, on the Day of Resurrection with written between his eyes: 'despairing of the mercy of Allah'."

It was narrated from al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba and Ibn Abbas, and this is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan, (and) Abu Salama, 'Ata', Qatada, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr, as Ibn Qudamah transmitted from them in *al-Mughni*: that a group is killed for one. Al-Bayhaqi also related it from Umar and Ali (may Allah be pleased with them both). No opponent among the Companions is known for these two, so it became a silent consensus (ijma' sukuti). Some objected to this, saying that it is established from Ibn al-Zubayr that a group is not killed for one, as Ibn al-Mundhir said.

If so, the disagreement is among the Companions, and it is established in the principles of jurisprudence that when the Companions disagree, it is not permissible to act on one of the two views except with a preponderance (tarjih).

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The view of the majority, which is the killing of a group for one, is preponderant, because Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And for you in retaliation there is life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 179]. That is, whoever knows that he will be killed if he kills will be deterred by that and restrained from killing. If two persons were not retaliated against for one, then everyone who wished to kill a Muslim would take one of his helpers and kill him together with him, and there would be no deterrent from killing. By that, the wisdom of retaliation would be entirely lost from its root. Moreover, those who collude in killing are such that each of them is truly called a killer, so he is killed. What supports this is that if a group falsely accused one person, the legal punishment for slander (hadd al-qadhf) would be due on all of them. And Allah knows best.

The Qur'anic verse "And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein" does not specify here anything of what was revealed in the Gospel (al-Injil) that He commanded the People of the Gospel to judge by. In other places, however, He made clear that among that content is the good news of the sending of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), the obligation to follow him, and to believe in him. Such as His saying: ﴿And when Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O Children of Israel, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you, confirming that which came before me of the Torah and giving good tidings of a Messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad"﴾ [Al-Saff: 6], and His saying: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [Al-A'raf: 157], and other verses besides these.

A subtle point related to this noble verse: some scholars mentioned that a Christian said to a scholar of the Muslims: "Debate me on which is better, Islam or Christianity." The scholar said to the Christian: "Come to the debate on that." The Christian said: "Is what is agreed upon more deserving of being followed, or what is disputed?" The scholar said: "What is agreed upon is more deserving of being followed than what is disputed." The Christian said: "Then it is incumbent upon you to follow Jesus along with us, and to abandon following Muhammad (ﷺ), because we and you agree on the prophethood of Jesus, and we disagree with you on the prophethood of Muhammad, may peace be upon them both." The Muslim said: "It is you who refrain from (p-411) following what is agreed upon, because what is agreed upon, which is Jesus, said to you: ﴿and giving good tidings of a Messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾. So if you were truly followers of Jesus, you would have followed Muhammad (ﷺ). Thus it became clear that it is you who did not follow what is agreed upon, nor anything else." So the Christian was silenced.

There is no doubt that if the Christians were followers of Jesus, they would have followed Muhammad (ﷺ).

As for His saying: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, then they are the defiers﴾, we have already mentioned that this verse concerns the Christians, the one before it concerns the Jews, and the one before that concerns the Muslims, as the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates.

We have also mentioned that disbelief (kufr), wrongdoing (zulm), and defiance (fisq) are all applied to sin short of disbelief, and to disbelief that takes one out of the religion itself. From disbelief in the sense of sin is His saying (ﷺ) when a woman asked him about the reason women are the majority of the people of the Fire: "Indeed that happens because of their disbelief," then he explained it as their being ungrateful to their husbands (kufr al-'Ashir). From disbelief in the sense of what takes one out of the religion is His saying: ﴿Say: "O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship"﴾ [Al-Kafirun: 1–2], and from wrongdoing in the sense of disbelief is His saying: ﴿And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 254], and His saying: ﴿And do not call upon other than Allah that which neither benefits you nor harms you, for if you did, you would then be among the wrongdoers﴾ [Yunus: 106], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, associating others with Allah is a great wrongdoing﴾ [Luqman: 13]. From wrongdoing in the sense of sin is His saying: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate﴾ [Fatir: 32]. From defiance in the sense of disbelief is His saying: ﴿And as for those who defied, their refuge is the Fire; every time they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it﴾ [As-Sajdah: 20], and from it in the sense of sin is His saying about those who slandered 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her): ﴿And do not accept their testimony ever after, and those are the defiers﴾ [An-Nur: 4].

It is known that slander does not take one out of the religion, and His saying supports this: ﴿Indeed, those who came up with the lie are a band among you﴾ [An-Nur: 11]. Also from defiance in the sense of sin is His saying concerning al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah: ﴿O you who believe, if a defiant one brings you news, verify it﴾ [Al-Hujurat: 6].

We have already stated that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasions of revelation. So whoever refrains from judging by what Allah has revealed, with the intention of opposing it and rejecting it, and refusing to commit to it, is a disbeliever, a wrongdoer, and a defier, all in their meanings that take one out of the religion. But whoever refrains from judging by it out of desire, while believing that his act is wrong, his disbelief, wrongdoing, and defiance are not those that take one out of the religion, unless what he refrained from judging by is a condition for the validity of his faith, like refraining from believing in what must be believed. This is the apparent meaning in the aforementioned verses, as we have already mentioned, and Allah knows best.

The commentary begins here: when Allah says, ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies; they are allies of one another﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51], He mentions in this noble verse that the Jews and the Christians are allies of one another. However, He clarifies in other places that the alliance of some of them with others is false and not sincere, because it does not rest on a sound foundation, which is the religion of Islam. He makes clear that enmity and hatred between the Jews and the Christians will last until the Day of Resurrection, by His saying: ﴿And from those who said, "We are Christians," We took their covenant, but they forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of. So We cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 14]. He made a similar statement about the Jews as well, when He said of them: ﴿The Jews say, "The hand of Allah is chained." Their hands are chained, and they are cursed for what they say. Rather, His hands are both outstretched; He spends however He wills. And what has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. And We have cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64]. The apparent meaning is that this enmity is among the Jews themselves, as the clear context indicates, contrary to those who said that it refers to enmity between the Jews and the Christians.

He also explicitly stated that the Jews do not agree with one another, giving as the reason their lack of understanding, in His saying: ﴿You think them united, but their hearts are divided. That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾ [al-Hashr: 14].

Caution

Some scholars derived from His saying, ﴿some of them are allies of others﴾, that a Jew and a Christian inherit from each other. Others rejected this, arguing that the verse means the alliance of Jews with Jews specifically and of Christians with Christians specifically. According to this meaning, there is no evidence in the verse for inheritance between Jews and Christians.

As for His saying, ﴿And whoever among you allies with them, then indeed he is one of them﴾: in this noble verse He mentions that whoever among the Muslims allies with the Jews and the Christians becomes one of them by virtue of that alliance. In another place He clarifies that their alliance necessitates the wrath of Allah and abiding in His punishment, and that if the one allying with them were a believer, he would not have allied with them. This is His saying: ﴿You see many of them allying with those who disbelieve. Evil is what their souls have put forward for them: that Allah has become wrathful toward them, and in punishment they will abide. And if they had believed in Allah, the Prophet, and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies; but many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 80–81].

In another place He forbade allying with them, explaining the reason for keeping away from it, in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not ally with a people with whom Allah has become angry; they have despaired of the Hereafter as the disbelievers have despaired of the companions of the graves﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 13].

He also clarified in another place that this prohibition applies when the alliance is not due to fear and taqiyyah (precautionary dissimulation to protect oneself from harm). If it is due to such fear, then the one who does it is excused. This is His saying: ﴿Let not the believers take disbelievers as allies instead of believers. Whoever does that has nothing with Allah, except when you fear a danger from them. And Allah warns you against Himself, and to Allah is the final destination﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28]. Here, ﴿except when you fear a danger from them﴾ is the Arabic phrase ﴿إلّا أنْ تَتَّقُوا مِنهم تُقاةً﴾, which means except when you take precaution against them with precaution. This noble verse clarifies and explains all the verses that absolutely prohibit allying with disbelievers, because that prohibition applies in a state of free choice. In a state of fear and taqiyyah, however, alliance with them is permitted only to the degree of outward courtesy by which their harm is averted, and this requires that the inner heart remain free of that alliance. The poet said:

*And whoever undertakes matters under compulsion is not like one who undertakes them by choice.*

It is understood from the apparent meanings of these verses that whoever deliberately and freely allies with the disbelievers, desiring them, is a disbeliever like them.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 52:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them, saying, "We fear lest a misfortune should befall us." But perhaps Allah will bring a conquest or a decision from Him, and they will become, over what they had concealed within themselves, regretful.﴾ ﴿And those who believe will say, "Are these the ones who swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths that they were with you?" Their deeds have become worthless, and they have become losers.﴾

In this noble verse, He mentions that those in whose hearts is a disease, namely the hypocrites, make excuses for their allegiance to the disbelievers among the Jews, saying that they fear that the circles (al-dawa'ir) will turn against them, meaning the turns of time (duwal al-dahr), the circling of fortune from one people to another, as the poet said: [al-Wafir]

؎When time drags its chest over a people, it makes another group kneel down.

They mean either by a famine, so that [the Jews] will not supply us with provisions nor show us favour, or by the victory of the disbelievers over the Muslims, so that the matter will not remain with the Prophet ﷺ and his companions. They suppose that, when fortune turns in the manner mentioned, they will have friends among [the Jews] who have maintained their friendship, so they will obtain from them what a friend hopes from his friend. And the Muslims marvel at their lying in their swearing by Allah their most emphatic oaths that they were with the Muslims. In this verse He makes clear that those circles for whose sake they maintained friendship with the Jews turn only against the Jews and the disbelievers, and do not turn against the Muslims, by His saying: ﴿But perhaps Allah will bring a conquest or a decision from Him﴾ to the end of the verse. And the "perhaps" (asa) from Allah is binding, because He is the Generous, the Mighty, for whom one can hope only for what He gives.

As for the conquest mentioned, it has been said that it is the Muslims' conquest of the lands of the polytheists. It has also been said that the conquest is judgment, as in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with the truth, and You are the best of deciders﴾ [al-A'raf: 89]. Accordingly, it is Allah's judgment to kill the fighting men of the Banu Qurayza, take their children captive, and expel the Banu al-Nadir. It has also been said that it is the conquest of Makkah, and this refers back to the first.

Allah the Exalted explains in another place that the cause of their swearing false oaths to the Muslims, that they are of them, is only fear (al-faraq), that is, dread, and that if they found a refuge in which to hide from the Muslims, they would hasten toward it, because of the intensity of their hatred for the Muslims. This is His saying: ﴿And they swear by Allah that they are surely of you, but they are not of you; rather, they are a people who are afraid. If they could find a refuge or caves or a place of entry, they would turn toward it while rushing headlong.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 56-57]. In this verse is an explanation of the cause of the hypocrites' oaths, and its parallel is His saying: ﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾ [al-Mujadila: 16].

Allah the Exalted explains in another place that they swear those oaths in order to win the approval of the believers, and that if the believers are pleased with them, Allah is not pleased with them. This is His saying: ﴿They swear to you that you may be pleased with them; but if you should be pleased with them, indeed Allah is not pleased with the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 96].

He explains in another place that they intend by their oaths to please the believers, while Allah and His Messenger have more right to be pleased. This is His saying: ﴿They swear to you by Allah to please you, but Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him, if they are believers.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62].

He explains in another place that they swear to them so that they will be pleased with them, because they have a valid excuse, and that Allah commanded them to turn away from them, not because they have a valid excuse, but with the information that they are impure (rijs), and their refuge is Hellfire because of what they earned of hypocrisy. This is His saying: ﴿They will swear by Allah to you when you return to them that you may leave them alone. So leave them alone; indeed, they are impure, and their refuge is Hell as recompense for what they used to earn.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 95].

He explains in another place that their false oaths are a cause of their own destruction. This is His saying: ﴿And they will swear by Allah, "If we had been able, we would have gone out with you." They destroy themselves﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Tawbah: 42].

All these causes of the hypocrites' oaths mentioned in these verses trace back together to the first cause, which is fear, because their fear of the believers is the reason for their desire to please them and to turn away from them, so that they will not harm them. Therefore they swore to them, in order to please them and to turn away from them, out of fear of their harm, as is evident.

Note

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿And those who believe will say, "Are these the ones who swore…"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 53] has three canonical readings (qira'at sab'iyyah).

The first: "yaqulu" without waw, with the nominative (raf'), and with it Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Ibn 'Amir read.

The second: "wa-yaqulu" with the waw affirmed and the verb also in the nominative, and with it 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read.

The third: with the waw affirmed and "yaqulu" in the accusative (nasb), as a conjunction coordinated with ﴿an ya'ti bil-fath﴾, and with it Abu 'Amr read.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 54:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, whoever among you turns back from his religion - Allah will bring forth a people whom He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾ and the rest of the verse.

In this noble verse, Allah, may He be exalted, informs the believers that if some of them apostatize, Allah will bring in place of that apostate a people whose attributes include humility toward the believers, lowliness and gentleness toward them, and harshness and severity toward the disbelievers. This is among the perfect attributes of the believers. Allah commanded His Prophet ﷺ with this, ordering him to be gentle toward the believers, saying: ﴿And lower your wing to the believers﴾ [al-Hijr: 88], and His saying: ﴿And lower your wing to those who follow you of the believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 215]. He commanded him to be harsh toward others, saying: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be stern with them. Their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73]. Allah, may He be exalted, also praised His Prophet for his gentleness toward the believers, in His saying: ﴿So by mercy from Allah, you were lenient with them. And if you had been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you﴾ and the rest of the verse [Ali 'Imran: 159]. He also declared explicitly that what was mentioned of gentleness toward the believers and severity toward the disbelievers are attributes of the Messenger ﷺ and his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, saying: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are severe against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29].

(p-416) The poet said about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, [from al-Tawil]:

*Never has a camel carried, atop its saddle,*
*one more faithful to his covenant or more fulfilling of his trust than Muhammad.*

*And he gives when the seeker of kindness comes to him,*
*and he strikes with the edge of the sharpened, Indian sword.*

Another poet said about him, [from al-Tawil]:

*Never has a camel carried, atop its saddle,*
*one fiercer against his enemies than Muhammad.*

From these verses it is understood that the believer must not be gentle except at the time suited to gentleness, and must not be harsh except at the time suited to harshness, because gentleness in a place requiring harshness is weakness and feebleness, and harshness in a place requiring gentleness is folly and recklessness. Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi said, [from al-Tawil]:

*When it is said, "Forbearance," say, "Forbearance has its place,"*
*but a young man's forbearance in the wrong place is ignorance.*

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 67:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ – the verse.

In this verse, Allah, may He be exalted, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to convey what was sent down to him, and He bore witness to his compliance in several verses, such as:

• His saying: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3],

• and His saying: ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the conveying [of the message]﴾ [al-Nur: 54],

• and His saying: ﴿So turn away from them; you are not to be blamed﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 54]. Had it been possible for him to conceal anything, he would have concealed His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you would conceal within yourself that which Allah is to disclose, and you fear the people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37].

Therefore, whoever claims that he ﷺ concealed a single letter of what was sent down to him has greatly slandered Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 71:

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَحَسِبُوا ألّا تَكُونَ فِتْنَةٌ فَعَمُوا وصَمُّوا ثُمَّ تابَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمْ ثُمَّ عَمُوا وصَمُّوا كَثِيرٌ مِنهم واللَّهُ بَصِيرٌ بِما يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ الآيَةَ.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they thought there would be no trial, so they became blind and deaf; then Allah turned to them; then many of them became blind and deaf again. And Allah is Seeing of what they do.﴾ (the verse).

ذَكَرَ تَعالى في هَذِهِ الآيَةِ الكَرِيمَةِ أنَّ بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ عَمُوا وصَمُّوا مَرَّتَيْنِ، تَتَخَلَّلُهُما (p-٤١٨)تَوْبَةٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِمْ، وبَيَّنَ تَفْصِيلَ ذَلِكَ في قَوْلِهِ: ﴿وَقَضَيْنا إلى بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ في الكِتابِ لَتُفْسِدُنَّ في الأرْضِ مَرَّتَيْنِ﴾ الآيَةَ [الإسراء: ٤]، فَبَيَّنَ جَزاءَ عَماهم، وصَمَمِهِمْ في المَرَّةِ الأوْلى بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿فَإذا جاءَ وعْدُ أُولاهُما بَعَثْنا عَلَيْكم عِبادًا لَنا أُولِي بَأْسٍ شَدِيدٍ﴾ الآيَةَ [الإسراء: ٥]، وبَيَّنَ جَزاءَ عَماهم وصَمَمِهِمْ في المَرَّةِ الآخِرَةِ بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿فَإذا جاءَ وعْدُ الآخِرَةِ لِيَسُوءُوا وُجُوهَكم ولِيَدْخُلُوا المَسْجِدَ كَما دَخَلُوهُ أوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ ولِيُتَبِّرُوا ما عَلَوْا تَتْبِيرًا﴾، وبَيَّنَ التَّوْبَةَ الَّتِي بَيْنَهُما بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿ثُمَّ رَدَدْنا لَكُمُ الكَرَّةَ عَلَيْهِمْ وأمْدَدْناكم بِأمْوالٍ وبَنِينَ وجَعَلْناكم أكْثَرَ نَفِيرًا﴾، ثُمَّ بَيَّنَ أنَّهم إنْ عادُوا إلى الإفْسادِ عادَ إلى الِانْتِقامِ مِنهم بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿وَإنْ عُدْتُمْ عُدْنا﴾، فَعادُوا إلى الإفْسادِ بِتَكْذيبِهِ ﷺ وكَتْمِ صِفاتِهِ الَّتِي في التَّوْراةِ، فَعادَ اللَّهُ إلى الِانْتِقامِ مِنهم، فَسَلَّطَ عَلَيْهِمْ نَبِيَّهُ ﷺ فَذَبَحَ مُقاتِلَةَ بَنِي قُرَيْظَةَ، وسَبى نِساءَهم، وذَرارِيَّهم، وأجْلى بَنِي قَيْنُقاعَ، وبَنِي النَّضِيرِ، كَما ذَكَرَ تَعالى طَرَفًا مِن ذَلِكَ في سُورَةِ الحَشْرِ، وهَذا البَيانُ الَّذِي ذَكَرْنا في هَذِهِ الآيَةِ ذَكَرَهُ بَعْضُ المُفَسِّرِينَ، وكَثِيرٌ مِنهم لَمْ يَذْكُرْهُ، ولَكِنْ ظاهِرُ القُرْآنِ يَقْتَضِيهِ؛ لِأنَّ السِّياقَ في ذِكْرِ أفْعالِهِمُ القَبِيحَةِ الماضِيَةِ، مِن قَتْلِ الرُّسُلِ، وتَكْذِيبِهِمْ، إذْ قَبْلَ الآيَةِ المَذْكُورَةِ: ﴿كُلَّما جاءَهم رَسُولٌ بِما لا تَهْوى أنْفُسُهم فَرِيقًا كَذَّبُوا وفَرِيقًا يَقْتُلُونَ﴾ [المائدة: ٧٠] .

The noble verse mentions that the Children of Israel became blind and deaf twice, with a repentance from Allah toward them in between. He explained the details of this in His saying: ﴿And We decreed for the Children of Israel in the Scripture that you would cause corruption on the earth twice﴾ (the verse) [al-Isra' 17:4]. He explained the requital of their blindness and deafness in the first instance in His saying: ﴿So when the promise of the first of them came, We sent against you servants of Ours of great might﴾ (the verse) [al-Isra' 17:5]. He explained the requital of their blindness and deafness in the last instance in His saying: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter came, to sadden your faces and to enter the Masjid as they entered it the first time and to destroy what they had subjugated with destruction﴾. He explained the repentance that lies between them in His saying: ﴿Then We gave you the return of victory over them and provided you with wealth and children and made you more numerous in manpower﴾. Then He explained that if they returned to corruption, He would return to punishing them, in His saying: ﴿And if you return, We will return﴾. They returned to corruption by denying him, peace be upon him, and concealing his attributes that are in the Torah, so Allah returned to punishing them, and He empowered His Prophet, peace be upon him, over them, so he slaughtered the fighting men of Banu Qurayzah, took their women and offspring captive, and expelled Banu Qaynuqa' and Banu al-Nadir, as He, may He be exalted, mentioned a portion of that in Surat al-Hashr. This explanation that we have mentioned in this verse was mentioned by some of the commentators, and many of them did not mention it, but the apparent meaning of the Qur'an requires it, because the context concerns the past ugly deeds of theirs, such as killing the messengers and denying them, since before the mentioned verse is: ﴿Every time a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, a group they denied and a group they killed﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:70].

The meaning of ﴿And they thought there would be no trial﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:71] is: they thought that no affliction or punishment from Allah would befall them, because of their disbelief and their killing of the prophets, due to their false claim that they are the sons of Allah and His beloved.

His saying ﴿many of them﴾ — the best of the grammatical analyses of it is that it is a substitute (badal) for the waw of the subject in His saying ﴿they became blind and deaf﴾, like your saying: "The people came, most of them."

His saying ﴿there would be no trial﴾ — it was read by Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr with the nominative (raf'), and the rest with the accusative (nasb). The reading with the accusative is clear, because al-husban (reckoning, thinking) means al-zann (supposing). The reading with the nominative is by treating their belief in that, even if false, as if it were knowledge, so that ﴿anna﴾ is the lightened form of the heavy one (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah). And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 74:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness? And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾

In this verse He indicates that those who said, ﴿Indeed, Allah is the third of three﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 73], if they were to repent to Him from that, He would accept their repentance and forgive them, because He invited them to that with the most gentle and tender invitation, by His saying: ﴿Will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness?﴾ Then He indicated that if they did that, He would forgive them, by His saying: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ He stated this meaning in general terms for all the disbelievers by His saying: (p-419) ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they cease, they will be forgiven what has already passed﴾ [al-Anfal: 38], and the verse continues.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 75:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And his mother was a truthful woman. They both used to eat food.﴾ In this noble verse He mentions that ʿIsa and his mother used to eat food. He mentions in other places that all the messengers were like this,

• such as His saying: ﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they certainly ate food and walked in the markets.﴾ [al-Furqan: 20],

• and His saying: ﴿And We did not make them bodies that do not eat food.﴾ [al-Anbiya: 8],

• and His saying: ﴿And they said, "What is this messenger that eats food and walks in the markets?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 7],

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Look how We make the signs clear to them; then look how they are turned away.﴾ The meaning of His saying "yu'fakun" (they are turned away) [dh/ 75] is that they are diverted from the truth. What is meant by their being diverted from it is the saying of some of them: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary,﴾ and the saying of some of them: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the third of three,﴾ and the saying of some of them: ﴿ʿUzayr is the son of Allah.﴾ Glorified is He and exalted far above that with a great exaltation. Upon whoever says that be the curses of Allah until the Day of Resurrection, for they say this matter, of which no one has said anything more abominable or greater, despite the clear evidences of Tawhid that make it plain. Therefore the Exalted said: ﴿Look how We make the signs clear to them; then look how they are turned away,﴾ as an expression of wonder at their condition: how are they turned away to this disbelief despite the clarity of the evidences of Tawhid?!

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 78:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed upon the tongue of Dawud and 'Isa, the son of Maryam﴾ to the end of the verse. Some scholars ('ulama') said: those who were cursed upon the tongue of Dawud were those who transgressed on the Sabbath, and those who were cursed upon the tongue of 'Isa, the son of Maryam, were those among the People of the Table (ahl al-ma'idah) who disbelieved. Accordingly, the cursing of the first group was their transformation into apes, as Allah, may He be exalted, explained in His saying: ﴿And you had already known those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so We said to them, "Be apes, despised and expelled"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 65], and His saying: ﴿So when they persisted in what they had been forbidden, We said to them, "Be apes, despised and expelled"﴾ [al-A'raf: 166]. The cursing of the others is what is mentioned in His saying: ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves after that, I will surely punish him with a punishment by which I have not punished anyone among the worlds﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 115]. Many have mentioned that He transformed them into swine (khanazir). This view is narrated from al-Hasan, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Baqir. Al-Alusi transmitted it in his tafsir and said: "Many have chosen it." Al-Qurtubi transmitted it from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and Abu Malik, and he mentioned that it was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Some of those who held this view said: when the people of Aylah transgressed on the Sabbath, "Dawud (peace be upon him) said: 'O Allah, clothe them with the curse like a cloak, and like a belt upon the loins,'" so Allah transformed them into apes. And as for the People of the Table, when they disbelieved, "'Isa (peace be upon him) said: (p-420) 'O Allah, punish whoever disbelieves after eating from the Table with a punishment You have not inflicted upon anyone among the worlds, and curse them as You cursed the people of the Sabbath, so they became swine.'"

This is the meaning of their being cursed upon the tongue of Dawud and 'Isa, the son of Maryam. There are other views concerning the verse besides this, which we have left aside, because they are not what we are concerned with here.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 89 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah will not impose blame upon you for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He will impose blame upon you for what you have intended in oaths⌋. We have already mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah that what is meant by "what you have intended in oaths" is that in which you intended to bind yourselves by an oath, not what passes over your tongues without intention, such as "No, by Allah" and "Yes, by Allah." From this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

[Al-Tawil]
You are not held to account for idle words you utter
when you did not intend the binding of resolutions.

This binding ('aqd) is figurative (ma'nawi). From this is the saying of al-Hutay'ah:

[Al-Basit]
A people who, when they bind a pact with their neighbour,
tie the knot (al-'inaj) and tie over it the strong cord (al-karaba).

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Shu'bah from 'Asim read ﴿'aqqadtum﴾ with light stress and without an alif (ʿaqadtum). Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn 'Amir read ﴿'aqqadtum﴾ with an alif in the pattern fa'ala (ʿāqadtum). The rest read it with the doubled letter and without an alif. Both the doubling and the mufa'alah form have the same meaning, the bare verb, as is shown by the reading ʿaqadtum without alif or doubling. The readings explain one another. The "mā" in His saying "bimā ʿaqqadtum" is, in verification, a verbal-masdar particle (maṣdariyyah), not a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), as some have claimed, supposing that the returning pronoun is omitted.

Regarding the meaning of "lagw" (idle or unintentional oath) in the verse, there are several opinions, the two most famous among the scholars being:

The first: that lagw is what passes over a person's tongue without intention, such as "No, by Allah" and "Yes, by Allah."

This view was held by al-Shafi'i, by 'A'ishah in one of the two narrations from her, and it is reported from Ibn 'Umar, from Ibn 'Abbas in one of his two opinions, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Ikrimah in one of his two opinions, from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, from Abu Salih, from al-Dahhak in one of his two opinions, from Abu Qilabah, and from al-Zuhri, as transmitted from them by Ibn Kathir and others.

The second opinion: that lagw is that a person swears to something he believes, but then it becomes evident that it is not so. This is the (p-421) view of Malik ibn Anas, who said it is the best that has been heard regarding the meaning of lagw. It is also narrated from 'A'ishah, Abu Hurayrah, Ibn 'Abbas in one of his two opinions, Sulayman ibn Yasar, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid in one of his two opinions, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i in one of his two opinions, al-Hasan, Zurarah ibn Awfa, Abu Malik, 'Ata' al-Khurasani, Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah, one of the two opinions of 'Ikrimah, Habib ibn Abi Thabit, al-Suddi, Makhul, Muqatil, Tawus, Qatadah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Yahya ibn Sa'id, and Rabi'ah, as transmitted from them by Ibn Kathir.

The two opinions are close in meaning, and lagw includes both: in the first, he did not intend to bind an oath at all; in the second, he intended only the truth and the right. I have omitted the other opinions because of their weakness in my view. Linguistically, lagw is speech with what has no benefit and no need for it. From this is the hadith: "If you say to your companion, while the imam is delivering the Friday sermon, 'Be silent,' you have engaged in idle talk (laghawta) or spoken frivolously (laghayta)."

And the saying of al-'Ajjaj:

[Al-Rajaz]
How many a host of pilgrims, restrained
from idle talk and obscene speech.

* *

Issues concerning the rulings on oaths

Know that oaths are of four kinds: two in which expiation is required without dispute, and two about which there is disagreement.

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir of this noble verse, and his words are: "Oaths in the Shari'ah are of four kinds: two kinds require expiation, and two kinds do not require expiation." al-Daraqutni recorded in his Sunan: 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz narrated to us, Khalaf ibn Hisham narrated to us, 'Abthar narrated to us from Layth, from Hammad, from Ibrahim, from 'Alqamah, from 'Abd Allah, who said: "Oaths are four: two oaths that are expiated and two oaths that are not expiated. The two oaths that are expiated: the man who swears, 'By Allah, I will not do such and such,' and then does it; and the man who says, 'By Allah, I will surely do such and such,' and then does not do it. The two oaths that are not expiated: the man who swears, 'By Allah, I did not do such and such,' when he did it; and the man who swears, 'By Allah, I did do such and such,' when he did not do it."

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Sufyan al-Thawri mentioned it in his Jami', and al-Marwazi also reported it from him. Sufyan said: "Oaths are four: two oaths that are expiated, namely a man saying, 'By Allah, I will not do,' and then he does; or saying, 'By Allah, I will surely do,' and then he does not. And two oaths that are not expiated, namely a man saying, 'By Allah, I did not do,' when he did; or saying, 'By Allah, I did,' when he did not."

Al-Marwazi said: As for the first two, there is no disagreement among the scholars about them, according to what Sufyan said. As for the latter two, the people of knowledge have differed about them. If the swearer swore that he had not done such and such, or that he had done such and such, believing himself truthful and thinking that what he swore was so, then there is no sin upon him and no expiation, according to Malik, Sufyan al-Thawri, and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y). Likewise Ahmad and Abu 'Ubayd said. Al-Shafi'i said: there is no sin upon him, but expiation is required.

Al-Marwazi said: al-Shafi'i's view on this is not strong. He said: If the swearer swore that he had not done such and such, when he had done it, deliberately lying, then he is sinful, and there is no expiation for him according to the general consensus of the scholars: Malik, Sufyan al-Thawri, the people of opinion, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abu Thawr, and Abu 'Ubayd.

Al-Shafi'i used to say: he must expiate. He said: It has been reported from some of the Followers the same view as al-Shafi'i's. Al-Marwazi said: I incline to the view of Malik and Ahmad. End of al-Qurtubi's words, quoted verbatim, which is the essence of the matter regarding a person's oath "I will surely do" or "I will not do."

As for swearing about the occurrence of a matter other than one's own action, or its non-occurrence, such as saying, "By Allah, such and such has come into existence," or "such and such has not come into existence": if he swears about a past matter that it has occurred, while he knows it has not, deliberately lying, then this is a perjurious oath (yamin ghamus). If he believes it occurred but it turns out not to be so, then it is of the idle oath (yamin al-lagw), as we have already mentioned. If he is in doubt, then it is like the perjurious oath, and some scholars counted it among the perjurious oaths.

If he swears about a future matter without knowing whether it will happen or not, it likewise falls under the perjurious oath. Most scholars hold that the perjurious oath is not expiated, because its sin is too great for an oath-expiation to cover it.

We have already mentioned al-Shafi'i's view that expiation applies to it. Among the Malikis there is a detailed position: expiation is obligatory in cases not connected to a past time.

Know also that oaths are further divided into an oath binding to do good (al-muntaqidah 'ala birr), and an oath binding to breach (al-muntaqidah 'ala hinth). The oath binding to good is the one whose swearer is not required to dissolve it, such as saying, "By Allah, I will not do such and such." The oath binding to breach is the one whose swearer must dissolve it by doing what he swore to, or by expiation, such as saying, "By Allah, I will surely do such and such." He is not judged to have breached an oath binding to breach until the possibility of doing what he swore to has passed, unless it is limited to a time, in which case he breaches it when that time passes. But if it is by divorce, such as saying regarding her divorce, "I will surely do such and such," then he is prevented from having intercourse with her until he does what he swore to, because he does not know whether he is keeping his oath or breaching it. It is not permissible to approach a doubtful private part according to a group of scholars, including Malik and his companions.

Some scholars said: he is not prevented from intercourse, because she is his wife and the divorce has not taken place by action. Among those who held this is Ahmad.

* *

Second issue: Know that an oath is not binding except by the names and attributes of Allah. It is not permissible to swear by a created being, because of his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever is swearing, let him swear by Allah, or let him keep silent." No oath is binding by a created being, whoever he may be, just as it is not permissible by the consensus of those among the people of knowledge whose opinion counts, and by the clear, authentic text prohibiting swearing by other than Allah. So the view of some people of knowledge that an oath is binding by him (ﷺ), on the ground that a person's Islam depends on belief in him, is manifestly false. And Allah knows best.

* *

Third issue: One is released from the obligation of an oath by one of three things:

The first: fulfilling it by doing what one swore to.

The second: expiation, which is permissible both before and after breaching, according to verification.

The third: the exception (istithna') by such words as "if Allah wills." Verification holds that it is a dissolution of the oath, not a substitute for expiation, as Ibn al-Majishun claimed. It requires the intention to pronounce it and its connection to the oath; a separation by anything other than a necessity, such as coughing or sneezing, is not accepted. This differs from the view of Ibn 'Abbas and others who permitted a delayed exception.

The verification of this is that what is meant is that the servant, when he says, "I will surely do such and such," must say, "if Allah wills," as He Himself stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," ﴿unless [adding], "If Allah wills."﴾ [al-Kahf: 23-24]. If he forgot the exception "if Allah wills" and remembered it, even after an interval, he should say "if Allah wills," so that he thereby escapes the liability of not having committed the matters to Allah and suspended them on His will, not because it dissolves an oath that has already passed and been binding.

(p-424) This is supported by His saying to Ayyub: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle and strike with it and do not breach [your oath]﴾ [Sad: 44]. Had it been possible to make up the exception afterwards, He would have told him to say "if Allah wills." It is also supported by the fact that, if this were so, the binding of an oath would not be known, since a later exception could always attach to it. And know that the exception with "if Allah wills" takes effect in oaths by Allah by consensus.

The scholars differed regarding other than that, such as oaths by divorce, zihar, and manumission, as when one says, "If you enter the house, then you are divorced, if Allah wills," or "You are to me like the back of my mother, if Allah wills," or "You are free, if Allah wills." Some scholars held that it has no effect in any of these, because these are not oaths but conditional statements of manumission, zihar, and divorce; the exception by will was only prescribed by the Shari'ah for oaths, not for conditional statements. This is the view of Malik and his companions, and al-Hasan, al-Awza'i, and Qatadah said so, and Ibn al-'Arabi and others preferred it.

A group of scholars held that it has effect in all of these, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah, Tawus, Hammad, and Abu Thawr, as Ibn Qudamah reported from them in al-Mughni. Some distinguished between zihar and manumission and divorce, because zihar carries expiation, so it is an oath that is dissolved by the exception, like an oath by Allah and a vow. Ibn Qudamah reported this in al-Mughni from Abu Musa, and he himself affirmed it.

* *

Fourth issue: If one does what one swore to abstain from, forgetfully, the scholars have three positions:

The first view: there is no oath-breaking (ḥinth) on him at all, because he is excused by forgetfulness. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And there is no blame on you for what you did in error﴾ (al-Aḥzāb 33:5). The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my ummah their error, their forgetfulness, and what they were forced to do." Although Imam Aḥmad and Ibn Abī Ḥātim criticized this ḥadīth as defective, scholars have accepted it from earlier and later times. It is supported by what is authentically recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim from Abū Hurayrah: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) recited ﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we forget or make errors﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:286), Allah said: 'Yes.'" And from the ḥadīth of Ibn ʿAbbās: Allah said: "I have done it." That one who acts forgetfully does not incur oath-breaking is the view of ʿAṭāʾ, ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, Ibn Abī Najīḥ, Isḥāq, and a narration from Aḥmad, as stated by the author of al-Mughnī. The basis of this view is clear from the evidences we have mentioned. However, some people held that he incurs oath-breaking in all cases. This is the well-known position of Mālik, and it was said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, al-Zuhrī, Qatādah, Rabīʿah, and Abū Ḥanīfah, and it is one of the two opinions of al-Shāfiʿī, as al-Mughnī's author reports from them [p. 425]. The basis of this view, according to its proponents, is that he did deliberately what he swore not to do. Since he intentionally did the act that caused the breach, he is not excused by forgetting the oath. Its weakness is not hidden.

Some scholars distinguished between divorce (ṭalāq) and manumission (ʿitq) on one side and other matters on the other. According to them, one is not excused by forgetfulness in divorce and manumission, but is excused in other matters. This is the apparent position of Imam Aḥmad, as al-Mughnī's author states. He said: al-Khallāl and his companion chose this view, and it is the view of Abū ʿUbayd.

The author of this commentary (may Allah pardon him) says: This last view has merit, because divorce and manumission involve both a right of Allah and a right of a human being. The one who swears may actually have acted deliberately while claiming forgetfulness, since intention is a hidden inner matter whose reality people cannot see. If forgetfulness were accepted as an excuse here, this could lead to the loss of human beings' rights. And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted.

* *

The fifth issue: If someone swears not to do a good act, such as reconciling between people or something similar, he is not permitted to refrain from it and hide behind the oath. Rather, he must expiate his oath and do what is better, because of the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle in your oaths to be righteous and fear Allah and make peace between people﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:224), meaning: do not let your oaths by Allah the Exalted prevent you from righteousness and maintaining family ties if you have sworn to abandon them. A parallel to this verse is the words of Allah the Exalted about the oath of Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) not to spend on Mistaḥ, because of what Mistaḥ said about ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her): ﴿And let not those of virtue and wealth among you swear not to give to the near of kin and the needy and the emigrants in the way of Allah. Let them pardon and overlook. Do you not like that Allah should forgive you? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (al-Nūr 24:22).

And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "By Allah, for one of you to persist in his oath concerning his family is more sinful for him before Allah than to give his expiation which Allah has made obligatory upon him." Agreed upon (Bukhārī and Muslim), from the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah.

And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "By Allah, if Allah wills, I never swear an oath and then see something else as better than it, except that I do what is better and expiate my oath." Also agreed upon, from the ḥadīth of Abū Mūsā.

And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Samurah: "ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Samurah, do not ask for leadership. For if you are given it without asking, you will be helped with it; and if you are given it upon asking, you will be left to handle it alone. And when you swear an oath and see something else as better than it, then do what is better and expiate your oath." Agreed upon as well. The ḥadīths on this subject are numerous.

This is the truth of the matter, contrary to those who said: its expiation is to abandon it, relying on ḥadīths reported on this topic. Abū Dāwūd said: All the ḥadīths from the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Let him expiate his oath," and these are the authentic ones. And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿the freeing of a neck﴾. Here He did not qualify the "neck" in the expiation of oaths with faith, whereas He did qualify it with faith in the expiation of killing by mistake.

This is one of the issues of the absolute (muṭlaq) and the qualified (muqayyad) in a situation where the ruling is the same but the cause differs. Many scholars hold that the absolute is to be interpreted in light of the qualified (ḥaml al-muṭlaq ʿalā al-muqayyad). Accordingly, the neck in oath-expiation and in ẓihār (the zihār formula) is qualified by the condition found in the neck for killing by mistake, applying the absolute to the qualified. Abū Ḥanīfah and those who agreed with him disagreed on this.

We have clarified this issue in our book Dafʿ Īhām al-Iḍṭirāb, in the chapter on Sūrat al-Nisāʾ at the verse: ﴿then the freeing of a believing neck﴾ (al-Nisāʾ 4:92). Therefore we have not extended the discussion here. The meaning of "taḥrīr" (freeing) is removal from slavery, though the Arabs sometimes use it for removal from captivity, hardships, the toil of this world, and similar things. Among its uses is the statement of Mary's mother: ﴿I have vowed to You what is in my womb, dedicated (muḥarraran)﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 3:35), meaning freed from the toil of worldly work. And among its uses is the verse of al-Farazdaq, Hammām ibn Ghālib al-Tamīmī:

Banū Ghudānah, indeed I have freed you,
so I have given you to ʿAṭiyyah ibn Jiʿāl.

He means: I have freed you from satire, so I will not satirize you.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 90:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe! Indeed, wine, gambling, stone altars, and divining arrows are only filth (rijs)...﴾ the verse.

It is understood from this noble verse that wine is najis (ritually impure) in its essence, because Allah, exalted is He, said that it is *rijs*, and *rijs* in the speech of the Arabs means everything loathsome that the soul recoils from.

It has also been said that its origin is from *al-raks*, which is dung and stench. Some scholars said: What supports this is the *mafhum al-mukhalafa* (the inferred meaning by contrast) in His saying, may He be exalted, concerning the drink of the people of Paradise: ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure (tahur) drink﴾ [al-Insan: 21]. For His describing the drink of the people of Paradise as *tahur* (pure) implies that the wine of this world is not like that. What confirms this is that all the attributes by which Allah, exalted is He, praised the wine of the Hereafter are negated of the wine of this world, such as His saying: ﴿neither will there be in it any intoxication (ghawl), nor will they be affected by it﴾ [al-Saffat: 47], and His saying: ﴿they will not be afflicted with headache from it, nor will they be intoxicated﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 19]. By contrast, the wine of this world has *ghawl* that seizes the minds, and its people are afflicted with headache (*yusadda'un*), meaning that the headache, which is pain of the head, befalls them because of it. As for His saying *la yunzafun* (they will not be intoxicated), according to the reading with a *fath* (fatha) on the *zay*, making it passive (*mabniyyan lil-maf'ul*), its meaning is that they will not become drunk. *Al-nazif* is the drunkard, and from it is the saying of Humayd ibn Thawr: [Tawil]

> A drunkard (nazif): you see the trace of the perfume (al-'abir) answering her,
> as the hunting dog stains the wounded game with its blood.

He means that she, in the heaviness of her movement, is like a drunkard, and that the redness of the *'abir* (perfume), which is the scent in her bosom, is like the redness of blood on the prey that the hunting beasts have stained with their blood, so that the bleeding from the wounds inflicted by the beasts has befallen it. From it also is the saying of Imru' al-Qays: [Mutaqarib]

> And when she walks like the walk of the nazif
> whom the panting of the sand-dune throws down.

And also his saying: [Tawil]

> A nazif, when she stands before a face, sways,
